A sovereign root of trust goes live

The National Agency for Information Systems Security of Côte d’Ivoire (ANSSI-CI) announced the commissioning of the national public key infrastructure on 23 July 2026 in Abidjan. The new PKI now sits at the top of the certification tree for all electronic certificates recognised internationally on Ivorian territory.

It becomes the trust foundation for every certification authority operating in the country. ANSSI-CI said the system guarantees authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation of electronic exchanges between the administration, businesses and citizens.

The agency described the launch as a structuring milestone in the National Cybersecurity Strategy and the 2026–2028 roadmap of the Ministry of Digital Transition and Digitalisation. ANSSI-CI is already recognised by the International Telecommunication Union and the International Organization for Standardization as the national registration authority for object identifiers, a technical prerequisite for running a sovereign PKI.

The legal architecture behind the digital-trust PKI

The PKI does not float in a legal vacuum. It rests on a stack of laws and decrees built over more than a decade, starting with Law No. 2013-546 of 30 July 2013 on electronic transactions, which gave legal value to electronic signatures meeting security and reliability requirements.

Decrees in 2014 and 2016 added rules on cryptology services, electronic signatures and electronic archiving. A parallel data-protection law from June 2013 created obligations enforced by the telecoms regulator ARTCI.

The most consequential recent change came with Ordinance No. 2024-950 of 30 October 2024, ratified unanimously by the National Assembly on 24 April 2025. It repealed the article that had given ARTCI responsibility for network security, audits and electronic certificate issuance, transferring all those powers to ANSSI-CI and consolidating cybersecurity and trust-service authority in a single specialised agency.

Where the PKI plugs into the digital economy

The national digital-trust PKI is not a standalone project. It is the cryptographic backbone for several flagship programmes that together aim to double the digital sector’s contribution to GDP by 2030, a target set by President Alassane Ouattara.

The Electronic Administration Support Project (PARAE), backed by a 49 billion CFA franc (about US$80 million) investment from the African Development Bank Group, explicitly couples a government Security Operations Centre with the PKI to ensure the reliability of digital transactions. The Public Administration Interoperability Platform, launched in October 2025 and built on Estonia’s X-Road model via Cybernetica’s Unified eXchange Platform, relies on the same trust layer to connect tax, civil-status, social-security and trade-court systems securely.

In the justice sector, the e-Justice platform went live in January 2025 in pilot jurisdictions. It uses a cryptographically signed Visible Digital Seal that citizens can verify worldwide through the AIGCEV/VDSIC global trust network, and since September 2025 only nationality certificates obtained online through e-Justice are accepted for national ID card applications.

Digital identity and the great-power contest over trust

Côte d’Ivoire is rolling out a foundational digital ID system, including the ECOWAS National Biometric ID Card, designed to be interoperable across services and payments. At the ID4Africa 2026 General Assembly in Abidjan, Interior Minister Vagondo Diomandé called digital identity a strategic infrastructure for reducing inequalities in access to finance, healthcare and social programmes.

The PKI is what makes such identity systems cryptographically secure and legally enforceable. ANSSI-CI’s Director General, Guelpétchin Moussa Ouattara, has compared PKI’s importance for digital identity to that of roads for an economy, an analogy that underscores why control over the trust layer is control over the country’s digital traffic.

The vendor landscape reveals a clear alignment with European technical ecosystems. Estonia’s Cybernetica supplies the interoperability platform, Entrust and Semlex handle biometric eID production with embedded PKI, and the Visible Digital Seal standard ties into a European-centric trust network. This configuration places Abidjan firmly inside Western-aligned digital-governance norms, even as Chinese firms dominate other layers of African telecoms infrastructure—a pattern explored in our pillar on Africa: The New Scramble.

Money, markets and the regional play

Beyond the AfDB’s US$80 million PARAE commitment, the government has projected a digital-strategy budget exceeding 1 trillion CFA francs (about US$1.8 billion) through 2030. World Bank diagnostics have flagged PKI deployment as essential for strengthening digital financial services, including the TreasorPay government-payment platform and customer identification for mobile money.

Regionally, the PKI positions Côte d’Ivoire as a digital hub in francophone West Africa. As a core member of ECOWAS and WAEMU, the country participates in harmonised frameworks for digital signatures and cross-border trust services. By moving relatively quickly on PKI, interoperability platforms and e-ID, Abidjan gains leverage in regional negotiations over mutual recognition of digital credentials and transactions.

Risks, exposure and what to watch next

Côte d’Ivoire remains one of the African countries most exposed to cyber threats, according to analysts tracking its AI-driven digital transformation. The national security operations centre and PKI were still under development while the broader digitisation push accelerated, creating a gap between ambition and defensive maturity.

From a governance perspective, the concentration of cyber and trust-service powers in ANSSI-CI raises familiar questions about oversight. The UN Economic Commission for Africa has warned that digital ID systems must address risks of surveillance and discrimination, and while Côte d’Ivoire’s legal framework includes data-protection safeguards, the PKI also gives the state powerful capabilities to authenticate, track and potentially control access to digital services.

The next milestones to watch are the full integration of the PKI with the interoperability platform, the expansion of e-Justice beyond pilot jurisdictions and the rollout of the biometric eID card with embedded cryptographic credentials. Each step will test whether the sovereign trust layer delivers the secure, inclusive digital economy that Abidjan has promised.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a national digital-trust PKI and why does it matter?

A public key infrastructure is the technical system that creates, manages and revokes digital certificates used for authentication, encryption and digital signatures. A national PKI places the state at the top of the certificate hierarchy, meaning the government controls the root of trust for all electronic transactions, identity verification and e-government services within its borders, rather than relying on foreign commercial certificate authorities.

How does the Ivorian PKI connect to digital identity and e-government?

The PKI provides the cryptographic backbone for the national digital ID system, the e-Justice platform and the public administration interoperability layer. It enables secure online authentication, legally binding electronic signatures and encrypted data exchange between government agencies, businesses and citizens, making services such as online nationality certificates and biometric ID cards cryptographically verifiable.

Who is funding and supplying Côte d’Ivoire’s digital-trust infrastructure?

The African Development Bank is the lead development-finance partner, committing 49 billion CFA francs (about US$80 million) to the PARAE project that couples the PKI with a government security operations centre. Technology vendors include Estonia’s Cybernetica for the interoperability platform, and Entrust and Semlex for biometric eID production with embedded PKI, reflecting a predominantly European and North American supplier base.

World.title: Angola Convicts Two Russians in Spy Trial, Exposing Information Warfare
World.content:
Africa · Southern

Key Facts —Verdict. Igor Ratchin and Lev Lakshtanov were convicted on 21 July 2026 in Luanda. —Sentences. Ratchin received 11 years; Lakshtanov received 8 years for terrorism and espionage. —Alleged network. Prosecutors linked the men to “Africa Politology,” a group with Wagner-era roots. —Payments. Over $24,000 was allegedly paid to local journalists to spread disinformation. —Target. The operation aimed to influence Angola’s 2027 presidential election and destabilise the state.

A Luanda court has convicted two Russian nationals for terrorism and espionage, pulling back the curtain on a new phase of Russia-Africa information warfare that targets elections, media, and strategic minerals.

Angola Spy Trial Exposes New Phase of Russia-Africa Information Warfare (Photo internet reproduction)

The Verdict in Luanda

On 21 July 2026, an Angolan court sentenced Igor Ratchin to 11 years in prison and Lev Lakshtanov to 8 years. The two Russian men faced 11 charges, including terrorism, espionage, and influence peddling.

They were arrested in August 2025 and their trial opened on 24 March 2026. Prosecutors alleged the pair paid local journalists and experts over $24,000 to spread propaganda designed to incite unrest.

The case marks one of the most explicit legal confrontations with alleged Russian information operations on the African continent. It signals that Angola is willing to draw a hard line against foreign interference.

The Alleged Network: Africa Politology

Prosecutors connected the defendants to a group called “Africa Politology.” Investigators describe it as a Russian influence network that emerged from the Wagner ecosystem after Yevgeny Prigozhin’s death in 2023.

Some reporting suggests the network was later absorbed into structures linked to Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service. Those claims remain attributed to investigators and have not been independently verified by court documents.

What is clear is the method: low-cost payments to local intermediaries, online narratives, and an attempt to shape political conditions without overt military action. It is a playbook that mirrors Russia-Africa information warfare tactics seen elsewhere on the continent, as detailed in our pillar Africa: The New Scramble.

Angola’s Strategic Pivot

The trial unfolds against a backdrop of profound realignment. President João Lourenço, in power since 2017, has steered Angola closer to the United States and Western partners.

That shift reduces a decades-long dependency on Moscow’s orbit. French and German diplomatic sources frame the verdict as a message that Luanda will no longer tolerate the kind of influence operations it once quietly accepted.

The timing is sensitive. Angola’s next presidential election is scheduled for 2027, and any credible allegation of external interference immediately raises the political temperature in a competitive pre-election environment.

The Lobito Corridor and the Minerals Angle

Several reports connect the alleged influence operation to efforts to undermine the Lobito Corridor. This rail and logistics project links the copper and cobalt belts of Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo to Angola’s Atlantic coast.

The corridor is a flagship American geoeconomic project in Africa. It is central to exporting minerals essential for the global energy transition, and Washington has invested significant political capital in its success.

If Moscow-linked actors wanted to slow Angola’s Western integration, disrupting confidence in such projects would be a logical target. Prosecutors’ claims in this area remain allegations, but the strategic logic is unmistakable.

A Transactional, Not Ideological, Play

Prosecutors reportedly said the defendants explored influencing both the ruling MPLA and the opposition UNITA. That suggests the aim was not ideological but transactional.

The goal appeared to be retaining access and leverage regardless of who wins the 2027 election. For a relatively small sum, the alleged operation sought high-value political and economic outcomes.

This pattern fits a broader Russian strategy in Africa. It combines security partnerships, disinformation, private military networks, and resource diplomacy to build influence while working around Western sanctions imposed after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

What Brazil and Latin America Should Watch

For readers in Brazil and across Latin America, the Angola case offers a preview of how great-power competition is evolving in the Global South. Information warfare is cheap, deniable, and easily exported.

Both regions sit on critical minerals, both face pre-election sensitivity, and both are arenas where Moscow, Washington, and Beijing compete for access. The Angola trial shows one government’s decision to criminalise the playbook rather than ignore it.

The BRICS dimension adds another layer. Angola is not a BRICS member, but its realignment away from Moscow complicates Russia’s narrative of a rising anti-Western bloc in the developing world.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who were the two Russians convicted in Angola?

Igor Ratchin and Lev Lakshtanov were convicted on 21 July 2026 in Luanda. They received sentences of 11 years and 8 years respectively for terrorism, espionage, and influence peddling. Prosecutors alleged they were part of a Russia-linked disinformation network called Africa Politology.

What is the Lobito Corridor and why does it matter in this case?

The Lobito Corridor is a rail and logistics project connecting the mineral-rich regions of Zambia and the DRC to Angola’s Atlantic coast. It is backed by the United States as a flagship geoeconomic initiative. Several reports allege the influence operation sought to undermine confidence in the corridor to slow Angola’s Western integration.

How does this trial fit into the wider Russia-Africa pattern?

The case reflects a broader Russian strategy that mixes security partnerships, disinformation, private military networks, and resource diplomacy. The alleged network, Africa Politology, is said to have emerged from the Wagner ecosystem after Prigozhin’s death. The trial shows one African government choosing to criminalise that playbook rather than accommodate it.

World.title: Ghana Vindicated as South Africa Confirms Identity of Slain Citizen
World.content:
Africa · Western

Key Facts —The victim. Bashiru Isak, a 40-year-old Ghanaian tailor and father of three, had lived in South Africa for roughly 20 years. —The killing. Ghana says he was fatally shot on 30 June 2026 in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, during anti-immigrant demonstrations. —The dispute. South African police initially identified the dead man as Kwabena Bwagin, killed a day earlier in a different suburb in an extortion incident. —The confirmation. On 27 July 2026, South African authorities formally accepted that the deceased is indeed Bashiru Isak. —The wider stakes. The row has delayed a presidential visit, reached the African Union, and exposed tensions over migration and continental leadership.

Ghana has been vindicated after South Africa formally confirmed that the Ghanaian shot dead in Cape Town is Bashiru Isak, ending a weeks-long factual dispute that had spiralled into a full-blown diplomatic crisis between two of Africa’s leading economies.

Ghana Vindicated as South Africa Confirms Identity of Slain Citizen (Photo internet reproduction)

A death, a name, and two competing narratives

Ghana’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs first went public on 1 July 2026, condemning the killing of a Ghanaian national in South Africa. The ministry identified the deceased as Bashiru Isak, a 40-year-old tailor and father of three who had lived in the country for roughly two decades.

Accra stated that Isak was “fatally shot in Khayelitsha, Cape Town, on Monday, June 30, during anti-immigrant demonstrations linked to ongoing xenophobic attacks.” South African authorities immediately pushed back with a different story.

The South African Police Service told media that the victim was a 35-year-old Ghanaian named Kwabena Bwagin, killed on 29 June in Nyanga, not Khayelitsha. Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi insisted that “no fatalities have been recorded during the day of these demonstrations” and described the killing as extortion-related.

Ghana vindicated as Pretoria accepts the facts

The factual turning point came on 27 July 2026, when Ghana’s Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced that South African authorities had confirmed the deceased is indeed Bashiru Isak. “The name that was provided by the South African authorities, being Kwabena Bwagin, which really is not a Ghanaian name; nobody is called Bwagin in Ghana, they clearly got it wrong,” Ablakwa said.

He declared that Ghana had been vindicated and had “at no time engaged in misinformation and disinformation.” The identity of Mr Isak, he added, had now been confirmed “beyond any scintilla of doubt.”

Isak’s remains had already been repatriated, arriving in Accra on 14 July 2026 at 6:40 pm. Ghana’s Foreign Ministry used the moment to state that “this irrefutable fact is contrary to false claims initially made by some South African officials.”

A diplomatic crisis that reached the African Union

The identity dispute did not unfold in a vacuum. Ghana had already summoned South Africa’s acting High Commissioner on 23 April 2026 over viral videos showing Ghanaian nationals being harassed in KwaZulu-Natal and told to “fix your country.”

Once the killing became public, Accra escalated sharply. Ghana turned down a requested state visit by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, explicitly citing xenophobic attacks on Ghanaians and the death of a national.

Accra also took the matter to ECOWAS and requested discussion at the African Union. South Africa’s presidential spokesperson Vincent Magwenya responded by accusing Ghana of leading a “false” campaign to portray South Africa as increasingly isolated and xenophobic.

What remains contested after the identity confirmation

Even with the name settled, significant disagreements persist. Ghana continues to link Isak’s killing to xenophobic tensions and anti-immigrant demonstrations.

South African officials still contend there is no credible evidence connecting the killing to the protests and maintain it appears extortion-related. Pretoria also insists that no one died during the demonstrations themselves.

At the time of writing, Ghana was still awaiting the full autopsy report and SAPS case file. The forensic and prosecutorial record remains incomplete.

Trade, migration, and the contest for continental influence

The row carries real economic weight. Ghana and South Africa have one of the strongest bilateral trade relationships in Africa, with South African firms deeply invested in West African mining, telecoms, and financial services.

Diplomatic rifts of this kind threaten investor confidence and complicate African Continental Free Trade Area ambitions. As one Ghanaian analyst noted, the spat “has dire implications for continental trade and integration efforts.”

Beneath the surface lies a subtle power struggle. South Africa sees itself as the continent’s heavyweight and resents efforts by Ghana and Nigeria to turn its domestic migration politics into a pan-African debate. Ghana, home to major Pan-African institutions, is leveraging moral authority to position itself as a norm-setter on migrant rights. This dynamic fits squarely within the broader patterns explored in Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch next

The autopsy report and SAPS investigation will determine whether the killing was a targeted crime or connected to the broader anti-migrant unrest. That finding will shape the next phase of the diplomatic conversation.

The AU and ECOWAS discussions Ghana has requested will test whether African multilateral bodies can mediate such disputes effectively. For investors, the episode is a reminder that social unrest over migration in South Africa carries a direct risk premium for intra-African trade and labour mobility.

Connected Coverage Africa: The New Scramble

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was the Ghanaian killed in South Africa?

The victim was Bashiru Isak, a 40-year-old tailor and father of three who had lived in South Africa for roughly 20 years. South African authorities initially identified him as Kwabena Bwagin before formally confirming his true identity on 27 July 2026.

Why did Ghana and South Africa disagree over the killing?

The two governments differed on the victim’s name, the date and location of the shooting, and the motive. Ghana said Isak was killed on 30 June in Khayelitsha during anti-immigrant protests.

South African police said a man named Kwabena Bwagin was killed on 29 June in Nyanga in an extortion-related incident.

What does this dispute mean for African trade and diplomacy?

The row has delayed a presidential visit, reached the African Union, and exposed tensions over migration and continental leadership. It threatens investor confidence in two of Africa’s largest economies and complicates efforts to advance free movement and trade under the African Continental Free Trade Area.

World.title: Yara Ghana’s New Fertilizers Boost Smallholder Crop Yields
World.content:
Africa · Western

Key Facts —Products. Yara Winner Plus targets rice and cereals; Yara Legume targets soybeans, cowpeas and groundnuts. —Location. The launch took place in Walewale, North East Region, a key smallholder farming zone. —Infrastructure. Yara has invested over US$15 million in a blending terminal at Tema port with 50,000-tonne storage. —Geopolitics. The Grow Ghana initiative distributed 18,000 tonnes of free Yara fertiliser after the Russia-Ukraine war. —Yield data. Field trials show Yara protocols can lift maize yields by roughly 38 percent versus blanket NPK.

Yara Ghana fertilisers are moving the country’s smallholder farmers away from generic NPK blends and toward crop-specific nutrition, a shift that promises higher yields but also deepens a Nordic multinational’s footprint in West African food systems.

Yara Ghana introduces two crop-specific fertiliser solutions to improve farmers’ yields (Photo internet reproduction)

Two new blends, one clear strategy

In July 2026, Yara Ghana Limited gathered farmers and retailers in Walewale, a commercial hub in the North East Region, to unveil Yara Winner Plus and Yara Legume. The event was part product demonstration, part market activation, with discounted prices offered to seed adoption.

Winner Plus carries an NPK ratio of 15-9-20, fortified with magnesium, sulphur, calcium and zinc. It is optimised for rice and other cereals. Legume, formulated at 4-18-13 with added boron, targets soybeans, cowpeas and groundnuts, aiming to improve flowering, pod set and nitrogen fixation.

Why Yara Ghana fertilisers matter for smallholder economics

Ghanaian agriculture is dominated by smallholders who typically apply blanket NPK fertilisers with mixed results. Yara’s model replaces that one-size-fits-all approach with blends mapped to specific crops and local soil deficiencies.

Independent field trials in the Ashanti Region found that Yara protocols produced an average maize yield of 5,875 kg per hectare, compared with 4,241 kg under the national blanket recommendation. Five of seven Yara treatments delivered value-to-cost ratios above two, meaning farmers more than doubled their money.

The Tema terminal and the infrastructure of influence

Behind the Walewale launch stands a physical asset that few competitors can match. Yara International ASA has poured more than US$15 million into a fertiliser terminal and blending facility at Tema, Ghana’s main port.

The site stores over 50,000 tonnes and blends more than 100 tonnes per hour. It allows Yara to import bulk ingredients, mix Ghana-specific formulas and bag them under its own brands, controlling the supply chain from ship to smallholder.

Grow Ghana and the fertiliser-as-geopolitics lens

When Russia’s invasion of Ukraine disrupted global fertiliser supply, Ghana’s food system faced a shock. Yara responded with Grow Ghana, a US$20 million emergency initiative backed by USAID, AGRA and the African Fertiliser and Agribusiness Partnership.

The programme distributed 18,000 metric tonnes of YaraMila Actyva fertiliser free of charge, reaching over 111,000 smallholders. It helped produce more than 500,000 tonnes of cereals while cementing Yara’s reputation as an indispensable partner for Ghanaian food security.

The dependency question behind Yara Ghana fertilisers

Yield gains come with a structural trade-off. Farmers who adopt Yara’s branded blends and agronomic protocols may find it difficult to switch back to generic inputs, especially when donor-subsidised programmes build familiarity and trust.

This dynamic fits a broader pattern across Africa, where Western agribusiness and development finance shape input markets. As explored in Africa: The New Scramble, fertiliser has become a strategic asset in the contest for influence between Western, Russian and Chinese supply chains.

What to watch next

Yara’s Ghana portfolio now spans maize, rice, cocoa, oil palm and legumes. Each crop-specific blend reinforces the company’s position as a premium agronomy partner rather than a commodity supplier.

The next test is whether Ghana’s government uses the Planting for Food and Jobs programme to diversify input sources or deepens its reliance on imported, branded fertiliser. For investors and policymakers watching West African agriculture, Walewale is a signal worth reading.

Frequently Asked Questions

What crops do Yara Winner Plus and Yara Legume target?

Yara Winner Plus is designed for rice and other fruiting cereals, with an NPK ratio of 15-9-20 plus micronutrients. Yara Legume targets soybeans, cowpeas and groundnuts with a 4-18-13 formula that includes boron for flowering and pod development.

How much did Yara invest in its Ghana fertiliser terminal?

Yara International ASA invested over US$15 million in a blending and storage terminal at Tema port. The facility holds more than 50,000 tonnes and can blend over 100 tonnes of fertiliser per hour.

What was the Grow Ghana fertiliser initiative?

Grow Ghana was a US$20 million emergency programme launched after the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted fertiliser supply. It distributed 18,000 metric tonnes of YaraMila Actyva free of charge to over 111,000 smallholder farmers, supporting cereal production of more than 500,000 tonnes.

World.title: Rulay Fusion Video: Dominican-Colombian Salsa Collab in Cali
World.content:
Music & Culture

Key Facts —The track. “Rulay” is a 2026 single merging Dominican salsa with Colombian salsa choke. —The artists. Menteabierta represents Dominican tropical sound; Cali Flow Latino brings Pacific Colombian rhythms. —The video location. Filmed in Siloé, a culturally significant hillside neighbourhood in Cali, Colombia. —The concept. The production integrates local residents and dancers, avoiding commercial-clip conventions. —The album. The single appears on Cali Flow Latino’s project “Colombia en el Beat.”

The Rulay fusion video brings together Dominican salsa group Menteabierta and Colombian salsa choke pioneers Cali Flow Latino in a cross-border collaboration that signals growing commercial appetite for experimental tropical music across Latin America.

A new Dominican-Colombian single, ‘Rulay,’ drops. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What “Rulay” Represents for Tropical Music

“Rulay” is not a standard salsa track. It deliberately fuses two distinct rhythmic traditions: the classic Dominican salsa sound carried by Menteabierta and the faster, street-born salsa choke style that Cali Flow Latino has championed since forming in Cali in 2000.

The result is a danceable, experimental piece built on Dominican melodic structures and Pacific Colombian cadences. The title itself draws from Caribbean urban slang for having a good time, being relaxed, or moving in a state of enjoyment.

The collaboration lands inside Cali Flow Latino’s broader album “Colombia en el Beat,” a project positioning Colombian urban and tropical sounds for international audiences. For Menteabierta, it marks a strategic step into the Colombian market, where salsa consumption remains among the highest in the region.

Why the Video Was Shot in Siloé

The production team chose Siloé, a hillside neighbourhood in western Cali, as the visual anchor for the Rulay fusion video. The choice is deliberate and carries cultural weight: Siloé is one of the city’s most historically complex barrios, known for community resilience and deep salsa roots.

Rather than building a polished studio set, the video integrates residents and local dancers directly into the frame. The camera follows movement through streets and communal spaces, capturing what the producers describe as the essence of salsa in its natural community context.

This approach departs from the glossy aesthetic common in Latin urban music videos. It reflects a growing trend among tropical artists to ground visual storytelling in real places, betting that authenticity resonates more with streaming audiences than high-budget artifice.

The Business Logic Behind Cross-Border Salsa Collaborations

Cross-border tropical collaborations make commercial sense in 2026. Streaming data consistently shows salsa and its variants holding strong listener bases in Colombia, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, and diaspora communities in the United States and Europe.

By pairing a Dominican act with a Colombian group, “Rulay” opens playlist access in two distinct national markets simultaneously. For Cali Flow Latino, the track reinforces their standing as international ambassadors of salsa choke, a genre that emerged from Cali’s Pacific-influenced barrios and has steadily gained streaming traction outside Colombia.

For Menteabierta, the collaboration provides entry into Colombia’s live-music circuit, where salsa festivals and club dates in Cali, Bogotá, and Medellín generate consistent touring revenue. The single’s digital release across Amazon Music and Apple Music positions it for algorithmic discovery on tropical and Latin dance playlists.

Cali’s Enduring Role as a Salsa Capital

Cali’s identity as a global salsa hub is not new, but it continues to generate economic and cultural returns. The city hosts major annual events including the Feria de Cali and the World Salsa Festival, which draw international visitors and sustain a local ecosystem of dance schools, musicians, and recording studios.

Salsa choke, the specific variant Cali Flow Latino represents, evolved from this environment. It incorporates faster beats, Afro-Pacific percussion patterns, and a street-dance vocabulary distinct from the classic salsa dura associated with New York or Puerto Rico.

The “Rulay” video’s Siloé setting reinforces Cali’s claim as a living salsa city rather than a museum piece. For investors watching Latin America’s creative economy, the city’s music sector offers a replicable model of how local genre innovation can generate exportable cultural product.

What Expats and Visitors Should Know About Siloé

Siloé carries a complicated reputation. For decades it was associated with violence and limited state presence, but community-led cultural initiatives have reshaped parts of the neighbourhood’s image, particularly through music and dance projects.

The area has produced notable salsa dancers and musicians, and community tourism efforts now offer guided visits focused on its musical heritage. Foreign residents in Cali should approach Siloé with the same situational awareness they would apply in any hillside barrio, but the neighbourhood’s cultural output is genuine and increasingly recognised.

The “Rulay” video adds another layer to Siloé’s cultural resume, documenting the barrio not as a backdrop but as a participant in the creative process.

What to Watch Next

The release of “Rulay” and its video sets up several threads worth following. First, streaming performance data over the next quarter will indicate whether the Dominican-Colombian fusion connects with playlists and listener algorithms beyond the artists’ existing fan bases.

Second, Cali Flow Latino’s “Colombia en el Beat” album rollout will reveal whether the group can sustain momentum across a full project. Third, Menteabierta’s next moves in the Colombian market will signal how seriously Dominican tropical acts are pursuing cross-border expansion.

For the broader Latin music industry, “Rulay” tests a proposition: that tropical fusion, rooted in specific neighbourhoods and traditions, can compete for streaming attention in a landscape dominated by reggaeton and Mexican regional. The answer will arrive in the numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does “rulay” mean in the song?

In Caribbean and urban Spanish slang, “rulay” refers to having a good time, being relaxed, or moving in a state of enjoyment and euphoria. The song uses the term to capture the carefree, danceable energy of the Dominican-Colombian fusion.

Who are Cali Flow Latino and Menteabierta?

Cali Flow Latino is a Colombian group formed in Cali in 2000, known as key exponents of salsa choke and Pacific Colombian rhythms. Menteabierta is a Dominican act that brings classic salsa and urban tropical sounds to the collaboration.

Where was the “Rulay” video filmed and why does it matter?

The video was shot in Siloé, a hillside neighbourhood in Cali, Colombia, with deep cultural and historical significance. The production integrated local residents and dancers rather than using professional sets, aiming to capture authentic community salsa culture.

World.title: Buenos Aires This Week: Free Art, Fairs & Tango
World.content:
City Guide

Key Facts —Live Agendas. Time Out Buenos Aires and BuenosAiresConnect refresh their event listings every few days with current exhibitions, concerts, and ferias. —Museums Any Week. Malba, MACBA, and Bellas Artes offer world-class art collections with guided visits and new exhibitions throughout the year. —Sunday Classic. The San Telmo street fair runs every Sunday with antiques, crafts, street musicians, and tango bars open all afternoon. —Free Culture. Centro Cultural Recoleta hosts free open-air concerts every Sunday at 6 p.m., spanning rock, jazz, folk, and classical music. —Green Spaces. The Rosedal de Palermo, Reserva Ecológica Costanera Sur, and Parque Centenario offer walking paths, picnics, and cycling routes year-round.

Buenos Aires this week rewards visitors with a dense cultural calendar, from museum exhibitions and open-air concerts to design ferias and gastronomic markets that repeat reliably every weekend.

Buenos Aires offers a full week of events. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)
