How to Find What Is On in Buenos Aires This Week

The most reliable way to plan your days is to consult two live agendas that update every few days. Time Out Buenos Aires publishes a “Qué hacer esta semana” guide alongside a weekend-specific edition.

BuenosAiresConnect offers a day-by-day breakdown of events, from Tuesday cinema cycles to Sunday ferias. Cross-check both with QueHacemos Buenos Aires for a broader list of concerts, theatre, and nightlife.

For a foreign visitor, this habit of checking live, locally maintained agendas is essential because Buenos Aires cultural programming is famously fluid. Venues often confirm details only a few days ahead, and printed guides can be out of date before they reach your hands. The three platforms mentioned above are free to access and cover everything from major institutional shows to neighbourhood pop-ups that never appear in formal tourist brochures.

Museums and Cultural Centres Worth Your Time

Malba, MACBA, and the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes anchor the city’s art scene with permanent collections and rotating exhibitions. Time Out and BairesSecreta frequently highlight guided visits and new openings at these institutions.

Centro Cultural Recoleta remains a standout for free programming, including open-air concerts every Sunday at 6 p.m. The CCK, Usina del Arte, and Centro Cultural 25 de Mayo also offer free music, theatre, and family activities most weekends.

What makes these cultural centres particularly valuable for a week-long stay is their concentration in walkable neighbourhoods. A visitor can reasonably visit the Recoleta complex in the morning and still reach the CCK in the afternoon without relying on taxis, which also makes it easier to adapt plans if a particular exhibition turns out to be closed or fully booked.

Theatre, Cinema, and Live Music in Buenos Aires This Week

Avenida Corrientes, the city’s theatre district, runs dozens of plays from Friday to Sunday, with matinée shows for children on weekends. Independent theatre venues such as Nün, Regio, and the Teatro San Martín offer smaller productions throughout the week.

For live music, the Palermo circuit — Niceto, La Trastienda, and C Art Media — programmes rock, indie, and electronic acts on Friday and Saturday nights. Larger shows at Movistar Arena and Luna Park are announced on venue social media and ticketing platforms.

Theatre on Avenida Corrientes has a particular rhythm worth understanding: many productions are in Spanish without subtitles, but the visual and musical spectacle often transcends language barriers. Independent venues in neighbourhoods like Villa Crespo and Almagro tend to programme more experimental work, and tickets are typically available at the door for a fraction of the price of a big Corrientes production.

Ferias, Markets, and Gastronomic Outings

The San Telmo street fair is the quintessential Sunday plan, stretching along Defensa Street with antiques, crafts, and street performers. Combine it with a coffee or a tango bar visit in the surrounding cobblestone streets.

On Saturdays, design ferias and organic markets such as Sabe la Tierra set up in plazas across the city, including Aristóbulo del Valle, Irlanda, and Las Heras. Gastronomic patios like Bonpland, Belgrano, and Costanera Norte offer street-food options ideal for a casual lunch.

These markets serve a dual purpose for the visitor: they are a place to eat, but they are also a window into how porteños — as Buenos Aires residents are known — spend their leisure time. The organic and design fairs rotate among different plazas, so checking the specific location on a live agenda before heading out is always wise.

Outdoor Plans for Any Weekend

The Rosedal de Palermo and the Reserva Ecológica Costanera Sur provide green escapes within the city limits. The ecological reserve occasionally hosts guided visits, talks, and workshops on Saturdays.

The Planetario Galileo Galilei runs family-friendly shows on weekends, including “Top 5: lo mejor del universo,” and organises open-air cinema and astronomy activities. Parque Centenario’s amphitheatre also schedules live music on select weekends.

The Reserva Ecológica is particularly notable because it sits right on the Río de la Plata, offering a waterfront perspective of the city that contrasts sharply with the dense urban neighbourhoods just a few blocks away. Its flat, well-marked trails make it accessible even for visitors who are not regular hikers, and the birdwatching opportunities along the lagoons can be a quiet counterpoint to a busy cultural itinerary.

How to Structure Your Days

On weekdays, pair a museum visit with a café stop in Palermo or Recoleta, then catch independent theatre or an auteur film at Sala Lugones. The CCK and Usina del Arte also run free evening concerts and film cycles from Tuesday to Thursday.

Saturday works well for a morning park walk, a midday gastronomic market, and an evening theatre show or concert. Sunday is ideal for the San Telmo fair in the morning, followed by the free 6 p.m. concert at Centro Cultural Recoleta or a family session at the Planetarium.

This rhythm mirrors how locals themselves approach the week: cultural consumption in Buenos Aires is rarely rushed, and the best experiences often come from leaving space between planned stops. A visitor who tries to cram three museums and a concert into a single day may find the distances and late-starting evening events work against them. Building the day around one anchor activity — a morning fair, an afternoon museum, or an evening show — and letting the neighbourhood fill in the rest tends to yield a more satisfying visit.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best way to find current events in Buenos Aires this week?

Check Time Out Buenos Aires and BuenosAiresConnect, both of which refresh their listings every few days with exhibitions, concerts, ferias, and theatre. Cross-reference with QueHacemos Buenos Aires for a broader selection of nightlife and cultural events.

Are there free cultural activities in Buenos Aires on weekends?

Yes, Centro Cultural Recoleta offers free open-air concerts every Sunday at 6 p.m., and the CCK, Usina del Arte, and Centro Cultural 25 de Mayo host free music, theatre, and film cycles most weekends. The San Telmo street fair is also free to wander.

Which parks are best for an outdoor afternoon in Buenos Aires?

The Rosedal de Palermo, Reserva Ecológica Costanera Sur, and Parque Centenario are the top choices for walking, picnics, and cycling. The ecological reserve occasionally adds guided visits and workshops on Saturdays.

World.title: Researchers in Costa Rica Document a Remora Clinging to a Nesting Turtle
World.content:
On a dark night last September on the Osa Peninsula, a female olive ridley sea turtle dragged herself out of the Pacific to nest at Playa Pejeperro carrying a passenger that should not have been able to survive the trip.

Research assistants with Comunidad Protectora de Tortugas de Osa (COPROT)met the turtle at 10:29 p.m. on September 24, 2025, moments after she cleared the surf. Clamped to the left side of her shell was a large common remora, the suckerfish that spends most of its life stuck to sharks, rays, whales and turtles.

The patrol watched the pair for 19 minutes. The fish stayed almost motionless, working its gill covers open and shut, and only shifted position on the shell when a researcher moved in to detach it. Lifted free and carried back to the water, the remora writhed, then swam off. It had been out of the sea for the better part of a third of an hour and was still alive. The turtle appeared entirely untroubled by any of it. She went about the standard business of digging a body pit and began laying eggs at 10:48 p.m.

The observation has now been published as a brief research report in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science by Megan J. Bullock of the University of West Florida and COPROT, Vicente Peña Eisele of COPROT, and Emily A. Yeager of the University of Miami, who is the corresponding author. The paper appeared on June 8 and drew wider attention this month after the journal featured the night photograph in a monthly roundup of images from its research.

The turtle measured an average of 68.4 centimeters (26.9 inches) along the curve of her shell and 72.6 centimeters (28.6 inches) across it. Using those figures as a known scale, the team estimated the remora at roughly 28 centimeters (11 inches) from photographs taken later. Because the entire encounter was observed under red light, which is used on nesting beaches to avoid disorienting turtles, no reliable note could be made of the fish’s color.

Remoras attach with a modified dorsal fin that works as an adhesive disc, and the arrangement saves them the energy of swimming while putting them close to a host’s meals. Whether the relationship benefits both animals, only the fish, or actively costs the host is still argued over in the scientific literature.

What is not in dispute is that a remora out of water cannot breathe, and following a turtle onto a beach can kill it. That has happened in the handful of previous cases on record, which involved nesting leatherbacks in French Guiana in the late 1970s and olive ridleys in Mexico. The Costa Rican observation adds a Central American record to a list that already spanned North and South America, which suggests the behavior may be far more widespread across turtle populations than the thin documentation implies.

The authors read the risk-taking as a clue about how tightly these fish bind themselves to particular hosts. Recent work has tracked individual remoras staying with one animal for extraordinary stretches, including a sharksucker that remained with the same parrotfish for 238 days while much larger potential hosts swam past.

Other studies have followed remoras riding manta rays and sharks into deep water once thought physiologically off limits to them. Taken together, the researchers argue, the picture is less of a fish that opportunistically grabs whatever passes and more of one that will not risk losing the specific animal it has chosen, even when staying attached is dangerous.

Playa Pejeperro sits inside the Río Oro National Wildlife Refuge on the Pacific side of the Osa Peninsula, on a stretch of largely undeveloped coastline that COPROT patrols nightly from June through April. The study reports about 7,000 olive ridley nests and 600 green turtle nests laid at the beach in 2024, making it one of the most important nesting sites on the country’s Pacific coast. COPROT was founded in 2018 and describes its model as training and paying local residents, including people who had been working in the area’s illegal gold mining, to run the monitoring and hatchery work.

The record itself came out of nothing more elaborate than that routine. A crew walking sand in the dark with a red light, writing down carapace measurements, noticed something on a shell that did not belong there and logged it. Much of what is known about the ordinary traffic of the ocean has been assembled the same way, one incidental line in a field notebook at a time.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Widen Extradition of Its Own Citizens
World.content:
President Laura Fernández asked lawmakers on Monday to widen the narrow list of crimes for which Costa Rica may hand its own citizens over to foreign courts, proposing a constitutional amendment that would add money laundering, human trafficking, arms trafficking, contract killing and cybercrime to the two grounds that exist today.

The president arrived at the Legislative Assembly mid-morning accompanied by her cabinet, police directors and members of the unit the government calls Fuerza Élite, and delivered a second package of six security bills. The extradition proposal was the centerpiece of her presentation but was not among the files formally handed over, because legislative procedure does not allow constitutional reforms to be processed during extraordinary sessions. The government said it will file that text on Monday, August 3.

Costa Rica has permitted the extradition of its nationals only since 2025, and only for international drug trafficking and terrorism. Fernández wants to add seven further categories: money laundering; human trafficking and migrant smuggling; illegal arms trafficking; trafficking in organs, tissues and human stem cells; contract killing and homicides linked to organized criminal structures; participation in transnational criminal organizations; and cybercrime, cyberterrorism and cyberfraud that compromise national security or the critical infrastructure of the Costa Rican state.

Fernández framed the proposal as a move against criminal structures rather than a general loosening of protections for citizens, telling lawmakers that Costa Rican nationality is a right and a source of pride for millions of honest citizens and <cite index=”1-1″>not a shield for members of transnational criminal organizations.

She said the mechanism would remain exceptional and would require a final ruling from Costa Rican courts in every case, describing it as not an automatic or generalized extradition of nationals. The proposal also preserves the dual criminality requirement, meaning the conduct must be a crime both in Costa Rica and in the country requesting the person.

The prohibition Fernández is seeking to narrow further dates to the aftermath of the 1948 civil war, when the drafters of the current constitution barred the forced removal of citizens from national territory. That ban held for more than seven decades. The Legislative Assembly approved the amendment to Article 32 unanimously in its final debate on May 15, 2025, and the reform was promulgated as Law 10730 and published on May 28 of that year. A companion reform harmonizing the 1971 Extradition Law with the new constitutional text cleared Congress the following November.

On March 20 of this year, former Supreme Court magistrate and former security minister Celso Gamboa Sánchez and Edwin Danney López Vega were handed to United States agents at the San Jose Airport and flown to Texas aboard a DEA aircraft, the first extraditions of Costa Rican nationals in our history.

Both face cocaine conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of Texas. The appeals court that authorized the transfer required written assurances from Washington that neither man would face life imprisonment or a sentence longer than 50 years, the ceiling permitted under Costa Rican law, and that time served in pretrial detention here would be credited against any sentence.

That same ruling exposed a question the courts have not settled. Judges accepted a defense argument on non-retroactivity in the case of a third man, Álvarez Alfaro, declining to apply the 2025 reform to conduct predating it. Whether nationals can be extradited for acts committed before May 2025 remains contested, and any expansion of the grounds would inherit the same dispute.

Constitutional amendments move slowly in Costa Rica by design. The text must win a two-thirds majority in three debates, then be taken up again and approved in three more debates after the Assembly’s annual turnover, meaning no reform filed in August could take effect before the second half of the current legislative period at the earliest.

The five bills Fernández did file on Monday address the ordinary criminal system. One would replace the preliminary hearing in the Criminal Procedure Code with a single pre-trial hearing before the same court that will hear the case, which the president said would cut duplicated steps that delay resolutions. Another would require electronic ankle monitoring for anyone granted an alternative to prison after a final sentence, replacing arrangements such as signing in every fifteen days.

A third would classify illegal mining as organized crime and raise penalties for extraction, processing, financing, transport or storage to between six and ten years, with confiscation of machinery and registry freezes on linked properties. A fourth would allow parents jailed over unpaid child support to serve under electronic monitoring instead, on the reasoning that a father in prison cannot earn the money he owes.

The fifth restores older police rank titles and requires a university degree and fifteen years of service for senior command posts. A planned reform of the Dirección de Inteligencia y Seguridad Nacional was pulled from the package and deferred to a third round of bills.

The government has now sent twelve security bills to Congress since mid-June. Homicides, meanwhile, are running below last year’s pace. The Judicial Investigation Agency counted 401 killings through July 6, fifty-two fewer than the same point in 2025, with settling of scores recorded as the leading motive and San José, Limón and Puntarenas the most affected provinces.

World.title: Costa Rica Reworks $400 Million Limón Hospital Tender After Failed Bid
World.content:
Costa Rica’s public health system is preparing to relaunch the tender for a new hospital in Limón during the final week of July, seven months after the first competition for the roughly $400 million project closed without a single company submitting an offer.

The Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social (CCSS) has rewritten the terms of the competition to address the objection contractors raised most consistently the first time around. Under the original terms, the winning firm would have been locked into its quoted price for the full life of a project expected to run several years, with no mechanism to recover cost increases if the exchange rate moved, if steel and cement rose, or if freight became more expensive. Jorge Granados, the CCSS manager of infrastructure and technology, confirmed that the institution has secured a change to that provision for the new tender.

The absence of a price-adjustment clause was not an oversight. The first competition was structured as a turnkey contract covering design, construction and equipment in a single award, and the regulations accompanying the General Public Contracting Law bar price readjustment mechanisms in contracts of that type. Granados told the CCSS board earlier this year that when the institution surveyed the companies that had declined to bid, the inability to adjust prices was the reason they named most often. On a project of this size and duration, he said, ordinary movement in input costs becomes a risk the bidder alone would have to absorb.

Construction firms cited additional concerns. Security conditions in the province and the repeated closures of Route 32, the highway that connects the Caribbean coast to the Central Valley, both came up in the CCSS survey, along with uncertainty over the colón’s behavior against the dollar. The institution has characterized those as secondary to the pricing question, though they help explain why a project in Limón in particular drew no takers.

The second change to the tender is structural. The first competition was open only to companies that had cleared an earlier international prequalification round, which in practice narrowed the field to five Costa Rican firms. Representatives of all five visited the 19-hectare (47-acre) site in June of last year, and none of them bid when the window closed in December. The new process discards prequalification entirely and will be run as an open public tender, which allows companies beyond that original group, including foreign firms, to compete alongside them. Mónica Taylor, the CCSS executive president, has said the institution intends to draw bidders from abroad.

The financial figures attached to the project have shifted with the currency. The tender declared unsuccessful was valued at approximately ¢208.78 billion, a figure set when the colón stood considerably weaker against the dollar than it does now. The CCSS currently describes the project as costing close to $400 million, which at the Banco Central de Costa Rica reference rate of ¢455.40 to the dollar would translate to roughly ¢182 billion. The gap between those two numbers over a period of months is a fair illustration of the exposure contractors said they were unwilling to carry.

How quickly the relaunch translates into visible work on the ground is the open question. Taylor has previously indicated that awarding a contract of this scale would take about a year. Granados has since offered a longer estimate, warning that even with the tender published in the coming days, the contracting and award process for a project of this magnitude can run up to two years before construction begins. Once building starts, he has estimated roughly two and a half years to completion, with late 2029 as a tentative date for the hospital to open its doors.

That timeline sits well beyond what the institution promised the province. In a 2023 press statement the CCSS said the facility would be ready by the end of 2027. President Laura Fernández has asked whether groundbreaking could be scheduled for August 31, 2027, the Day of the Black Person and Afro-Costa Rican Culture, a date that would now mark the start of construction rather than the opening the province was originally told to expect.

The failed tender has drawn official scrutiny. The Defensoría de los Habitantes opened an investigation into the process, requesting that the CCSS submit an improvement plan for the project along with the specific adjustments planned to the tender terms, the contracting model and the participation conditions, and the corrective measures it intends to take in the short, medium and long term. The ombudsman’s office framed the review as a matter of verifying efficiency, reasonableness and transparency in a project it described as essential to the right to health for the population of Limón.

The current Hospital Tony Facio Castro serves the entire Caribbean province, including the cruise port at Limón, the beach communities of Cahuita and Puerto Viejo, and the agricultural districts along Route 32. Its physical condition has been the central argument for replacement for years, and every month the new tender does not produce a contract is another month the province waits on a building the CCSS itself has called urgent.

Whether the revised terms are enough to attract offers will be visible within weeks of publication. If the second competition also closes without bids, the institution will be back at a starting point it has now reached twice.

World.title: Costa Rica’s First Gold Lands as Four Clubs enter Copa Centroamericana
World.content:
The Concacaf Copa Centroamericana kicks off its fourth edition Tuesday, and although opening night belongs to clubs from Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama and Guatemala, Costa Rica’s four entrants follow within 48 hours. Alajuelense, Saprissa, Herediano and Cartaginés all open group play midweek in the tournament that has become the country’s most dependable route into continental competition.

Saprissa is first out, away to UMECIT of Panama at 6 p.m. Costa Rica time Wednesday, followed the same evening by Alajuelense at home against Xelajú of Guatemala at 8 p.m. Herediano hosts Marathón of Honduras at 7 p.m. Thursday, and Cartaginés closes matchday one away to Municipal in Guatemala City at 9 p.m. Costa Rica sits at UTC-6 with no daylight saving adjustment, which puts the Wednesday opener at 8 p.m. on the United States East Coast and 7 p.m. in the Central time zone.

Twenty clubs from the seven countries of the isthmus are split into four groups of five. Each team plays four matches, two at home and two away, and the top two in every group advance to the quarterfinals. The group phase runs from July 28 through August 27, knockout rounds begin in September, and the two-legged final is scheduled for December 2 and December 6. Six clubs — the four semifinalists plus the two Play-In winners — earn places in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup, and the eventual champion goes straight into the round of 16 of that competition, which is where the real financial upside sits for a Central American club.

Alajuelense arrives as three-time defending champion chasing a fourth consecutive regional title, and the May draw in Miami handed the Manudos the hardest assignment of the four Costa Rican sides. Group A pairs them with Plaza Amador of Panama, Luis Ángel Firpo of El Salvador, Diriangén of Nicaragua and Xelajú, the Guatemalan side they beat on penalties in last year’s final.

Herediano heads Group B alongside Antigua GFC, Marathón, Real Estelí and Alianza FC of El Salvador. Saprissa landed in Group C with Olimpia of Honduras, Deportivo Mixco, Alianza FC of Panama and UMECIT. Cartaginés drew Group D with Municipal, Motagua, FAS of El Salvador and Verdes FC of Belize. No two Costa Rican clubs can meet before the knockout rounds.

The regional schedule lands on top of a domestic season that only just started. Matchday one of the Apertura produced a 5-1 win for Saprissa over Pérez Zeledón, a 3-1 Cartaginés victory over Inter San Carlos in the newcomers’ first top-flight fixture, and a 1-1 draw between Sporting and Alajuelense at Puente Piedra in Grecia. All four Copa entrants now face the familiar Central American squeeze of league and continental fixtures inside the same week, a workload that has historically thinned squads by September.

Costa Rica’s other sporting story of the weekend came from the Dominican Republic, where the XXV Central American and Caribbean Games are underway. Taekwondo athlete Jaycee Bassett, 18, won our first gold medal of the Games on Sunday, taking the women’s -46 kg division (about 101 pounds) with a 2-0 win over Mexico’s Fernanda Hernández.

The first round finished 7-7 and went to Bassett on tiebreak criteria; she then took the second 10-2 to close the final without needing a third. Bassett has had an unusually strong year, winning the G4 Pan American Championship in Rio de Janeiro and the Canada Open before competing at the Rome Grand Prix as the only Central American entrant, and she was a world junior runner-up in 2024. The National Olympic Committee, which reported the result, has begun framing her as a genuine prospect for Los Angeles 2028.

Laura Sancho added a bronze in taekwondo the same day, beating Nicaragua’s Erika Narváez 2-1 in rounds after dropping the second 10-4 and recovering to take the decider 3-0. Both medals followed a strong Saturday for the delegation. Open-water swimmer Jeison Rojas, a 22-year-old from Cartago and one of Costa Rica’s flagbearers at the opening ceremony, took silver in the men’s 10-kilometer (6.2-mile) event in 2:05:03.0, finishing 2 minutes and 29 seconds behind Mexico’s Paulo Strehlke and holding off the bronze medalist by four seconds.

Because only gold and silver carried qualification, the result secured Rojas a place at the Lima 2027 Pan American Games. He returned Sunday in the 3-kilometer knockout and finished seventh in 7:33.4. Víctor Camilo Cantillano also took silver Saturday in men’s individual traditional poomsae.

The Games mark the centenary of the competition, which began in Mexico City in 1926, and this edition is the largest yet with 40 sports on the program — more than are scheduled for the Los Angeles Olympics. Competition in Santo Domingo continues through August 8, overlapping almost entirely with the Copa Centroamericana group phase, which means five straight weeks in which Costa Rican results will be arriving from two directions at once.

World.title: Rincón de la Vieja volcano raised to caution level after 38 eruptions
World.content:
If you have a Rincón de la Vieja hike or a hot springs day trip on your calendar, the volcano’s official activity level went up last week — and the change is worth not only knowing about but understanding before you drive out there.

The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVISCORI) moved Rincón de la Vieja from warning to caution on 24 July, the third rung on a four-step scale. Since 2 July the observatory has counted 38 phreatic eruptions at the crater. Three of them sent lahars down the northern flank. The strongest, on 20 July, was the most energetic eruption the volcano has produced all year.

Volcanologist Geoffroy Avard said the decision rested on more than the eruption count. Seismic activity has picked up. The shape of the volcano itself is changing measurably and to get technical, the Sulphur dioxide output is up. Put together, those three signals point the same direction, and the observatory said further eruptions of equal or greater intensity are possible. In a nutshell, this is not a report that something happened but a report that something is more likely to happen again.

What caution actually means

Costa Rica’s volcano scale runs from one to four. Level one is calm. Level two, warning, is where Rincón de la Vieja has spent most of the last several years — small eruptions, gas, hot springs bubbling harder than usual, mild swelling of the summit. Ash falls lightly if it falls at all.

Level three, caution, is a step up in what the volcano is capable of on short notice, not a declaration that it is erupting now. It means bigger explosions are on the table, rocks can be thrown further from the crater, ash can travel, and lahars are an expected consequence rather than a surprise. Level four is reserved for a major eruption in progress.

Nothing about level three closes the area, cancels flights or triggers evacuations. What it does is shrink the margin for error close to the crater, which is exactly where the hardest hiking in the park goes.

Why the rivers turn grey

Those downhill from the volcano reported the Azul and Pénjamo rivers running a milky grey earlier this month after eruptive episodes. That color is the most reliable early warning system in the area, and it is worth knowing what it signals.

Rincón de la Vieja has an acidic lake sitting inside its active crater. A phreatic eruption happens when groundwater or lake water hits something hot enough to flash it to steam, and the pressure blows out through the top. There is no lava involved. What comes out is steam, gas, rock and a great deal of water and sediment.

That water and sediment goes somewhere. The crater’s northern rim is the lowest, so the flow spills that way and races downhill as a lahar — essentially a fast-moving slurry of water, ash, mud and rock with the consistency of wet concrete. It picks up more material from the riverbed as it goes. By the time it reaches the lowland farming communities on the Upala side, the river is grey, smells of sulphur and is running higher than it was an hour earlier.

Rain makes this worse rather than better, which is important to know in late July. Heavy rain at the summit mobilizes loose volcanic material that is already sitting on the slopes, so a lahar can come down without a fresh eruption to announce it.

The historical record shows what these flows can do. In November 1995 a lahar took out the bridge over the Pénjamo entirely. In 2019 the same river rose more than four metres (13 feet) in minutes and widened by six metres (20 feet) on each bank. Dead fish have turned up in the Río Niño, 15 kilometres (nine miles) from the crater, after past events.

If you are near one of these rivers and the water changes color, rises or starts to smell of sulphur, get away from the channel and onto higher ground. Do not wait to see how big it gets. That is the whole safety rule, and it works because lahars travel much faster than people can outrun them along a riverbed.

What is open in the park

Rincón de la Vieja National Park covers 14,300 hectares (35,300 acres) and is the busiest protected area in the Guanacaste Conservation Area. It sits about 23 kilometres (14 miles) from Liberia, which is why it shows up on so many itineraries. Visitation splits between two sectors, Las Pailas and Santa María.

The Active Crater trail — eight kilometres one way, 16 kilometres (10 miles) round trip, climbing roughly 1,000 metres (3,300 feet) — has been closed for years. Volcanic activity and unsafe crater gases keep it shut, and last week’s level change does nothing to reopen it. Anyone selling you a summit hike is selling you something the park is not permitting.

The Las Pailas loop is the main draw and the reason most visitors come. It runs three kilometres (1.9 miles) on a circuit past fumaroles, boiling mud pots and steam vents that sit between 78 and 106 degrees Celsius (172 to 223 degrees Fahrenheit). It is well marked and partly paved. The waterfall trails to La Cangreja, five kilometres (3.1 miles) out, and Catarata Escondida, 4.3 kilometres (2.7 miles), are longer and harder.

Confirm the day before you go. Area and trail closures at this park have historically arrived with no notice, sometimes on the morning of, and travelers have turned up at the gate to be told a trail shut days earlier. Park staff at the entrance know the current status. A tour operator’s website from last season does not.

All tickets must be bought in advance through the park service’s online reservation system. There is no cash or card payment at the gate.

What closes first if the level rises

The pattern here in Costa Rica is consistent, and it works outward from the crater. Summit and crater-adjacent trails go first — those are already shut here. Next come the longer backcountry trails that put hikers hours from an exit, which is where the waterfall routes sit. Then the visited sectors themselves close, sometimes one at a time, sometimes both.

Hot springs resorts and private reserves on the volcano’s flanks operate independently of the park and make their own calls, so a park closure does not automatically mean your hot springs booking is cancelled, or the reverse. Full closures of an entire area have happened repeatedly at active volcanoes and have lasted anywhere from a day to several weeks. Build that possibility into a tight Guanacaste itinerary rather than assuming a single fixed day at the park will hold.

Poás is active too

Rincón de la Vieja is not the only volcano the observatory is watching. Poás, far more accessible from the Central Valley and San José, is producing low-intensity eruptions of its own. Poás has its own history of abrupt closures over gas emissions and ashfall, including multi-week shutdowns. If you are choosing between the two on a short trip, check both before committing.

Where to check

The observatory monitors Rincón de la Vieja continuously through seismic stations, gas-measuring equipment, cameras and field observation, and publishes changes as they happen. Level changes in either direction are announced rather than quietly applied — the volcano was moved down from caution to warning in a previous cycle, and it could go either way again.

The behavior on display now is not new for this mountain. Rincón de la Vieja has run through active phases and quiet ones since 2011, with stretches of daily small eruptions followed by months of little. What the level change records is that the current stretch is more energetic than the last one, and that the instruments suggest it has further to run.

World.title: Why Two Fitness Veterans Chose Costa Rica to Launch a New Peptide Company: Peptides Costa Rica
World.content:
Costa Rica is known internationally as one of the healthiest places on the planet. Its pura vida lifestyle, outdoor recreation, and its focus on wellness has made it a magnet for athletes, entrepreneurs, and retirees looking for a healthy and active way of living.

As this evolution of wellness and health accelerates, one topic comes up more and more among fitness professionals, wellness practitioners, and anyone looking to age healthy and gracefully: peptides. While research continues to expand and validate these compounds, Costa Rican residents have been running into a consistent roadblock: finding a dependable local supplier they can trust.

That challenge inspired the launch of Peptides Costa Rica, a new company dedicated to serving customers throughout Costa Rica with quality peptide products, educational resources, and responsive local customer service.

More information about the company can be found at https://peptidescostarica.net/.

A Growing Need for Local Access

In the past, many Costa Ricans interested in peptides relied on international suppliers. While ordering from overseas is possible, the experience can be confusing and even hard to trust.. Customers waiting on deliveries may face customs delays, communication can be difficult, and there are often unanswered questions and concerns.

If you’re researching peptides for wellness, recovery, or performance-related goals, confidence in both the supplier and the purchasing process is a major issue.

Peptides Costa Rica was founded to simplify that experience.

The company operates locally, understands the Costa Rican market, and places customer support at front and center of its business. Instead of waiting weeks for international shipments or wondering about the status of an order, customers can reach out quickly and expect orders promptly.

The company’s mission extends beyond offering products. Education, transparency, and long-term relationships are equally important priorities for Peptides Costa Rica.

From Personal Experience to Business Vision

For co-founder Joey Webster, launching Peptides Costa Rica wasn’t just a business opportunity. It grew from years of personal experience. Webster has spent much of his life involved in competitive athletics. Beginning as a successful wrestler who competed at both the state and national levels, he later moved into amateur mixed martial arts while continuing to pursue strength training and overall fitness.

Like many athletes who spend years pushing their bodies to perform, injuries eventually became part of the reality of his journey. Multiple surgeries and long recovery periods happened, but this is how Webster was introduced to the growing body of research surrounding peptides and the conversations taking place within sports, performance, and wellness circles. Rather than accepting marketing claims as truth, he dedicated himself to learning about peptide science, manufacturing standards, product sourcing, and quality control.

That educational journey became the foundation for Peptides Costa Rica. “We wanted to build the kind of company we wished had existed when we first started learning about peptides,” Webster says. “People deserve access to reliable information, responsive customer service, and products sourced with quality in mind.”

Rather than focusing only on sales, Webster believes education should be part of every customer’s experience.

A Partnership Built on Decades of Experience

Joining Webster is co-founder Sean McCully, whose name is well known throughout the fitness and martial arts industries. McCully founded LA Boxing and has spent decades helping people improve their health through structured training, coaching, and discipline. As one of the early pioneers of Muay Thai, kickboxing, and mixed martial arts instruction in the United States, he has worked with thousands of students ranging from beginners to competitive athletes.

Throughout his career, McCully has seen firsthand how proper recovery, consistent training, and informed decision-making help make long-term health more achievable. Those same values now guide Peptides Costa Rica. “Our goal is to earn people’s trust,” McCully says. “That starts by treating customers with honesty, answering questions, and providing reliable service every step of the way.”

Together, Webster and McCully bring decades of combined experience in athletics, coaching, business development, and customer education.

More Than an Online Store

Although peptide products are the focus of the business, Peptides Costa Rica was never meant to function as just another online retailer. Instead, the founders pictured a resource where customers could learn about peptides, understand the different categories available, and make research-based decisions based on credible information instead of social media trends or online speculation.

The company continues to expand its educational content to help visitors better understand commonly discussed peptide applications. That educational focus has become one of the company’s most important and unique characteristics.

Quality Comes First

Quality and transparency have been crucial principles for the business from the start. Peptides Costa Rica carefully selects products from reputable manufacturing partners while maintaining consistency and quality throughout the purchasing process. When available, customers may request Certificates of Analysis (COAs), providing additional confidence regarding product identity and manufacturing standards.



The company believes that transparency is one of the most important ways to build lasting customer relationships. And this is what sets this company apart from the rest. Responsive communication and local support, along with a deep commitment to transparency, helps distinguish the business from many overseas suppliers.

A Growing Product Catalog

As customer demand has expanded, so has the company’s selection of peptide products. Visitors can browse the complete catalog at:

https://catalog.peptidescostarica.net/

The catalog continues to grow as new products become available and customer interest evolves. Among the company’s most popular offerings is Retatrutide, which has generated significant attention within the wellness and medical research communities over the past several years.

If you’re interested in learning more about Retatrutide, you can visit:

https://peptidescostarica.net/retatrutide-costa-rica/

Serving Costa Rica’s Diverse Community

Costa Rica’s population includes both Spanish-speaking residents and a large international community. Recognizing that reality, Peptides Costa Rica has developed resources in multiple languages to better serve customers across the country. The company’s Spanish-language website can be found here:

https://peptidescostarica.net/es

Providing bilingual resources is another way the founders show their commitment to accessibility and customer education for everyone interested in learning more about peptides.

Looking Toward the Future

Although Peptides Costa Rica is a new company, Webster and McCully see it as a long-term investment in Costa Rica’s growing wellness community. Future plans include expanding educational content, introducing additional peptide products, strengthening customer support, and continuing to build relationships throughout the country.

For the founders, success won’t be measured by growth or sales figures alone. It will be measured by their reputation. They hope customers come to associate the company with reliable information, honest communication, and dependable service, which are qualities they believe are sometimes difficult to find in an industry that continues to evolve rapidly.

Their goal is to become the trusted local resource for Costa Ricans seeking high-quality peptide products while maintaining the personal service that only a locally focused business can provide.

Learn More

Peptides Costa Rica welcomes customers from across the country who are interested in learning more about peptides or exploring the company’s growing catalog. For additional information, educational resources, product availability, questions, or assistance, contact the team directly:

Phone / WhatsApp: 8404-6973

As interest in peptides continues to grow throughout Costa Rica, Peptides Costa Rica hopes to become more than a supplier. It wants to become a trusted local partner committed to education, transparency, and exceptional customer service for years to come.

World.title: Bail denied for Manuel De Jesus Flores, accused of sexually assaulting 10-year-old girl
World.content:
Bail denied for Manuel De Jesus Flores, accused of sexually assaulting 10-year-old girl

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A resident of the Lords Bank area, Ladyville, was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Monday morning after appearing in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on sexual assault charges involving a 10-year-old minor.

Manuel De Jesus Flores appeared in Court #5 before a Senior Magistrate to answer to two counts of sexual assault. Allegations are that on July 18, 2026, Flores intentionally and unlawfully touched the female minor, who is 10 years and 5 months old, without her consent.

Court details reveal that Flores allegedly pressed his body against the child before grabbing her with his right hand, pulling down her blouse, and touching her breast.

Flores was represented by attorney Sharon Pitts-Robateau, who submitted a strong application for bail. Pitts-Robateau argued that her client is gainfully employed as a mason and emphasized that he remains presumed innocent until proven guilty, as the charges against him are currently allegations. She argued that the functional purpose of bail is to ensure a defendant’s attendance in court, which could be managed through strictly enforced court conditions.

Police Prosecutor Sergeant Ayala vigorously objected to bail, urging the court to consider the extreme vulnerability of the young victim, the serious nature and prevalence of sexual offenses, and the risk that Flores might reoffend or interfere with the victim or the ongoing police investigation, given that the alleged incident took place at around 12:30 a.m.

After weighing submissions from both the defense and prosecution, the sitting Senior Magistrate denied bail due to the severity of the charges. Flores has been remanded to prison until his next court appearance scheduled for September 17, 2026.

World.title: Police officer pleads guilty to having sex multiple times with 13-year-old girl; Had sex with her in her mother’s house – showed up in police uniform
World.content:
Police officer pleads guilty to having sex multiple times with 13-year-old girl; Had sex with her in her mother’s house – showed up in police uniform

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 29-year-old police officer is behind bars tonight after pleading guilty in the High Court to four counts of Unlawful Sexual Intercourse (USI) involving a minor.

Police Constable Dexter Diego admitted to the charges on Monday morning before Justice Nigel Pilgrim. The trial was expected to begin on Monday but concluded in less than an hour when Diego entered guilty pleas on all counts. Diego had sex with the victim once when she was 13 years old and three times when she was 14 years old.

According to the agreed facts presented in court, Diego was a family friend who first became acquainted with the victim in 2022. Over a 10-month period, the two maintained regular communication and developed a close relationship in secret without the knowledge of the child’s mother.

The incidents took place between late 2022 and early 2023. The first instance occurred between late December 2022 and January 2023, when the 13-year-old victim was babysitting a relative’s children. Diego visited the home and engaged in sexual acts and repeated intercourse with the minor throughout the night, leading to a single charge for that date.

The remaining charges stem from three separate incidents in early 2023. Between mid-February and March 2023, Diego visited the victim’s home uninvited while her mother was away and had sexual intercourse with her. On February 27, 2023, Diego again visited the minor at her home around 9:00 a.m. and engaged in sexual intercourse. The final incident took place on March 26, 2023, when Diego visited the victim’s house while dressed in his police uniform and had sexual intercourse with her.

Diego was represented in court by attorney Hurl Hamilton. The prosecution was represented by Crown Counsel Shannel Fernandez-Peyrefitte.

Justice Pilgrim has deferred sentencing until September 8, 2026. Before delivering the sentence, the court has ordered the preparation of a Prison Report, a Social Inquiry Report, and a Victim Impact Statement. Diego remains in custody pending his sentencing hearing.

World.title: Gunman fires at GI3 officers during Belize City pursuit
World.content:
Gunman fires at GI3 officers during Belize City pursuit

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed confrontation in which a gunman allegedly opened fire on members of the Gang Intelligence, Investigation and Interdiction Unit, commonly known as GI3.

The incident occurred on July 23, 2026, while GI3 officers were conducting mobile operations in the Saint Martin’s and Port Loyola areas of Belize City.

Police say officers attempted to intercept a vehicle of interest, but its driver refused to stop, prompting a pursuit. The fleeing vehicle eventually crashed into a lamp post, after which three people exited and ran.

Investigators allege that the front-seat passenger fired at the officers, who returned fire. All three occupants managed to escape, but no police officers were injured.

The vehicle was subsequently impounded, and police say significant progress has been made in the investigation. Separate reporting placed the incident in the Police Street area behind the Foam Factory and indicated that it occurred during the early-morning hours.

World.title: Baby placed in Human Services care after mother allegedly failed to return for the infant
World.content:
Baby placed in Human Services care after mother allegedly failed to return for the infant

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A baby has been placed in the care of the Human Services Department after the child’s mother allegedly left the infant with a woman in Belize City and failed to return.

Police became involved after responding to a report of a small fire on the stairway of a residence. After extinguishing the fire, the occupant found a birth document near the area where the blaze had occurred.

The document was eventually linked to a baby who had been left at another nearby residence. The caretaker told investigators that a woman she knew only by her first name had visited and asked her to call a taxi. While they waited, the child fell asleep and was placed inside the home.

The mother reportedly left the premises and did not return for the child. Police have since located her, while the baby has been handed over to Human Services.

Authorities say a welfare assessment and consultation are being conducted to determine what caused the mother to leave the child. Police have not established that the stairway fire was intended to harm the baby.

World.title: Fire contained at downtown Belize City’s Abdo Building
World.content:
Fire contained at downtown Belize City’s Abdo Building

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Fire officials are investigating a fire that broke out inside the Abdo Building at the corner of Albert and Orange streets in downtown Belize City.

Police were alerted to the blaze at approximately 12:44 a.m. on Sunday, July 26, 2026. Criminal Investigation Branch personnel responded and found National Fire Service officers already working to extinguish the flames.

The businessman occupying the affected ground-floor premises told police that he had left the property and was later alerted to the fire. He reportedly rents the building, while the contents of the store belong to him and are insured.

The quick response prevented the blaze from spreading extensively to the building’s upper level. Police are awaiting an official report from the National Fire Service to determine whether the fire was caused by an electrical fault or was deliberately set.

World.title: Police investigate break-in at Atlantic Bank’s Ladyville branch
World.content:
Police investigate break-in at Atlantic Bank’s Ladyville branch

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a burglary at the Atlantic Bank branch in Ladyville that caused damage to the building and its automated teller machine.

Investigators were called to the branch on Thursday, July 23, 2026, after signs of forced entry were discovered. Police say nothing of significance appears to have been stolen.

The ATM was damaged, apparently after the intruder or intruders had already gained entry to the building. Police have declined to reveal how the building was entered.

Scenes of Crime technicians processed the location and lifted several fingerprints that investigators hope will help identify those responsible. Atlantic Bank subsequently advised customers that the Ladyville branch was open and its ATM service had been restored.

World.title: Mexican motorcyclist Nidia Hernandez killed in collision near Belize–Mexico border
World.content:
Mexican motorcyclist Nidia Hernandez killed in collision near Belize–Mexico border

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have issued notices of intended prosecution following a traffic accident that claimed the life of 31-year-old Mexican national Nidia Hernandez near Belize’s northern border.

The accident occurred at approximately 9 p.m. on Sunday, July 26, 2026, as Hernandez was riding a motorcycle toward the Mexican border.

Investigators say a green Chevrolet was travelling behind Hernandez when she allegedly swerved into the opposite lane and collided with a Dodge Attitude travelling from the direction of Mexico toward Belize.

Hernandez sustained fatal injuries in the collision. Police say urine samples were obtained from the drivers of both motor vehicles as the investigation continues.

World.title: Notice of intended prosecution issued to driver after Tatiana Alvarado’s fatal crash
World.content:
Notice of intended prosecution issued to driver after Tatiana Alvarado’s fatal crash

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have issued a notice of intended prosecution as investigations continue into the road traffic accident that claimed the life of 39-year-old Tatiana Alvarado of Bella Vista Village.

The collision occurred at approximately 4:35 p.m. on Saturday, July 25, 2026, near the Independence Junction on the Thomas Vincent Ramos Highway.

Police say Alvarado was riding a motorcycle toward Punta Gorda when the driver of a Ford Escape travelling behind her allegedly attempted to overtake. Investigators now allege that Alvarado suddenly turned left during the overtaking manoeuvre, resulting in the collision.

Earlier reports identified the driver of the Ford Escape as 26-year-old Daunte Oliver Eden Noralez of a Belmopan address. Alvarado’s motorcycle caught fire following the collision, and she was pronounced dead after being transported to the Southern Regional Hospital.

Police say the driver has been cooperating with investigators. Authorities have not yet confirmed whether a urine sample was obtained from him.

World.content:
Jamaica Observer Limited is advising the public of an unauthorised and deceptive website that is unlawfully using our name, logo, and other brand elements to imitate our official platform and mislead individuals.

The article references former Cabinet minister Lisa Hanna and a purported investment platform, and it improperly uses the image and likeness of the public figure, purporting to create the appearance of an endorsement or affiliation with the platform described in the article. These claims are entirely false. The website and related social media posts are fraudulent and have no connection to the Jamaica Observer. How to Protect Yourself
