World.title: MMA fighter founds ‘Defence of Traditional Values’ movement in Georgia. What do lawyers say?
World.content:
MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, together with several associates, has announced the creation of a new civic movement in Georgia aimed at “protecting traditional values, culture and national identity.”

Kartvelishvili unveiled the initiative at a special briefing, saying the organisation would “respond immediately” to issues involving the country’s ancestors, religion, history and other matters that the group considers offensive.

“If necessary, we’ll even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

It remains unclear who will join the movement, how it will operate or what form it will take. Kartvelishvili said those details would be announced at a later date.

Kartvelishvili’s rhetoric has already won the backing of Archil Gorduladze, an MP from the ruling Georgian Dream party, who said the initiative was “important and positive” but stressed that it “must operate within the law and fully comply with it.”

Lawyers, however, argue that the proposed group amounts to an illegal formation, and that establishing, leading or joining such an organisation is a criminal offence under Georgian law.

Kartvelishvili has previously been accused by some activists of mobilising titushky — organised groups of aggressive enforcers often used to intimidate opponents. Several days ago, pro-government media also described him as a friend of Niko Khurtsilava, who recently attacked comedian Onise Okriashvili.

What Kartvelishvili said

According to Kartvelishvili, Georgia’s identity, traditions, religion and cultural heritage have come under deliberate attack in recent years.

“Our identity, traditions, values and religion, as well as the achievements that have enriched Georgian culture throughout its history, have repeatedly been the target of coordinated attacks,” the MMA fighter said.

Giorgi Kartvelishvili (third from left) at the briefing

According to Kartvelishvili, these developments are being driven by “foreign-funded groups, politicians, activists and media representatives” seeking to undermine Georgian values.

He said the new movement would begin confronting individuals and groups that are “under the influence of external interests” and called on supporters to join the initiative.

Lawyers’ comments

Lawyer Boris Kurua told Netgazeti that it was unlikely Kartvelishvili had launched such an initiative without the approval of the security services.

Kurua said: “If anyone still had even the slightest doubt that they might not actually be planning to commit a crime, the statement made at the briefing — ‘we’re ready to go to prison’ — makes everything more than clear.

“If members of this group arm themselves with nothing more than wooden sticks, it would already fall under Article 223 of the Criminal Code. In other words, this would constitute an illegal formation, and establishing, leading or joining such a group is a criminal offence.

“Article 223 of the Criminal Code covers the establishment of an illegal formation, its leadership, joining such a formation, participating in it, or carrying out any other activities on its behalf. The offence is punishable by three to seven years in prison. If such actions result in serious consequences, the prison sentence increases to between four and eight years.

“If, for a moment, we imagine that this group is being created without the approval of the security services, then, assuming law enforcement is functioning effectively, those involved should be prosecuted even at the stage of preparing the crime. It’s difficult for me to imagine Kartvelishvili taking such an initiative without the security services’ approval.”

Lawyer Omar Purtseladze also commented on the situation for Netgazeti. In addition to the potential criminal offence, he argued that Giorgi Kartvelishvili’s briefing amounted to a political statement.

“The creation by individuals or groups close to the authorities of an organisation whose purpose is to persecute people on ideological grounds is not only a serious legal issue but also a political statement. I hope someone will show at least a minimum degree of prudence to prevent the situation from becoming even more radicalised in an already deeply polarised environment,” Purtseladze said.

Protecting traditional values in Georgia

World.title: More than $7 million laundered in Georgia, prosecutors say after uncovering transnational crime network
World.content:
Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has brought criminal charges against four foreign nationals and five companies in connection with a transnational organised crime and large-scale money laundering case involving 21.5 million lari (about $7.8m).

According to prosecutors, the suspects carried out criminal activities in several countries before transferring the illicit proceeds to Georgia in an attempt to conceal their origin and legalise the funds.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the suspects established companies in Georgia without any intention of carrying out genuine business activities. Using forged documents and fictitious payment descriptions, they gradually transferred funds of illicit and unexplained origin from abroad into Georgian bank accounts. The total amount, held in various currencies, was equivalent to 21.5 million lari.

Prosecutors said that part of the money was later transferred abroad using forged documentation and fictitious payment descriptions, while the bulk of the allegedly illicit assets has been frozen as part of the investigation.

The defendants have been charged with laundering criminal proceeds on an especially large scale. The offence carries a prison sentence of between nine and 12 years for individuals, while companies found guilty may face liquidation, a ban on conducting business activities or a fine.

The Prosecutor’s Office said it would ask the court, within the timeframe set by law, to place the defendants in pre-trial detention. If the court grants the request, the suspects will be placed on a wanted list.

According to prosecutors, the investigation has so far resulted in the seizure of foreign currency worth around 14 million lari (about $5.1m) and real estate valued at more than 1 million lari (about $363,000).

The Prosecutor’s Office said it would initiate the necessary legal procedures to confiscate the seized assets in favour of the state.

money laundering in Georgia

World.title: Georgian parliament speaker: ‘What’s the point of EU membership if you’re stripped of its main benefit?’
World.content:
Georgian parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili says the country’s EU membership should not become an end in itself, and has criticised proposals which, he argues, would weaken the principle of consensus in the bloc’s decision-making process.

Papuashvili said that if such changes were introduced, remaining outside the EU could become more advantageous for some smaller states, as they would retain greater freedom to make independent decisions.

“The question will become increasingly relevant: what’s the point of membership if you’re stripped of its main advantage and leverage from the very beginning?” Papuashvili wrote on social media.

He said there was a growing perception that Europe’s larger states were seeking to reshape the EU’s system of governance, warning that such changes would threaten both the continent’s political balance and the bloc’s enlargement process, as well as the principles on which the European Union was founded.

Papuashvili was commenting on remarks by Germany’s foreign minister, who said several countries had joined Berlin’s initiative to abolish unanimity in EU decision-making.

According to Papuashvili, if such a reform were implemented, the European Union could evolve from a union of equal member states into one dominated largely by its biggest countries.

“EU membership is not an end in itself. That is true neither for current member states nor for candidate countries. Brexit was the clearest proof of that,” the parliament speaker wrote.

According to Papuashvili, the main purpose of joining the European Union is to expand a country’s opportunities, better protect its national interests and increase its influence over international decision-making. He argued that the principle of consensus is one of the key guarantees of that influence for smaller states, as it allows them to block decisions they consider harmful and defend their national interests.

“If the principle of consensus is abolished and decision-making comes to depend entirely on the will of larger states or a stable majority, smaller countries will lose this fundamental lever,” he wrote.

In his view, EU membership would then cease to represent the voluntary delegation of part of a country’s sovereignty in pursuit of shared economic and political goals, and could instead become a process that significantly reduces the influence of smaller states.

Papuashvili argued that a country which can no longer prevent decisions it considers harmful gradually loses both its political freedom and its ability to make sovereign decisions.

He said such a model could benefit larger states, whose economic and political weight already gives them considerable influence, but would represent a “catastrophic change” for smaller countries.

“That is why the question will become increasingly relevant: what’s the point of membership if you’re stripped of its main advantage and leverage from the very beginning?”

Papuashvili argued that the EU’s value lies precisely in allowing member states to defend their interests, influence decisions and block measures they consider undesirable.

He said the debate over changing the unanimity rule could also result in a slowdown of the EU’s future enlargement.

“Candidate countries are being offered not equal membership in the existing union, but a pre-designed system in which they will assume all the obligations of membership while their rights and influence are curtailed.”

According to Papuashvili, the key question for Georgia should not only be when it joins the European Union, but also what kind of European Union it joins and what rights new members will have.

“Membership that deprives a country of its sovereign rights and offers no mechanisms to defend them is not integration – it is the abolition of sovereignty.”

Papuashvili concluded his statement with an apparent reference to Greek mythology: “It seems that even Jupiter’s abduction of Europa is forgiven.”

Papuashvili questions value of EU membership

World.title: EU sanctions Inter RAO, Russian company controlling energy assets in Georgia
World.content:
The European Union has imposed sanctions on Russian state-owned energy company Inter RAO, which indirectly owns Georgia’s Telasi, Telmico, Khrami HPP I and Khrami HPP II through its subsidiaries.

The decision could affect Inter RAO’s assets in Georgia as well as ongoing corporate transactions.

Telasi and Telmico both operate in Georgia’s electricity sector, but they perform different roles. Khrami HPP I and Khrami HPP II (the Khrami hydropower cascade) form one of Georgia’s largest hydropower complexes. Located on the Khrami River in the Kvemo Kartli region, the two plants generate electricity and are an important part of Georgia’s power system, contributing significantly to the country’s domestic electricity production. Telasi is the electricity distribution network operator for Tbilisi. The company owns and manages the capital’s power distribution infrastructure—including power lines, substations and other grid assets—and is responsible for delivering electricity to consumers. Telmico is an electricity supply company. It purchases electricity on the wholesale market and supplies it to residential and commercial customers in Tbilisi. The company issues electricity bills and signs supply contracts with consumers.

Inter RAO was added to the EU sanctions list on 23 July as part of the bloc’s 21st package of sanctions against Russia.

According to the Council of the European Union, the Russian government-controlled company is one of the country’s largest energy groups and plays a significant role in the Russian economy.

According to the Council, the Russian Federation benefits financially from Inter RAO through both the taxes paid by the company and the dividends received by its owners. For that reason, the EU considers the company to be providing financial support to the Russian authorities, which Brussels holds responsible for the aggression against Ukraine and the annexation of Crimea.

According to the company’s ownership structure, Inter RAO is the indirect owner of 100% of the shares in the Netherlands-registered Silk Road Holdings B.V. The company directly owns a 75.108% stake in Telasi and a 75.471% stake in Telmico.

Inter RAO also indirectly owns the Netherlands-registered Gardabani Holdings B.V., which has full ownership of Khrami HPP I and Khrami HPP II.

At the same time, Silk Road Holdings has launched a tender offer to acquire the remaining 24.892% stake in Telasi. The offer closes on 31 July, applications will be reviewed until 7 August, and the transaction is scheduled to be completed on 21 August.

What impact could the sanctions have?

The inclusion of Inter RAO on the EU sanctions list could also affect the operations of the companies it indirectly controls in Georgia. Under EU sanctions, banks and companies based in the bloc may be prohibited from carrying out financial transactions, providing economic resources or delivering certain services to legal entities that are directly or indirectly controlled by a sanctioned company.

The restrictions could also limit Inter RAO’s ability to exercise its shareholder rights through its Netherlands-registered subsidiaries. This could affect voting rights, the appointment of directors, the approval and receipt of dividends, the acquisition or disposal of shareholdings, and other key corporate decisions.

Particular attention is also being paid to the planned acquisition of the remaining stake in Telasi. Because the tender offer is being made by the Netherlands-registered Silk Road Holdings, the transaction may require approval from the relevant Dutch regulatory authority, increasing the risk of delays or even suspension of the deal.

At the same time, the EU has not listed Telasi, Telmico or the Khrami hydropower plants as separate sanctioned entities. However, under EU sanctions rules, asset-freezing measures generally extend to companies that are directly or indirectly owned or majority-controlled by a sanctioned individual or entity.

Inter RAO sanctioned by the EU

World.title: $94.3m in violations: What Azerbaijan’s mid-year audit reveals
World.content:
Report by the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan

In the first half of 2026, the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan identified financial violations and shortcomings worth a total of 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) following state financial oversight activities.

The figures were published in the chamber’s report on its activities for the first six months of the year and were also reported by several media outlets.

The chamber said it had ordered the recovery of 35 million manats ($20.5m) linked to the identified violations. Materials concerning violations worth 14.8 million manats ($8.71m) were referred to law enforcement agencies. The remaining 110.5 million manats ($65m) were classified as “other violations.”

During the reporting period, the chamber carried out 33 oversight activities, including 20 compliance audits, two financial audits, eight performance audits and three analytical reviews.

The audits covered the sectors of education, capital investment, public administration, water supply and irrigation, agriculture, and social protection. Twenty-one of the audited entities were inspected for the first time.

Comparison with previous years

These figures are significantly higher than those reported for the same period in previous years. In the first half of 2024, the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan identified financial violations worth 91 million manats ($53.5m). In the first half of 2025, the figure was estimated at around 65–70 million manats ($38–42m). For the whole of 2025, the chamber reported violations totaling 1.554 billion manats ($915m).

The 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) recorded in the first six months of 2026 is higher than the figures for the corresponding periods of both 2024 and 2025. This may reflect an increase in the number of audits or an expansion in the scope of inspections. At the same time, the data suggests that the scale of detected violations has not decreased.

The public classification of the identified violations remains limited. Reports from previous years, particularly for 2025, showed that the largest share involved breaches of budget legislation, accounting for around 50%, while violations of public procurement rules made up about 24%.

The data for the first half of 2026 does not provide a category-by-category breakdown of the violations. It only identifies the sectors covered by the audits, including capital investment, education and social protection. Previous reports indicate that audits in the construction and public procurement sectors have repeatedly uncovered violations such as inflated project costs, breaches of contract terms and improper documentation.

The role of the Accounts Chamber and the impact of its reports

The Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan is the country’s highest external public financial oversight body. Its reports are submitted to the Milli Majlis and, in principle, can influence the budget process. In practice, however, a significant share of the identified violations is classified as “other violations.”

Of the total 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) in identified violations, the chamber ordered the recovery of funds in only 35 million manats ($20.5m), or about 22% of the total. Materials relating to violations worth 14.8 million manats ($8.71m), around 9%, were referred to law enforcement agencies. The fate of the remaining amount has not been disclosed, and it remains unclear what action, if any, was taken by the relevant institutions or whether any officials were held accountable.

The issue appears to be systemic. Reports from previous years reveal a similar pattern: while violations involving substantial sums have been identified, the amount of recovered funds and the scale of legal action have remained limited. The same types of irregularities continue to be recorded year after year in public procurement, construction projects and the management of public funds, including incomplete documentation, inefficient spending and breaches of contract terms.

The chamber has also repeatedly pointed to weaknesses in internal audit mechanisms. However, the limited public discussion of its reports and the lack of detailed disclosure reduce the practical impact of state financial oversight.

Against the backdrop of Karabakh reconstruction and major government programmes

In recent years, funds allocated for the reconstruction of territories retaken from Armenian control have accounted for a significant share of Azerbaijan’s state budget spending. Billions of manats have been earmarked for capital investment under the Great Return programme and other large-scale government initiatives.

Notably, some of the violations identified in the first half of 2026 were linked to capital investment projects. However, the report does not specify which projects were involved, the sums affected or the nature of the violations.

This makes questions of transparency and the efficient use of public funds even more pressing. The risks of misuse or inefficient spending are particularly significant in large infrastructure and social projects, as these investments are directly tied to the return of displaced residents, the restoration of living conditions and the long-term development of the region.

The absence of a separate, detailed assessment of these programmes in the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan report—or the lack of public disclosure of such information—makes it difficult to objectively assess the risks involved.

Why do the violations recur year after year?

The repeated discovery of financial violations involving large sums may be explained by several factors.

First, insufficient oversight and weak internal audit mechanisms.

Second, a lack of transparency in public procurement and construction projects.

Third, limited accountability. A significant share of the identified violations does not result in disciplinary or legal action against individual officials or the institutions involved.

Based on publicly available information, it is not possible to clearly distinguish between corruption, poor management and procedural violations. However, the scale of the violations and their repeated occurrence suggest that the problem is systemic rather than isolated.

In this context, the limited public scrutiny of the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan’s reports is also significant. As a rule, the full reports, the names of specific projects, the list of audited institutions and detailed information about the identified violations are not made public. This limits opportunities for independent analysis and public oversight.

What does this mean for the public?

The 160.3 million manats ($94.3m) in identified violations involve public funds financed through taxpayers’ money and other state revenues. If part of these funds was spent in breach of financial rules, it means that the money could otherwise have been used for education, healthcare, social protection or infrastructure projects. The recovery of 35 million manats ($20.5m) represents a positive step, but the lack of clarity over the remaining amount raises further questions.

The findings underscore the need for greater transparency, stronger independent audit mechanisms and broader public scrutiny of audit reports.

Key questions remain unanswered: which institutions and projects were responsible for the violations; what became of the 110.5 million manats ($65m) classified as “other violations”; what concrete outcomes resulted from referring cases to law enforcement agencies; and what systemic measures, if any, will be introduced to prevent similar problems from recurring in the same sectors.

Report by the Accounts Chamber of Azerbaijan

World.title: From Avlabari to parliament: new route for pro-European marches in Tbilisi. Video blog “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Another activist in Georgia convicted over insulting Facebook post: doctor Giorgi Akhobadze
World.content:
Georgia: activist Giorgi Akhobadze sentenced over FB post

On July 24, another person in Georgia was sentenced to administrative detention over a Facebook post containing profanity. Giorgi Akhobadze, a doctor and active participant in the country’s pro-European protests, was sentenced to 25 days in detention.

Giorgi Akhobadze

The ruling was issued by Tbilisi City Court. Giorgi Akhobadze did not attend the hearing.

He was represented by his lawyer, Mikheil Zakareishvili.

A few hours after the ruling, Akhobadze was arrested during a special police operation at his home.

Administrative proceedings against Giorgi Akhobadze were initiated following a complaint by the Interior Ministry’s recently established Department for Monitoring Hate Speech.

Akhobadze was sentenced over a Facebook post in which he used profanity to insult police officers who had testified against him in an earlier criminal case.

In December 2024, Akhobadze was returning home from a pro-European protest (which has continued in Georgia for nearly two years) when he was detained by police. He was searched and charged with purchasing and possessing drugs.

Akhobadze and his lawyers maintained that the drugs had been planted on him during the arrest. After an eight-month trial, he was acquitted and released from the courtroom in August 2025.

The Facebook post that led to his current administrative sentence referred specifically to the police officers whom Akhobadze accuses of planting the drugs.

“I stand by every word of that post,” Akhobadze told TV Pirveli after learning of the court’s decision, repeating the profane insult directed at the police officers.

“I’ll spend 25 days in a cell, get some rest, and if they think I’ll come out thinking differently, they’re very much mistaken,” Akhobadze said before his arrest.

On fines and detention for offensive social media posts

Giorgi Akhobadze is the second person to receive a jail sentence over comments posted on social media.

A few days earlier, on July 22, Tbilisi City Court sentenced well-known journalist and Formula TV host Vakho Sanaia to 14 days of administrative detention.

Sanaia had published a Facebook post containing profane and insulting language directed at senior officials of the ruling Georgian Dream party.

Administrative cases over opinions expressed in public are being initiated on the basis of reports filed by the Interior Ministry’s new Department for Monitoring Hate Speech, which began operating on June 1.

The department’s mandate is to monitor and proactively identify statements that violate human dignity, are insulting, or incite hatred, where they may constitute an administrative offence.

According to the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, between June 1 and July 2 the department identified 170 alleged administrative offences and referred 150 cases to court.

Courts have already ruled on 33 of those cases: 31 people were fined and two received verbal warnings. Most of those fined are activists taking part in the mass protests demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration.

News in Georgia

World.title: The 'strange, anomalous, anachronistic' Commonwealth Games
World.content:
"It's just a square."

That's the three-star review of Nelson Mandela Place in Glasgow by someone named Katie Nicholson on Google.

Katie isn't entirely wrong. A statue for the freedom fighter and former South African president is set to be unveiled in October, but for now there's not a whole lot to see at the spot, listed as a tourist attraction on Google Maps.

But the couple of street signs tacked to buildings on West George Street, not far from the city centre, sit as an elegant and understated middle finger to apartheid South Africa.

The South African consulate left this location for some reason. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 1986, while Mandela was still in prison on Robben Island, the Glasgow City Council changed the name of St George's Place to Nelson Mandela Place.

It meant that the South African consulate under the then-ruling National Party was forced not only to see the name of one of their chief antagonists as they entered the Stock Exchange building every day, but also send out correspondence bearing his name.

They opted to use a PO Box address before moving from the location in the early 90s.

After Mandela was released, he came to the city to thank the people for their solidarity in 1993.

Nelson Mandela thanked Glasgow in 1993, between being released from prison and becoming president of South Africa. (Getty Images: Chris Bacon/PA)

"While we were physically denied our freedom in the country of our birth, a city 6,000 miles away, and as renowned as Glasgow, refused to accept the legitimacy of the apartheid system, and declared us to be free."

That cry of freedom is as synonymous with the Scottish as it is with Mandela himself.

So, how does a celebration of this Commonwealth sit with a city and country that has always had a fraught relationship with oppressors generally and the English specifically?

ABE – Anyone but England

Andy Murray got to represent Scotland in the 2022 Battle of the Brits. (Getty Images: Mark Runnacles/Battle of the Brits)

Tennis great Andy Murray once perplexed some (read: Americans) less au fait with the unique rivalries within the UK when he was asked who he'd be supporting at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and replied: "Anyone but England."

Scotland isn't on its own in this regard.

In the Ashes last summer, Australia's injury-plagued men's Test team scored a triumphant professional 4-1 victory, but more Australian joy was derived from watching another epic capitulation of an England team that had declared itself the saviour of Test cricket, teaching us all how to entertain, if not actually win much of anything.

We cheered every humiliating faceplant and fumble at least as much as we celebrated the all-time world-class performances of Travis Head and Mitchell Starc.

The recently completed World Cup was another reminder of the collective glee shared by so many in watching England stumble.

The Sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

There's just something about the schadenfreude for Scots, Aussies and dozens of other nations in watching England lose.

Sure, you've got the Parthenon Sculptures and Rosetta Stone, but we've got Ellyse Perry and Steve Smith.

"There is this standard, reflexive idea of that they would prefer almost everybody to win other than England, as the most powerful part of the United Kingdom," Western Sydney University emeritus professor of culture and research David Rowe told ABC Sport.

"I think for some people it's serious, for some people it's just a bit of fun."

Loading Instagram content

There are jokes to be made, but also reflections on the very real subjugation that went on for centuries, and arguably only ended in 1997 when Hong Kong gained its independence.

This celebration of empire remains a peculiarity as calls grow to decolonise our language and our lives.

For a perfect example, the Parthenon Sculptures mentioned earlier are more famously known as the Elgin Marbles, named for the lord who nicked them from Greece and brought them back to Old Blighty at the start of the 19th century.

"I mean, the Commonwealth of Nations is, let's face it, anachronistic," Rowe said.

Flags that don't always get to fly wave prominently at the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"There are people who … don't know much about it or, if they schooled up on it, educated themselves about it, would realise that this is an anachronistic organisation based on an empire that no longer technically exists."

Although, many in the still-constituent Scotland would tell you the legacy, if not the actuality, of the empire remains in many ways.

"There are plenty of people in Scotland, including its leading Scottish National Party, who really would prefer to separate from the United Kingdom and who are mightily displeased by Brexit," said Rowe, a sports sociologist who consulted on the Glasgow Life team tasked with helping boost the city's standing on the global sporting stage.

"There are plenty of Scots who felt a greater affinity with the European Union than with England."

Strange, anomalous and anachronistic

A time machine is perhaps a fitting vehicle of entry of an event harking back to the past. (AAP: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

At the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were warmly welcomed by the packed crowd at Glasgow's Hydro, perhaps surprisingly considering the same crowd's hearty refrains of Flower of Scotland barely an hour later.

The Scottish anthem retells Robert the Bruce's legendary victory over King Edward II of England at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.

The thrust of the rousing choon, and Scotland's identity more broadly, is about how this small but mighty land of hard folk repelled the crown time and again on the back of sheer grit and pride.

So ingrained in their identity is sticking it to the English that, instead of tearing down statues of old royals and dignitaries like the Duke of Wellington, they have simply given up on removing the traffic cones placed on his head.

The Games have never opened like this – maybe they always should The 2026 Commonwealth Games are like no other that came before them and the opening ceremony was similarly unique in a way that will make it hard to go back.

And yet, twice in the past 12 years, Glasgow has gone out of its way to host what is correctly dubbed the Friendly Games, welcoming dozens of nations whose primary unifying theme is that they were once conquered by the "bastards" from that anthem.

"It does strike me as something of an irony that it's not that very long ago that Scotland had a referendum to sever its ties with the United Kingdom and the British Crown, and now it's hosting a Commonwealth Games," Rowe said.

"I think it's having a bit of fun, all the kilts and all the Scottish culture, reminding people that Scotland has its own identity and has not just been subsumed by the United Kingdom."

The Commonwealth Games has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

If you need more evidence of the strange bedfellows in effect, Rowe said you need only look at the event's original name.

It was called the British Empire Games from 1930 to 1950, the British Empire and Commonwealth Games until for the next four editions, and the British Commonwealth Games until 1972.

"So even more coded British," Rowe told ABC Sport.

"And it's a strange body in some ways, if you consider that it is a monument to colonialism and imperialism. And yet the members, most of whom were formerly under the jurisdiction of the British crown, were colonised, have now voluntarily agreed to join an organisation which was formed out of that imperial arrangement."

It also provides those in the British Isles a chance to beat England while representing Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man.

Scottish knights of the British Empire Chris Hoy and Andy Murray have won a combined 13 Olympic medals for Great Britain.

Duncan Scott is Team GB's most decorated Olympic swimmer, Mark Cavendish has won a world championship and Olympic silver with the Union Jack next to his name, but both turned around to beat the English while flying the Scottish saltire and Isle of Man's triskelion during the Commonwealth Games.

Duncan Scott has won more Olympic medals than any other British swimmer. (Supplied: Commonwealth Sport)

So how does the home crowd feel watching their sporting heroes flying those flags?

"I think it means more to them to compete for Scotland," one Glasgow local, Peter, told ABC Sport.

"You can see it in their faces when they do better. It does mean a lot more to them to represent their home country."

There's perhaps a hint of personal projection in this fan's assessment, as summed up by his mate, Pat.

"I would hope that it does [mean more] for them, because it would for me," he said.

Duncan Scott with the 2014 and 2026 mascots, the latter sporting a traffic cone for a horn. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

No amount of raucous crowd support or national pride is going to turn a 45-year-old bricklayer who's had a hot dog for breakfast into a 10-flat 100m runner. But at the tippy-top of sport, where the margins are at their finest, it's got to be worth a few hundredths of a second.

Angharad Evans swam for Team GB at the 2025 world championships in Singapore, missing the semifinals and finishing a brutal 18th overall in the 100m breaststroke as she went almost two seconds slower than her time at the national trials.

She carried those scars with her until she exorcised them with a spectacular victory at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre, winning her first international gold medal and thanking the crowd for getting her to the wall 0.12 of a second ahead of Aimee Canny.

Angharad Evans said the Tollcross crowd carried her for the final 10 metres. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"Scotland was there to witness that and that was a very, very special moment for me," she said.

"I thanked them because leading into competitions it's so easy for doubts and negative thoughts to play a part in my mindset leading up, and I walk out and they just really uplift me and give me the confidence I need and boost me up.

"They often talk about how proud they are of us bringing back gold medals and PBs, but I'm immensely proud to have the Tartan Army supporting me in the crowd.

"Wearing the blue and white, hearing the crowd, being part of Scotland just carries you to the end. I don't think I would have had the strength and the courage I did in the last 10 metres if I wasn't in the blue and white and didn't have that crowd behind me.

"They absolutely helped me get to the end and finish in first place. So it's a medal for me but it's also a medal for Scotland."

All that from an English-born 23-year-old who is still learning the words to that famous Scottish anthem.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Breaking: Origin Energy believes 900,000 customers' data accessed in breach
World.content:
Origin Energy believes the information of approximately 900,000 current and former customers was accessed during a recent data security breach.

The energy provider confirmed it first became aware of a potential security threat in early July but initially did not believe it credible.

The company has urged customers to be vigilant to scams and said specialist identity and cyber support services were available to affected customers.

"We have now completed the initial phase of our review into Origin's customer data security incident," Origin chief executive Frank Calabria said in a statement.

" To our customers, I am sorry. We don't take for granted the trust customers place in Origin and our safeguarding of their information. "

Customers whose information has been accessed will be contacted, Origin said, and customer support hours extended.

"We are working with cyber security and forensic specialists to ensure the incident is contained, and we've taken a number of steps to secure our system," Mr Calabria said, confirming Origin was working with government and other agencies, and continuing its review into the incident.

Threat investigated since early July

Origin said it had been reviewing a "potential security threat" since early July.

"We worked to confirm its credibility and potential impact; however, based on the information available, it was not assessed to be credible," the statement said.

"On 22 July, new information emerged that indicated a potential security incident may have occurred.

"We acted immediately, providing updates to the market and notifying our customers as a precaution."

Mr Calabria said it was a "criminal matter" that was now being investigated by the relevant authorities.

"Given this, we are constrained by the level of information we can provide about the incident at this time," the chief executive said.

Shares in Origin Energy were down more than 2 per cent by 11am AEST on Tuesday.

World.title: US and Iran in 'good talks' Trump says as support for war wanes
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says the United States is having "good talks" with Iran, and there is a chance of a deal over their conflict, but he warns that US strikes will resume if the negotiations fail to deliver.

Despite Mr Trump's optimism, Tehran appeared to quickly test the pause in the US military campaign, with Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq reporting drone attacks on Monday, local time.

Washington abruptly suspended a two-week campaign of air strikes on Iran on Saturday in Mr Trump's latest strategic U-turn in the five-month-old conflict.

"We're having good talks," Mr Trump said.

"I think there's a good chance that something could happen, and if it does, good, if it doesn't, we go back to doing what we were doing two days ago."

At a campaign rally in Michigan later the same day, Mr Trump said of Iran: "You can't bribe them. You've got to beat them, and we'll beat the hell out of them. But we'll see how it turns out. Right now, there are very friendly negotiations going on."

Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said that messages were still being passed between the sides through mediators and Iran had not forsaken diplomacy, but reports that it requested negotiations were "fabricated".

"This is not in our DNA," he said.

A senior Iranian official said on Sunday that Iran would halt its own attacks as long as Mr Trump's self-imposed ceasefire continued, Reuters reported.

Iran says it remains in control of the contested Strait of Hormuz. (ISNA via AP: Razieh Poudat)

Iran's central military command later on Monday accused the US of threatening vessels and oil tankers in its territorial waters and of "attempting to implement an illegal maritime blockade", which it said, "constitutes an escalation of the conflict in the region."

Saudi Arabia said it shot down drones aimed at petroleum targets, including in Riyadh. It said they had been launched from Iraq by Iran-backed armed groups, and it reserved the right to respond.

Separately, Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen said they had targeted the East-West Pipeline carrying oil to Saudi Arabia's main Red Sea port of Yanbu in retaliation for Saudi drone incursions.

Tehran also said it remained in control of the contested Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for global energy supplies, which Trump has demanded vessels be able to pass through freely.

Oil prices tumble

Public disapproval of the war has been weighing on Mr Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections in which they have to defend slim congressional majorities.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted over the weekend showed Mr Trump's approval rating ticking higher to 37 per cent, up three points from last month when it tied the lowest of his presidency.

However, just one in three Americans support the Iran war, the lowest Reuters/Ipsos reading since the conflict's early days, with most saying Mr Trump has failed to explain his goals.

The end of the US campaign after 13 successive nights of intensifying bombing and Mr Trump's remarks on talks sent oil prices tumbling.

Treasury war impact warning The federal government is yet to reveal whether it will extend the fuel excise discount, which is set to expire this week.

US Crude fell 8.21 per cent to $US81.98 ($117) a barrel, and Brent Crude to $US87.77 ($125) per barrel, down 9.31 per cent on the day.

Mr Trump's decision to suspend US attacks reflected advice from his military that the bombing had reached the limits of what it could achieve, according to several US media reports and a US official speaking to Reuters.

The US official said military commanders had advised Mr Trump they were running out of targets and that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had expressed concern over the depletion of air munitions, Reuters reported.

Mr Trump dismissed suggestions that the US faced munitions shortages, saying the military was rapidly rebuilding inventories depleted by shipments to Ukraine. He said he would like more of "the more sophisticated stuff".

Iran media says ships turned back

Iranian state media outlets cited an "informed source" as saying that Iran had turned around six "offending ships" on Monday that had attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without permission.

Mr Trump launched his renewed bombing campaign to punish Iran after Tehran fired on ships using a route promoted by the US, which told vessels to sail close to the coast of Oman.

The United States insists Iran should allow free travel through the Strait of Hormuz. (ISNA via AP: Razieh Poudat)

Iran says ships may pass only through a Hormuz channel that runs closer to its own coast, which it controls and where it intends to impose transit fees.

The two weeks of renewed US bombing killed scores in Iran and destroyed bridges and tunnels across the south as well as military targets.

Iran could mark 'end of an era' for US military Five months into a war Donald Trump said would last only weeks, the Iran conflict has so far cost the United States tens of billions of dollars.

Four US service members were killed in return fire against US bases in neighbouring states.

Iran also struck civilian infrastructure in Gulf countries, calling it retaliation for US strikes.

It remains unclear what leverage Washington can exert to break Iran's grip on the strait.

Washington and Tehran reached an agreement in June on a framework for talks meant to take place by the end of August to resolve major issues such as Iran's nuclear programme.

But they have disputed the meaning of the memorandum's language about the strait, with Washington insisting it requires Tehran to allow free travel, while Iran says it grants it the authority to supervise transit.

Reuters

World.title: Who is the man who wants to be Victoria's 50th premier?
World.content:
Only a short drive from Darryl Kerrigan's fictional home in the classic comedy film The Castle, Airport West has shaped the political story of Victoria's new premier.

Live updates: Jacinta Allan stands down, paving the way for Ben Carroll to become the Victorian premier.

Ben Carroll's parents built their family home in the north-western Melbourne suburb back in 1974, a year before Victoria's 50th premier was born — and two years before his future electorate of Niddrie was created.

The 51-year-old former lawyer and political adviser is now vying to take the leadership of the Victorian Labor Party, with premier Jacinta Allan resigning ahead of an expected spill motion.

Jacinta Allan and Ben Carroll when they became premier and deputy premier respectively following Daniel Andrews's resignation in September 2023 . (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Like the members of the cinematic Kerrigan clan, Carroll has previously spoken about how his parents established a proud family business under the Essendon Airport flight path.

"In addition to building their family home, Mum and Dad also started their own small business, G B K Electrics — the initials stand for Greg, Ben and Kay," Carroll said in his inaugural speech in parliament after being elected the Member for Niddrie in 2012.

"Raising a family and establishing a small business at the same time is hard work. Mum and Dad succeeded at both.

" When I was growing up, dinner time was characterised by Dad putting the telephone off the hook so the family could sit down and have a meal together without interruption. "

A 36-year-old Ben Carroll won pre-selection to run in the 2012 Niddrie by-election. (ABC News)

When The Castle first hit cinemas in 1997, a young Carroll was studying law at La Trobe University and working part-time as a checkout operator.

"I spent eight years at Kmart in Airport West, which greatly assisted me during my college and university years," he said in that first speech.

"At this time, I also joined the union covering the retail sector — that is, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association — and got a good understanding of the importance of unions in helping working people."

His union experience inspired him to become a political adviser under Steve Bracks, Victoria's Labor premier from 1999 to 2007.

Both Bracks and his successor John Brumby (who was premier from 2007 to 2010) have offered effusive praise of their former staffer.

Author and speechwriter Joel Deane said Carroll's leadership approach was likely to be more inspired by the Bracks-Brumby era, rather than a simple continuation of the Andrews-Allan years.

Deane wrote Catch and Kill about Labor's "golden four" of the 2000s — Bracks, Brumby, John Thwaites and Rob Hulls — and how they steered Victoria in a centre-left direction from the 1990s Kennett revolution.

"In some ways, Ben Carroll could be a throwback to the Bracks-Brumby era — socially progressive and fiscally conservative — but you never truly know until someone becomes leader," he said.

"You see some in politics, Labor and Liberal, and you don't know exactly what they stand for and wonder if it's just a career path.

"That's not the case with Ben. He's shown both a clear vision balanced with a pragmatic approach to progressive politics."

Former Victorian premier John Brumby on the day he was elected Labor leader to replace Steve Bracks in 2007. (Julian Smith: AAP)

Deane said Carroll's outlook has also been shaped by his work for federal MPs Bill Shorten and Stephen Conroy.

"Dan Andrews was a somewhat impulsive politician, always on the front foot and that certainly worked for many years. Bracks was inspired by Bob Hawke and in turn, Ben has been inspired by Bracks — a first-among-equals, chairperson type of approach of consultative government."

Carroll enters Victorian parliament

Carroll won the Niddrie Labor pre-selection battle in 2012 against future cabinet colleague Jaclyn Symes, who is now treasurer.

He then entered Victorian parliament after winning a by-election that was triggered by the resignation of Rob Hulls.

Ben Carroll, Jacinta Allan and Jaclyn Symes following a tour of Parkville Station during construction of the Metro Rail Tunnel in 2025. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

Monash University politics professor Zareh Ghazarian said Carroll has held more than a dozen portfolios since Labor returned to power at the 2014 state election, most notably Education since 2023.

He became deputy premier under Allan that same year, but not before aiming for the top job himself — a move that reportedly infuriated Andrews, Ghazarian said.

"Ben Carroll attracted some interest as a future leader in the final years of Dan Andrews as premier," he said.

"But he showed significant tenacity in trying to run for the premiership in 2023, despite Dan Andrews's firm, unwavering backing of Jacinta Allan as his successor.

"Andrews wanted Jacinta Allan as premier and Tim Pallas as deputy, but Ben Carroll managed to secure the deputy role and established himself as heir apparent.

"Having said that, Labor's transition from Andrews to Allan was reasonably seamless while the Victorian Liberals have cycled through John Pesutto, Brad Battin and Jess Wilson in less than four years.

"Now Labor will have to deal with the difficulties of leadership change."

Lessons for Carroll ahead of leadership

Carroll has faced several hurdles in the education portfolio, notably the inadvertent release of year 12 exam results and two statewide teacher strikes amid an ongoing pay dispute that showed no sign of being resolved.

Victoria's teachers and education staff have walked off the job twice as part of an unresolved pay dispute. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

But Ghazarian said law and order would be the main issue the new Labor leader would need to tackle before polling day, a factor the incoming premier has acknowledged.

"We know, as a 12-year-old government, we have to be the insurgent," Carroll said in early June.

"Focus on the fundamentals: community safety, growing the economy, being a state that’s open for business."

Ben Carroll has held multiple portfolios, and is currently education minister. (ABC News)

With social media and populism transforming campaigning in the 2020s, Deane said the Niddrie MP's suburban story could help Labor ahead of the November poll.

"Victoria was traditionally run out of Melbourne's eastern suburbs," he said.

"Bracks and Brumby changed that dynamic — they were very effective in securing Victoria's regional centres during the 2000s, whereas Dan Andrews saw the political potential of Melbourne's outer ring electorates.

" Labor's grip on the type of suburbs Ben represents — north, north-west — were Labor for generations but now stand a real chance of falling to an independent [or] minor party equivalent of what the teal movement has done to the Liberal Party. "

Victoria does not have a history of ditching a premier less than a year out from an election.

Lindsay Thompson was one of Victoria's longest serving parliamentarians but shortest serving premiers, spending only 307 days in the top job from 1981 to 1982. (ABC TV)

The exception is Lindsay Thompson in 1981 — like Mr Carroll, an education minister who was thrust into the top job to save the political day.

"Sometimes replacing a premier in an election year works," Ghazarian said.

"There's been examples interstate but, in Victoria, Lindsay Thompson lasted less than 12 months before losing the 1982 election to John Cain."

World.title: Jacinta Allan began her career as a star, but her premiership waned
World.content:
When Jacinta Allan was elected, aged 25, she became Victoria's youngest ever woman MP.

Ascending to the ministry when she was just 29, Allan has now spent half her life in Victoria's parliament.

Live updates: Jacinta Allan stands down, paving the way for Ben Carroll to become the Victorian premier.

But her stint in the state's top job quickly came to an end this morning, less than three years into her leadership.

Jacinta Allan was sworn in as premier by Victorian Governor Margaret Gardner in 2023. (ABC News)

Allan will not take Labor to an election, marking the end of a premiership marred by scandals that date back to the era of her predecessor, Daniel Andrews, and a collapse in successive polls.

Making history in Victorian parliament

Allan was elected the day before her 26th birthday, when she muscled out the Liberal Party to take Bendigo East in Jeff Kennett's shock election loss in 1999.

She was promoted to cabinet in the Bracks government in 2002.

Jacinta Allan gained her first ministry under then-premier Steve Bracks in 2002. (ABC News)

It was under Andrews that Allan took responsibility for what will be her legacy — transport infrastructure — having recently opened the Metro Tunnel and the West Gate Tunnel.

But this portfolio ultimately began to count against her.

Alleged criminality in the construction union has stalked her government.

Cost overruns on the infrastructure pipeline helped push the state's net debt to $167.8 billion.

Jacinta Allan was deputy premier under Daniel Andrews and held the transport infrastructure ministry during the Suburban Rail Loop, Airport Rail and Metro Tunnel projects. (AAP: Diego Fedele)

The opposition has also cast the Suburban Rail Loop as a burden on the state budget, to the detriment of the west and other services.

The Victorian Ombudsman in 2023 slammed "excessive secrecy" around the project.

Meanwhile, the Airport Rail has been repeatedly delayed.

Allan became Andrews's deputy premier in the lead-up to the 2022 election in a move that was unusual given they both came from the same faction, the Socialist Left, making her heir apparent.

A clutch of MPs from the party's Right faction moved to the Socialist Left not long after, assuring Allan became premier when Andrews resigned less than a year into his third term.

For a time, Victoria had both a female premier and opposition leader, with Jacinta Allan (in white) leading the government and Jess Wilson (standing, on the opposite side of the table from Ms Allan) the Liberal leader. (ABC News)

Allan became Victoria's 49th premier in September, 2023, describing the role as a "deep honour and a privilege".

She staked her leadership on housing affordability and residential development, declaring she wanted to be the premier that got millennials into homes.

But she was criticised internally for failing to differentiate her leadership from that of Andrews, who had led the state for more than nine years including the COVID-19 era.

Allan raised in Labor

Allan lives with her husband Yorick and their two children on a rural property south of Bendigo, the regional city she grew up in, having hailed from a prominent local Labor family.

Her grandfather Bill was president of the Bendigo Trades Hall.

In May, she told Labor faithful how her father Peter was made redundant in the early 90s when the State Electricity Commission (SEC) was privatised under Kennett.

Jacinta Allan and her father Peter at their Bendigo house in the early 1990s. (Supplied: Victorian Premier's office)

She joined the party when she was 19, studied arts at La Trobe University's Bendigo campus and, in 1997, led a campaign to stop a lap dancing bar from opening.

Otherwise, she worked for Labor MPs.

Then she entered parliament herself.

Jacinta Allan (centre) became the youngest female MP in Victorian history after being elected to the seat of Bendigo East in 1999. (ABC News)

In her inaugural speech to parliament in 1999, Ms Allan wore two brooches.

One was a poppet head — a logo for her hometown — which served as a totem of her dedication to the people of Bendigo.

The other was an Emily's List brooch, the Labor women support network that was established by Joan Kirner, Victoria's only other female premier.

On the day she became premier, Allan was emotional as she described the late Kirner as a mentor, and reflected on following in her footsteps.

"I hope ... it says to young women, older women, women from across different backgrounds of all parts of the state that leadership takes on different shapes and sizes," she said at the time.

Like Kirner, the outgoing premier has served in the role, but has missed her chance to win an election in her own right.

World.title: Jacinta Allan steps aside as Victorian premier
World.content:
Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan will resign from the top job, paving the way for her deputy Ben Carroll to become the state's next leader.

Ms Allan made the announcement this morning, ahead of an expected spill motion she was tipped to lose.

The meeting came after a whirlwind 24 hours, which saw Ms Allan write to Labor's state secretary to confirm she would contest any leadership ballot, and Mr Carroll say he had been approached to launch a challenge.

Speaking at parliament this morning, the outgoing premier said she would give her unqualified support to Mr Carroll should he put his hand up.

"I am making this decision because it is the right thing by the Labor Party and the Victorian people," she said.

"I was prepared to put my record and my plan to a ballot of members as our rules allow.

"I believe I would have won. But doing so this close to an election takes up valuable resources, including the most precious … one, time.

" At the end of the day, I am and always have been a team player. "

Ms Allan has led Victoria since she replaced Daniel Andrews in 2023.

Her term has been overshadowed by scandals that have followed her from the Andrews era, most notably allegations of corruption in the state's Big Build construction program.

Ms Allan was the state's youngest-ever female MP when she was elected on the eve of her 26th birthday in 1999, and only the second woman to hold the top job.

Speaking this morning, she encouraged more women to enter politics.

"Please don't look at what I have experienced this week and think, 'Stuff that. I don't want to be involved,'" she said.

"Look at the support I've experienced over my career, and think, 'I can make a difference here too.'"

Ms Allan was greeted by a round of applause as she entered the Labor party room after her speech.

She did not stop to take questions.

The caucus meeting is continuing this morning.

World.title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
World.content:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Scotland's Archie Goodburn did not win a medal, but he has won the respect of everyone as he competes in Glasgow while dealing with three brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport," they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final, but outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"Where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Abigail Roper won bronze first, but sister Emily got her own an hour or so later. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But, given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games, two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her sister, who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow, but everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media, Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

Loading...

All it takes is one look at the comment section to see people on either side of the heated debate: from supporters saying shorter dresses are easier to play in, to those who reckon the Diamonds look "silly".

Responding to haters, Bruce says it's a "good thing we're strong … fit, and we train hard".

I mean, it's not like they aren't wearing shorts under the dress... (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

5. Mollie O'Callaghan pulls out of the backstroke

Mollie O'Callaghan has withdrawn from the 50m backstroke. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Coming into this Commonwealth Games, Mollie O'Callaghan revealed she was managing a back injury, and it cost her a chance in her backup event, the 50m backstroke.

The 22-year-old was worried that she might not even be able to compete in Glasgow after scans revealed stress fractures and bone bruising on her lumbar spine.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

World.title: Singer D4vd to stand trial for allegedly killing and dismembering 14yo girl
World.content:
Content warning: this story involves the death of a minor, allegations of sexual abuse of a child and graphic violent details.

Singer D4vd will stand trial charged with killing and dismembering 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez, who authorities say had threatened to expose their sexual relationship.

Los Angeles Judge Charlaine Olmedo decided that the evidence that prosecutors presented at a five-day preliminary hearing provided probable cause for a trial on charges of murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains.

D4vd, the 21-year-old singer born David Burke whose career was steeply rising before the allegations emerged, has pleaded not guilty.

Celeste Rivas Hernandez's dismembered body was found in D4vd's car. (AP: Damian Dovarganes)

Held without bail

"The people have met their burden on all counts," Justice Olmedo said.

She ordered that Mr Burke continue to be held without bail.

US singer D4vd pleads not guilty to murdering 14yo girl found in his Tesla The 21-year-old, who rose to fame after going viral on TikTok, has pleaded not guilty to a murder charge of a 14-year-old whose dismembered body was found in his seemingly abandoned Tesla.

Justice Olmedo emphasised that the probable cause standard for a preliminary hearing like this is much lower than the threshold at trial.

However, prosecutors asserted that the evidence was overwhelming.

"Based on the mountains of evidence presented," Deputy District Attorney Beth Silverman said, "all of the allegations have been proved way beyond the standard required".

Mr Burke had no visible reaction to the decision and the defence team declined to comment outside court.

Prosecutors wrapped up their case by giving a moment-by-moment account of Celeste's last night, showing that, after a stream of text messages with Mr Burke, her phone went permanently silent when she arrived at his home.

As she neared his Hollywood home shortly after 10am on April 23, 2025, in an Uber he had sent to pick her up, she sent her final text: "girly pop i'm almost there open ur door if ur home".

Prosecutors allege Mr Burke stabbed her to death when she came through the door.

Fighting via text messages

D4vd has pleaded not guilty but is being held in custody. (AP: Bill Robles)

The night before, the two argued via text about his relationship with a woman.

Celeste sent him an angry and profane text saying she would tell her dad so many lies about him and "i will end ur career and ur life".

Los Angeles Police detective Corey Farrell, under questioning from the prosecution, read the texts that were obtained from warrants on Mr Burke's iPhone and iCloud accounts.

After the final witness on Monday, the defence argued that the evidence was insufficient and the murder charge should be dismissed.

d4vd charged with first degree murder and sexual acts against a minor d4vd was arrested in relation to the murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez, whose body was found in his abandoned car in late 2025.

"There's no evidence that Mr Burke harboured a deliberate intent to kill Miss Hernandez," Mr Burke's attorney Marilyn Bednarski said.

She said the communications between Mr Burke and Celeste showed "no threat, no evidence of a history of violence" and that he had "the opposite of homicidal malice" toward her.

She argued that a medical examiner ruling that her death was a homicide from two puncture wounds was too vague and inconclusive to be evidence of murder.

The defence did not directly give an alternative theory on how she died and was not required to.

Mr Burke's legal team showed several other texts from Celeste threatening him about their relationship, and saying she would go to his mother, talk to his friends and "leak" information about them.

No suggestion of legal action

Under questioning from defence lawyer Blair Berk, Detective Farrell said he saw no indication that she ever threatened to go to police or pursue any legal action against him.

The defence also established that Celeste had asked seven times to come to see Mr Burke in the days before her death, and he reluctantly agreed only after she demanded it, and that she had threatened to kill him and to mutilate him.

D4vd released his first full-length album, Withered, two days after authorities say Celeste was killed. (AP: Jordan Strauss/Invision)

Mr Burke's lawyers argued that all of the malice had come from Celeste.

Ms Silverman told the judge that "the defence tried numerous times throughout these proceedings to dirty up the victim" despite her being a child.

The detective also said under questioning from Ms Berk that the parents of both Mr Burke and Celeste knew about their relationship, that he had attended church with members of her family and that her parents had given their consent for her to go to London with him for a week.

After her phone went silent, Mr Burke sent Celeste several other messages that night asking where she was and expressing concern.

Prosecutors allege that those messages were sent as cover after he had killed her.

Body found in Tesla five months after death

Prosecutors allege Mr Burke dismembered Celeste's body in his garage.

A police analyst testified earlier in the hearing that samples pulled from apparent blood stains there matched her DNA.

Her body was found in a Tesla registered to him nearly five months later.

Lawyers for D4vd argued that the prosecution had not met the threshold for murder, but the judge disagreed. (Reuters: Arafat Barbakh)

In earlier testimony, Detective Farrell recounted dozens of sexually explicit photos of Mr Burke and Celeste and years of text messages that described the same things, along with conversations that indicated she had gotten an abortion in 2024 at 13 after he got her pregnant.

Detective Farrell described the photos that could not be shown in court, material so graphic that it left Celeste's mother in tears and prompted both parents to leave the courtroom on Friday.

They were back in court on Monday.

D4vd (pronounced "David") became an online musical phenomenon as a teen with a blend of indie rock, R&B and lo-fi pop.

He had huge followings on TikTok, SoundCloud and Spotify, where his top songs, including his 2022 breakthrough Romantic Homicide, have more than a billion plays.

In 2024, he played the Coachella music festival and released his first full-length album, Withered, two days after authorities say Celeste was killed.

AP

World.title: EV industry fights back against copper thieves targeting public chargers
World.content:
EnvironmentSustainabilityElectric vehicles EV industry fights back against copper thieves targeting public chargers Caitlin Fitzsimmons July 28, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thieves are chopping off public electric vehicle chargers to steal the copper – and getting caught. As scrap metal prices have soared, copper theft has too, and the criminals are moving beyond their traditional targets of rail infrastructure, telecommunications and building sites. Copper wires allegedly found at the arrest of a man in the Newcastle area. NSW Police “EV chargers are the new frontier in an old crime,” said Geoff Brady, chief operating officer at Evie Networks. In Victoria, there were 2592 incidents of copper and other scrap metal theft in 2025, up from 998 in 2016, the state’s Crime Statistics Agency said. In NSW there were 879 incidents specifically of copper theft, up from 612 in 2019, according to the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research.



Brady said copper thieves were increasingly getting caught because of security measures such as cameras and cooperation between competitors to crack down on vandalism. “Cable theft and vandalism is affecting every operator, and we’re no different,” Brady said. “At Evie, we’ve moved from reactive replacement of vandalised cables to layered prevention, and we’re working as an industry to move in that direction together.” At sites identified as vulnerable, Brady said, the company improved lighting and camera coverage, introduced protective cable sleeves and on-site security. Electric charging companies were sharing information on sites that have been hit, camera footage of incidents and police case incident numbers, he said. As a result, the criminals were often getting caught.



Earlier this month NSW Police arrested a man in the Newcastle area and charged him with 10 counts of stealing and 11 counts of destroying or damaging property, as well as drug and driving offences. He was alleged to have damaged EV charging stations in the Newcastle-Hunter region and Central Coast in June, from as far north as Raymond Terrace to Gosford and Erina in the south. Components of EV chargers allegedly found at the arrest of a man in the Newcastle area. NSW Police Police allegedly located and seized 17 EV charging handles (plugs), cutting tools, a taser and several large bags of stripped cables. The price of copper on the London Metal Exchange was $US13,732.50 a tonne on Tuesday, or $US13.73 ($19.62) a kilogram. Brady said a typical DC charger cable would contain two to four kilos of copper, meaning it was not a terribly lucrative crime. “The outcome in Raymond Terrace is great because it shows that this is a simple crime – they’re after a little bit of copper – and it’s just not worth it,” Brady said.



“The customer experience is the casualty in all of this because the copper value is small, but the impact is that people can’t charge when they need to charge because the site is offline for a period of time.” Brady said Evie Networks had also experienced spates of copper theft in western Melbourne and Toowoomba in Queensland, which led to successful arrests. Some public EV chargers, such as the EVX units on power poles, do not have a DC charging cable attached, but rely on the driver to bring an AC charger with them.
