World.title: Meet the man facing off one of his party’s biggest-ever threats
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If opposition leader is the most unenviable job in politics, then Nationals leader in opposition has to be a close second. Gurmesh Singh, a Coffs Harbour macadamia and blueberry farmer-turned-politician, was elevated to that position in November last year. Along with Liberal leader Kellie Sloane, who gained office only days later, he became a newly minted political leader just weeks before the country’s worst-ever terror attack. Now he’s the man tasked with saving his party’s regional NSW seats from a One Nation avalanche at next year’s election. He’s also the first Sikh elected to an Australian parliament and the first Sikh leader of a major party. He has a rich family history, and a portrait of Singh’s great-grandfather is plastered on walls around the country. When we sit down to lunch on a rainy Sydney Tuesday, One Nation has been surging in the polls, and most of the talk on Macquarie Street about the Nationals often concludes with something like “they’re in major trouble”. I know it’s probably not what Singh wants me to talk about but I can’t help but ask how he feels about Pauline Hanson’s surge in popularity and her calls for a monoculture, given his own background. “I grew up in the ’80s and ’90s in what we would describe as Australian culture, in what some of these people are saying they’d like us to be,” he says. “It’s a good culture that I would also like to live in again. “I look at myself [and my family] – we’ve got a different ethnicity, obviously we have different religious beliefs, and we might have slightly different festivals and religious celebrations, but I think you can do that while still being uniquely Australian as well, and I think that’s the more mature conversation that we should be having … how do we – and you can – do both.”



“I think what people are actually looking for is what we had back then. That’s safer streets, that was an economy that meant you could have a house with one income, it meant kids who were out on their bikes, meant you could go to the beach on a weekend – like, these are the things that people remember … It’s actually things that government should be striving for, right?” The most recent Resolve Political Monitor conducted over June and July found support for the Coalition at the lowest in recent memory, down to 23 per cent and trailing behind One Nation, which sat at 25 per cent despite not yet having a single endorsed candidate for the NSW election. Singh says he believes the tides will turn in the time between now and the March poll, and that Coalition policies like a reduction in payroll tax, released earlier than usual in this election cycle, will get people back on board with the core Nationals principles of smaller governments and better infrastructure for the bush. Related Article Editorial

Resolve Political Monitor NSW voters revolt against major parties The Herald's View Editorial We’re lunching at Matt Moran’s Chophouse in Sydney’s CBD, a sophisticated steak house a short walk from Parliament House where Singh is familiar with the menu. He has a secret passion for hot chips, a love so deep that in his younger years he tried his hand at building an online map of his best reviewed offerings in Sydney. The chips at Chophouse and Bondi’s Hotel Ravesis are up there among the best, he says, but so are those from parliament’s Long Bell Cafe. (I share this enthusiasm and am all too familiar with the salty, crunchy goodness, given the kitchen is mere steps from the Herald’s parliament office.) Another favourite is the KFC chip, which, he says, tastes best on a late-Thursday-night sitting day. So of course we share a bowl of chips. He also selects the 200g eye fillet, and I’m quick to order the same, plus we get a side of charred sweetcorn with fermented chilli butter. Singh asks for no cheese on the corn; he’s so averse to the stuff that even the smell of melted cheese is enough to make him unwell.



Our plates are identical other than the sauce: peppercorn for Singh and mushroom for me. Our waiter recommends a 2018 Barossa Valley shiraz before I get a chance to open the wine list. I’m more of a beer drinker and am always anxious about choosing the wrong wine, so I’m relieved to leave it in our waiter’s hands. The hot chips at Chophouse. Sam Mooy Singh teams chips with eye fillet. Sam Mooy Charred sweetcorn completes the meal. Sam Mooy Singh is a “saltwater Nat”, lingo for Nationals MPs with coastal electorates, as opposed to their freshwater colleagues. His family first settled in Australia when his great-grandfather Bella Singh arrived in Cairns from Punjab in the 1890s and went to Harwood Island in the Clarence River region. Singh excitedly tells me he’s spoken with John Howard about this – his great-grandfather just happened to live in the small country town at the same time as Howard’s grandfather. I’ve seen pictures of Singh’s great-grandfather long before we meet for lunch. His photograph is one of several used by artist Peter Drew for his famous “Aussie” series, taken from documents found in the National Archives of Bella Singh’s exemption from the White Australia policy language test. Getting in contact with the artist led Singh to spend hours poring over archives, finding troves of documents, some of which he is still yet to fully examine.



After World War II, Bella moved to the Coffs Harbour area to work and, a century later, that’s the electorate his great-grandson represents in the NSW state parliament. Trying to win back conservative voters drawn to the anti-immigration rhetoric of One Nation without alienating the diverse members of his own electorate (Woolgoolga has a significant population of Indian heritage and is home to Australia’s first Sikh temple) will be a difficult tightrope to walk. The political fight ahead will test his leadership. Bella Singh, Gurmesh Singh’s great-grandfather, is featured on a well-known series of posters. Peter Drew Singh finds respite from the pressure of NSW politics in what sounds to me like the grimmest of situations. He’s an RFS volunteer, who enlisted after the Black Summer bushfires, but he tells me that, rather than fighting fires, most of his work has been supporting people on the worst days of their lives. Not as the boss but as the one who follows orders. “It’s not something I’ve sought to promote necessarily but plenty of people have seen me out on the fires or at car accidents and stuff, and sometimes people were a little bit surprised to see me holding a Stop/Go sign or sweeping glass off the road or rolling up a pipe or whatever it is that we’re called to do on that day. “I find it pretty rewarding. Given that I’m fairly junior in the brigade, I go there and take orders.”



One of the most confronting scenes he has responded to happened over Christmas while at a family dinner at a local beach. The brigade got a call and so Singh left the venue and headed two beaches over. A man had suffered a medical episode in the water and drowned. Paramedics were trying to resuscitate him. As an RFS volunteer his job wasn’t to be the hero but to help retrieve supplies from the ambulance as others worked to save the man’s life. “That’s often what you’re confronted with rather than actual fire, although we’ve had some hairy fires as well.” For the man with a title like NSW Nationals leader, his path to politics was fairly cosmopolitan. He attended UNSW and worked in a newsagent’s in Bondi. Straight out of university, Singh went to work for Qantas, in the marketing team, before working in software. He found a passion for politics after moving back home to farming. Singh has been at the scene of local tragedies as a member of the RFS. Sam Mooy While previous media reporting has painted Singh as a humble blueberry and macadamia farmer, that’s only part of the story. He was actually director of the powerful blueberry farmers co-op Oz Group in Woolgoolga, and was vice president of the Australian Blueberry Growers’ Association. The blueberry industry’s rapid expansion on the Mid North Coast hasn’t been without controversy, drawing concerns around pesticide use and lack of planning oversight. Dealing with land-use conflicts in horticulture and running the co-op was how Singh got interested in state politics. “Even liaising with our local council, who had a couple of Greens councillors, their solution was to add more regulation when they weren’t satisfied the existing regulation were being followed.

World.title: ‘Rattled homes and sleep loss’: Inside Sydney bowlo’s noise war with its neighbours
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Rattled homes and sleep loss’: Inside Sydney bowlo’s noise war with its neighbours David Barwell July 28, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A three-year noise battle between an eastern suburbs bowling club and neighbouring residents has come to a head after nearby home owners complained that loud music, birthday parties, late-night functions and disorderly patrons were disrupting life in one of Sydney’s most sought-after suburbs. Liquor & Gaming NSW has issued Diamond Bay Bowling Club in Vaucluse with a formal warning over noise impacts from live entertainment and patron activity, but stopped short of imposing licence sanctions, ruling the legal threshold for an “unreasonable and serious disturbance” had not been met. Liquor & Gaming NSW has handed down a decision after an investigation into noise complaints relating to the bowling club. James Brickwood The dispute has become the first major test of the NSW government’s vibrancy reforms, which were designed to strengthen the state’s live music and hospitality sectors by giving greater protection to established venues facing complaints from residents. The ruling follows an 18-month investigation triggered by 57 official complaints lodged since 2023 by one primary complainant, supported by eight neighbouring residents. The complaints alleged amplified music, DJs, live bands, bass vibrations and patron noise from weekend functions regularly disrupted sleep and “caused vibration to nearby residential buildings and infrastructure”.



Residents claimed the club had changed since the pandemic, evolving from a traditional community bowling club into an entertainment venue hosting DJ nights, live music, private functions and outdoor events that attracted younger crowds, forcing neighbours to keep windows shut, avoid outdoor areas and sleep with earplugs. The club, which has operated on Old South Head Road since 1963 and typically trades until 10pm on weekends, strongly rejected those claims and argued the “order of occupancy” principle was firmly in its favour, given it had been operating in the area for decades before the lead complainant moved nearby about five years ago. Liquor and Gaming NSW found that the venue had “not seriously disturbed the quiet and good order of the neighbourhood.” James Brickwood The club’s general manager Neve Storey said the club had spent more than $200,000 on noise mitigation measures after becoming aware of the complaints, including installing double-glazed windows, acoustic treatments, sound barriers, building upgrades and introducing operational changes designed to reduce impacts on neighbours. “We ran in the red for two years to put money into the club to do everything we could to address the concerns that were raised,” she said. “We’re not a big RSL or a major club – it’s been very traumatic for a little club, the amount of scrutiny we’ve been under.”



Regulatory inspections of the venue revealed mixed findings. Liquor & Gaming NSW conducted multiple covert observations of the venue, including inspections in late 2024 when officers found intoxicated patrons stumbling as they left the club, while others were seen running across the bowling greens, yelling, late at night. The venue was also subject to separate assessments by Waverley Council environmental health officers, who concluded amplified music and patron noise were likely to be offensive inside nearby homes when windows were open. However, Eastern Suburbs Police reached a different view, reporting that while music was audible from nearby locations, noise levels were comparable to those generated by other licensed venues in Sydney’s east and were not considered offensive. In its submissions to the regulator, the bowling club argued one neighbour had been responsible for co-ordinating many of the complaints and had encouraged other residents to lodge reports with authorities.



Related Article Opinion

City life If you buy a house near a pub, don’t complain about the noise Elizabeth Barry Sydney writer The club also rejected suggestions it had become a nightclub, arguing it had expanded its food, beverage and entertainment offerings simply to remain financially viable and had never marketed itself as a dance venue targeting an 18-to-25-year-old demographic. Storey said responding to the investigation had come at a significant financial and emotional cost through legal fees, consultant reports and staff resources. “At one point we felt like we’d become the fun police, shushing customers at 9.30pm on a Saturday just so we didn’t inflame the situation any further,” she said. “We’ve never had an alcohol-related incident. We’ve never had violence. We’ve never had sexual misconduct. How could we, as a small bowling club in Vaucluse, be the most complained-about club in NSW?”



Liquor & Gaming NSW acting director of hospitality and gaming operations Darren Duke, in his ruling, concluded the complaint could not be upheld under the legal framework introduced through the vibrancy reforms, which established a higher threshold for regulatory action against long-established venues. NSW Night-time Economy Minister John Graham said the decision was in line with laws designed to protect entertainment venues from noise complaints. Michael Quelch While declining to impose additional licence conditions or other sanctions, Duke issued the club with a formal warning, saying it was intended “to formally remind the club of its obligations to minimise disturbance and ensure the operation of the club does not detract from the amenity of the surrounding community”. NSW Night-time Economy Minister John Graham said the ruling demonstrated the intent of the government’s reforms. “This ruling proves the days of moving in next to an established venue and complaining until it gets closed down are coming to an end,” Graham said.



“While this is a good outcome, this was a costly process for the venue, which shows there is still more work to be done to cut red tape and help our venues survive.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The omission in Jacinta Allan’s departing statement as premier
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election The omission in Jacinta Allan’s departing statement as premier Kieran Rooney Updated July 28, 2026 — 11:24am ,first published 11:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Follow live updates: ALP leadership showdown As Jacinta Allan bid farewell to the job she has held for the past 1036 days, she used her final speech as Victoria’s premier to highlight her government’s achievements: tougher bail laws, a budget back in surplus, free public transport and improvements in women’s health. But as she emphasised Labor’s record upgrading the state’s infrastructure, Allan remained defiant about the corruption scandal that has plagued those same Big Build projects, even as some of her colleagues publicly moved to call for a royal commission. Loading “We’ve removed 92 level crossings, finished the West Gate Tunnel. We’re building the North East Link and the Suburban Rail Loop, and then there’s the Metro Tunnel,” she told reporters.



“Not too many people get to see a project of this size and scale through from the start to the end. I am so goddamn proud of it.” Ben Carroll, who is set to be Victoria’s new premier, is expected to announce a royal commission into the scandal surrounding the Big Build and the CFMEU as one of his first acts. Several Labor ministers pressed for such an inquiry during a tense cabinet meeting on Monday, and then did so publicly on Tuesday morning before Allan’s resignation. Jacinta Allan during her final press conference on Tuesday. Getty Images In her statement to reporters, Allan did not mention the revelations in The Age that the scandal-plagued construction union inflated the cost of the government’s signature projects, delayed construction, and employed criminals, including bikies, to work on them. Forced from office in large part because of her refusal to call a royal commission into the Building Bad scandal, Allan intimated that Victorians were benefiting from completed projects without focusing on the corrupt conduct on building sites during their construction.

World.title: Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline
World.content:
MoneySavingBudgeting Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline Nina Hendy July 28, 2026 — 11:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Living at home with her parents well into her 20s has resulted in a huge financial saving that has helped 25-year-old Chloe Henry get ahead in life and also helped the communications professional save for her first overseas holiday. Henry doesn’t pay any rent to her parents, instead contributing by buying some groceries and helping with the housework. Other than that, her income is hers to do with as she pleases. Communications professional Chloe Henry says she hopes to take her parents on a holiday to thank them for letting her live at home. “I’m lucky that my parents have allowed me to stay at home for as long as I want and that they’re happy to have me there. I’m off to Japan in September for my birthday, and I can’t wait,” she says. Each morning, she travels via public transport from Berwick into Melbourne, a journey that takes 90 minutes each way. But the sacrifice has been worth it, enabling her savings to quietly grow.



“Living at home means I’m not feeling like I’m under a price crunch. I have a savings goal in mind, and I’ve been able to reach that goal a lot faster,” she says. But the future of life on her own isn’t entirely clear. The hope is that one day, she could be in a strong enough position to be able to rent with her partner, who is still in university. “I’m pretty pessimistic about the housing market and being able to save up to move out or put a deposit on a home. A lot of my friends still live at home and don’t have plans to move out anytime soon either.” Staying put Henry is not alone. New research from AMP shows that for many, support is no longer just about the bank of mum and dad, it’s also about the house of mum and dad, with extended families open to sharing housing, costs and care in more practical ways.



The shift has been driven mostly by younger singles as housing affordability, rate increases and cost of living pressures combine to make living alone increasingly unaffordable. Editor's pick Opinion

Housing affordability A new type of class divide is emerging – and property is to blame Victoria Devine Money columnist The growing number of shared living arrangements is in direct response to the constant rise in living costs, which shows no sign of easing. While common in some cultures, multi-generational living isn’t the norm in Australia. But what started during the pandemic as a way to save money as housing costs bolted has now become a way of life for many. At a time when so many people are seeking financial stability, it’s understandable that living with a flatmate could be undesirable for some given that factors outside their control – such as job losses or a large unexpected bill – could impact on their ability to cover rent.



Generational shift Ben Hillier, general manager of retirement solutions at AMP. Natalie Boog AMP’s research found that 68 per cent of 20- to 39-year-olds support multi-generational living, but fewer than two in five people aged 65 and over do. This points to a generational shift in expectations around independence and home ownership. “As housing pressures intensify and Australia becomes increasingly multicultural, younger Australians are rethinking what the ‘Australian dream’ looks like,” explains Ben Hillier, AMP’s director of retirement. “This shift also tells us something important about confidence for retirement, which in Australia has long been tied to home ownership. Alongside super, Australians’ sense of financial security will increasingly be shaped by the household around them – how families live, what support they can provide one another and how costs and care are shared.”



Mortgage brokers have noticed the change in property demand too as they’re asked to help families find homes that will accommodate extended family members, says Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton of Two Red Shoes. “Our job as brokers is no longer just about securing a rate – it’s about providing creative pathways, whether it’s navigating generational wealth when buying property, or helping families explore shared ownership,” she says. As for Henry, she admits she doesn’t have all the answers about housing in the future, but does hope that one day she can thank her parents for letting her stay home well into her 20s. “Maybe I can pay for them to take a holiday one day,” she says. World.title: Melbourne businessman found guilty of rape, but his name remains a secret
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCourts Melbourne businessman found guilty of rape, but his name remains a secret Erin Pearson July 28, 2026 — 11:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A high-profile Melbourne businessman has been found guilty of raping a 27-year-old personal assistant. The man, who cannot be named due to a suppression order preventing his identity from being released, had been on trial for rape and sexual assault in the County Court of Victoria since July 8. The man cannot be named as his lawyers argue it could be detrimental to him. Tamara Voninski The prosecution had alleged the much older man had offered the young woman work, including on his autobiography, when she attended his “larger than life” converted warehouse to discuss the role. It was alleged that after a night of drinking and consuming cocaine the man raped the woman.



Related Article Courts Rape trial begins for Melbourne man who cannot be named Defence barrister Dermot Dann, KC, maintained his client was innocent and urged the jury to find the complainant was an unreliable witness who had a financial motive to lie. “She’s like a fiction writer,” Dann said. “She was telling [the accused man] this night that she loved him for his spirit. “What the prosecution has served up to you is a horrible mixture of lies, fabrications, recent inventions, inconsistencies and evidence that had been proved to be demonstrably false.



“This case is a powerful demonstration that there are cases when complainants make false evidence, false statements. This is one of those cases.” However on Tuesday, a jury of nine women and three men rejected the defence argument and found the man guilty after three days of deliberations. The accused had pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of rape. The rapist was immediately taken into custody with the prosecution applying to revoke his bail minutes after the three guilty verdicts were returned because of the likelihood the man would ultimately be sentenced to an immediate term of imprisonment. During the trial, the court heard the pair met in 2022 after the woman contacted him to express interest in working for him while she studied. While the job was initially unavailable, when it opened up the student was told she could help work on projects including his autobiography and a film script.



Prosecutor Matthew Fisher said an Uber was sent to collect the woman and bring her to the man’s house to discuss the employment position. Related Article Courts Doctor charged with filming naked pool patrons wins three-month secrecy order But, when she arrived he attempted to kiss her, prompting her to reply, “If I let you do this, if I let you f--- me, you’ll never respect me as your employee. I don’t want that to be the role I play in your life. I’ll never want to have sex with you.” The woman quit months later before reconnecting with the man in March 2023 when she was again offered work on his book. When she visited the man’s home to discuss the project days later, the jury were told the two allegedly consumed wine and cocaine and watched television at an associate’s home in South Melbourne.



On their return to his home, the prosecution alleges the woman began to cry and speak of the breakdown of a recent relationship when the accused man pulled her from a lounge and onto his bed, telling her he’d take care of her. “You’re so sexy, I can’t stop, I need your help to sleep, help me, I need to,” he allegedly said. The woman, who gave evidence for more than a week, said she was then raped before she punched the man in the nose and was told to leave. The woman went to a spare room where she texted her mother, who called the police. The man will face a plea hearing at a later date.



Last month, this masthead revealed that almost 500 suppression orders in various forms were issued in Victorian courts last year, with the highest number being issued on safety grounds, including for mental health reasons. Of those suppression orders granted, 247 were made in the County Court. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘Completely unprecedented’: Europe races to fight out-of-control blazes ahead of new heatwave
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires ‘Completely unprecedented’: Europe races to fight out-of-control blazes ahead of new heatwave David Crowe Updated July 28, 2026 — 11:01am ,first published July 28, 2026 — 8:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has warned of more devastating wildfires across Europe, with climate change making heatwaves more frequent, as emergency crews raced to contain blazes in Spain and France before temperatures soar later this week. Sanchez pledged more funding for fire shelters ahead of a meeting of national ministers that is tipped to commit to new measures on climate change during a growing debate on the country’s worst wildfires in decades. Burnt vehicles in a parking yard in Chapinería, Spain, on Monday. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez A firefighter monitors flames in La Adrada, in Spain’s Avila province. Anadolu via Getty Images The Spanish fires appeared to slow on Monday after spreading over the weekend in the Avila province west of Madrid, but a fire near Valencia in the south of the country continued to burn out of control.



In south-western France, a vast fire heading toward Bordeaux slowed as winds died down, but government officials warned of mounting risks when temperatures reach 39 degrees in the coming days. French authorities have evacuated about 220,000 people, including local residents and people on holiday, while Spanish authorities have told some 100,000 people to leave their homes or seek shelter. A charred bicycle in Lège-Cap-Ferret, outside Bordeaux, France. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva Firefighters work to suppress a blaze near Lacanau, France, on Monday. AP Photo/Baz Ratner Sanchez visited La Vall d’Uixo in Castellon province, north of Valencia, to step up his calls for a “state pact” across governments to do more to address climate change.



“What we’re experiencing isn’t a succession of isolated events,” he said. “It’s the most painful expression of a climate emergency ​that is making sixth-generation wildfires more ferocious, heatwaves more frequent, and our territory more vulnerable.” The Spanish Civil Guard released dramatic drone footage on Monday (shortly after 10pm, AEST) that showed the Avila fire spreading quickly through dense forests. The agency has deployed more than 8000 personnel to fight the fires. The State Meteorological Agency in Spain, AEMET, forecast another heatwave – the fourth of this northern summer – to begin on Wednesday and continue until at least Sunday.



“The wildfire danger level will continue to increase, reaching extreme levels and making firefighting efforts more difficult due to high temperatures, locally gusty southerly winds and widespread low humidity,” it said in a statement. Fires across Spain have scorched 150,000 hectares and killed 13 people since the start of this year, according to Sanchez. Waterbombing outside Bordeaux. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva Houses destroyed in Navas del Rey, Spain. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez The Avila blaze alone, which is now within 100 kilometres of Madrid, has burned an estimated 47,000 hectares, which would make it the country’s worst wildfire since official records began in 1968.



While the fires heightened arguments about climate change, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu revealed concerns about arson in police investigations into suspected criminals. Related Article Updated

Extreme weather Fire ‘at the gates’ of Bordeaux as Europe battles blazes Lecornu said fires across France had burned 116,085 hectares since January, surpassing the record year of 2022, when 72,000 hectares burned. “Our country is going through an unprecedented fire season,” he said, noting that there had been 13,566 “fire starts” recorded since January. “The fight against wildfires begins with prevention. Nine out of 10 fires are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution.



“But not all these fires are accidents. Some are deliberately set. Since July 6, 162 arrests have already taken place. “Security forces are fully mobilised to identify arsonists. They will be found, arrested, and held accountable for their actions before the courts.” Loading Lecornu said deliberately lighting a fire was a crime punishable by 15 years in prison.



In a visit to Bordeaux, French President Emmanuel Macron thanked firefighters for their hard work, warning the coming weeks would remain difficult. French President Emmanuel Macron at the fire and rescue operational centre in Bordeaux on Monday. Kenzo Tribouillard/Pool AFP via AP “We must hold on. We are going ​to win this battle together. The whole nation is behind you,” he said. “We’re facing a completely unprecedented fire,” Macron added, describing the situation as the country’s worst fire-related crisis since World War II. A pyrocumulonimbus – a giant cloud created by a large bushfires – near France’s Lège-Cap-Ferret late last week. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg



Macron said more than 200 houses had burned down and that “all those who have lost everything” would be supported by the government. Smoke emanating from the Lege-Cap-Ferret fire in south-west France. AFP The fire in French south-west remains about 15 kilometres west of the main entry points to Bordeaux, a city of about 1.3 million people across metropolitan region. Officials said 80 firefighters had been injured tackling the blaze. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready The fire was so powerful its smoke column became a thunderstorm that generated lightning that struck the ground and ignited new fires beyond the original blaze, French officials told the Associated Press.



The thundercloud also produced violent, erratic winds capable of driving the flames in new directions. The phenomenon, called a pyrocumulonimbus, is rare in Europe and more commonly documented in North America and Australia, where it occurs only over some of the most extreme fires. France’s national firefighters federation said it had never before recorded one in the country. Scientists in Australia drew attention to the pyrocumulonimbus events, also known as pyroCb firestorms, in February 2020 after some of the country’s most horrific bushfires that summer. World.title: EV industry fights back against copper thieves targeting public chargers
World.content:
EnvironmentSustainabilityElectric vehicles EV industry fights back against copper thieves targeting public chargers Caitlin Fitzsimmons July 28, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thieves are chopping off public electric vehicle chargers to steal the copper – and getting caught. As scrap metal prices have soared, copper theft has too, and the criminals are moving beyond their traditional targets of rail infrastructure, telecommunications and building sites. Copper wires allegedly found at the arrest of a man in the Newcastle area. NSW Police “EV chargers are the new frontier in an old crime,” said Geoff Brady, chief operating officer at Evie Networks. In Victoria, there were 2592 incidents of copper and other scrap metal theft in 2025, up from 998 in 2016, the state’s Crime Statistics Agency said. In NSW there were 879 incidents specifically of copper theft, up from 612 in 2019, according to the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research.



Brady said copper thieves were increasingly getting caught because of security measures such as cameras and cooperation between competitors to crack down on vandalism. “Cable theft and vandalism is affecting every operator, and we’re no different,” Brady said. “At Evie, we’ve moved from reactive replacement of vandalised cables to layered prevention, and we’re working as an industry to move in that direction together.” At sites identified as vulnerable, Brady said, the company improved lighting and camera coverage, introduced protective cable sleeves and on-site security. Electric charging companies were sharing information on sites that have been hit, camera footage of incidents and police case incident numbers, he said. As a result, the criminals were often getting caught.



Earlier this month NSW Police arrested a man in the Newcastle area and charged him with 10 counts of stealing and 11 counts of destroying or damaging property, as well as drug and driving offences. He was alleged to have damaged EV charging stations in the Newcastle-Hunter region and Central Coast in June, from as far north as Raymond Terrace to Gosford and Erina in the south. Components of EV chargers allegedly found at the arrest of a man in the Newcastle area. NSW Police Police allegedly located and seized 17 EV charging handles (plugs), cutting tools, a taser and several large bags of stripped cables. The price of copper on the London Metal Exchange was $US13,732.50 a tonne on Tuesday, or $US13.73 ($19.62) a kilogram. Brady said a typical DC charger cable would contain two to four kilos of copper, meaning it was not a terribly lucrative crime. “The outcome in Raymond Terrace is great because it shows that this is a simple crime – they’re after a little bit of copper – and it’s just not worth it,” Brady said.



“The customer experience is the casualty in all of this because the copper value is small, but the impact is that people can’t charge when they need to charge because the site is offline for a period of time.” Brady said Evie Networks had also experienced spates of copper theft in western Melbourne and Toowoomba in Queensland, which led to successful arrests. Some public EV chargers, such as the EVX units on power poles, do not have a DC charging cable attached, but rely on the driver to bring an AC charger with them. World.title: Meet the man facing off one of his party’s biggest-ever threats
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If opposition leader is the most unenviable job in politics, then Nationals leader in opposition has to be a close second. Gurmesh Singh, a Coffs Harbour macadamia and blueberry farmer-turned-politician, was elevated to that position in November last year. Along with Liberal leader Kellie Sloane, who gained office only days later, he became a newly minted political leader just weeks before the country’s worst-ever terror attack. Now he’s the man tasked with saving his party’s regional NSW seats from a One Nation avalanche at next year’s election. He’s also the first Sikh elected to an Australian parliament and the first Sikh leader of a major party. He has a rich family history, and a portrait of Singh’s great-grandfather is plastered on walls around the country. When we sit down to lunch on a rainy Sydney Tuesday, One Nation has been surging in the polls, and most of the talk on Macquarie Street about the Nationals often concludes with something like “they’re in major trouble”. I know it’s probably not what Singh wants me to talk about but I can’t help but ask how he feels about Pauline Hanson’s surge in popularity and her calls for a monoculture, given his own background. “I grew up in the ’80s and ’90s in what we would describe as Australian culture, in what some of these people are saying they’d like us to be,” he says. “It’s a good culture that I would also like to live in again. “I look at myself [and my family] – we’ve got a different ethnicity, obviously we have different religious beliefs, and we might have slightly different festivals and religious celebrations, but I think you can do that while still being uniquely Australian as well, and I think that’s the more mature conversation that we should be having … how do we – and you can – do both.”



“I think what people are actually looking for is what we had back then. That’s safer streets, that was an economy that meant you could have a house with one income, it meant kids who were out on their bikes, meant you could go to the beach on a weekend – like, these are the things that people remember … It’s actually things that government should be striving for, right?” The most recent Resolve Political Monitor conducted over June and July found support for the Coalition at the lowest in recent memory, down to 23 per cent and trailing behind One Nation, which sat at 25 per cent despite not yet having a single endorsed candidate for the NSW election. Singh says he believes the tides will turn in the time between now and the March poll, and that Coalition policies like a reduction in payroll tax, released earlier than usual in this election cycle, will get people back on board with the core Nationals principles of smaller governments and better infrastructure for the bush. Related Article Editorial

Resolve Political Monitor NSW voters revolt against major parties The Herald's View Editorial We’re lunching at Matt Moran’s Chophouse in Sydney’s CBD, a sophisticated steak house a short walk from Parliament House where Singh is familiar with the menu. He has a secret passion for hot chips, a love so deep that in his younger years he tried his hand at building an online map of his best reviewed offerings in Sydney. The chips at Chophouse and Bondi’s Hotel Ravesis are up there among the best, he says, but so are those from parliament’s Long Bell Cafe. (I share this enthusiasm and am all too familiar with the salty, crunchy goodness, given the kitchen is mere steps from the Herald’s parliament office.) Another favourite is the KFC chip, which, he says, tastes best on a late-Thursday-night sitting day. So of course we share a bowl of chips. He also selects the 200g eye fillet, and I’m quick to order the same, plus we get a side of charred sweetcorn with fermented chilli butter. Singh asks for no cheese on the corn; he’s so averse to the stuff that even the smell of melted cheese is enough to make him unwell.



Our plates are identical other than the sauce: peppercorn for Singh and mushroom for me. Our waiter recommends a 2018 Barossa Valley shiraz before I get a chance to open the wine list. I’m more of a beer drinker and am always anxious about choosing the wrong wine, so I’m relieved to leave it in our waiter’s hands. The hot chips at Chophouse. Sam Mooy Singh teams chips with eye fillet. Sam Mooy Charred sweetcorn completes the meal. Sam Mooy Singh is a “saltwater Nat”, lingo for Nationals MPs with coastal electorates, as opposed to their freshwater colleagues. His family first settled in Australia when his great-grandfather Bella Singh arrived in Cairns from Punjab in the 1890s and went to Harwood Island in the Clarence River region. Singh excitedly tells me he’s spoken with John Howard about this – his great-grandfather just happened to live in the small country town at the same time as Howard’s grandfather. I’ve seen pictures of Singh’s great-grandfather long before we meet for lunch. His photograph is one of several used by artist Peter Drew for his famous “Aussie” series, taken from documents found in the National Archives of Bella Singh’s exemption from the White Australia policy language test. Getting in contact with the artist led Singh to spend hours poring over archives, finding troves of documents, some of which he is still yet to fully examine.



After World War II, Bella moved to the Coffs Harbour area to work and, a century later, that’s the electorate his great-grandson represents in the NSW state parliament. Trying to win back conservative voters drawn to the anti-immigration rhetoric of One Nation without alienating the diverse members of his own electorate (Woolgoolga has a significant population of Indian heritage and is home to Australia’s first Sikh temple) will be a difficult tightrope to walk. The political fight ahead will test his leadership. Bella Singh, Gurmesh Singh’s great-grandfather, is featured on a well-known series of posters. Peter Drew Singh finds respite from the pressure of NSW politics in what sounds to me like the grimmest of situations. He’s an RFS volunteer, who enlisted after the Black Summer bushfires, but he tells me that, rather than fighting fires, most of his work has been supporting people on the worst days of their lives. Not as the boss but as the one who follows orders. “It’s not something I’ve sought to promote necessarily but plenty of people have seen me out on the fires or at car accidents and stuff, and sometimes people were a little bit surprised to see me holding a Stop/Go sign or sweeping glass off the road or rolling up a pipe or whatever it is that we’re called to do on that day. “I find it pretty rewarding. Given that I’m fairly junior in the brigade, I go there and take orders.”



One of the most confronting scenes he has responded to happened over Christmas while at a family dinner at a local beach. The brigade got a call and so Singh left the venue and headed two beaches over. A man had suffered a medical episode in the water and drowned. Paramedics were trying to resuscitate him. As an RFS volunteer his job wasn’t to be the hero but to help retrieve supplies from the ambulance as others worked to save the man’s life. “That’s often what you’re confronted with rather than actual fire, although we’ve had some hairy fires as well.” For the man with a title like NSW Nationals leader, his path to politics was fairly cosmopolitan. He attended UNSW and worked in a newsagent’s in Bondi. Straight out of university, Singh went to work for Qantas, in the marketing team, before working in software. He found a passion for politics after moving back home to farming. Singh has been at the scene of local tragedies as a member of the RFS. Sam Mooy While previous media reporting has painted Singh as a humble blueberry and macadamia farmer, that’s only part of the story. He was actually director of the powerful blueberry farmers co-op Oz Group in Woolgoolga, and was vice president of the Australian Blueberry Growers’ Association. The blueberry industry’s rapid expansion on the Mid North Coast hasn’t been without controversy, drawing concerns around pesticide use and lack of planning oversight. Dealing with land-use conflicts in horticulture and running the co-op was how Singh got interested in state politics. “Even liaising with our local council, who had a couple of Greens councillors, their solution was to add more regulation when they weren’t satisfied the existing regulation were being followed.

World.title: ‘Rattled homes and sleep loss’: Inside Sydney bowlo’s noise war with its neighbours
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Rattled homes and sleep loss’: Inside Sydney bowlo’s noise war with its neighbours David Barwell July 28, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A three-year noise battle between an eastern suburbs bowling club and neighbouring residents has come to a head after nearby home owners complained that loud music, birthday parties, late-night functions and disorderly patrons were disrupting life in one of Sydney’s most sought-after suburbs. Liquor & Gaming NSW has issued Diamond Bay Bowling Club in Vaucluse with a formal warning over noise impacts from live entertainment and patron activity, but stopped short of imposing licence sanctions, ruling the legal threshold for an “unreasonable and serious disturbance” had not been met. Liquor & Gaming NSW has handed down a decision after an investigation into noise complaints relating to the bowling club. James Brickwood The dispute has become the first major test of the NSW government’s vibrancy reforms, which were designed to strengthen the state’s live music and hospitality sectors by giving greater protection to established venues facing complaints from residents. The ruling follows an 18-month investigation triggered by 57 official complaints lodged since 2023 by one primary complainant, supported by eight neighbouring residents. The complaints alleged amplified music, DJs, live bands, bass vibrations and patron noise from weekend functions regularly disrupted sleep and “caused vibration to nearby residential buildings and infrastructure”.



Residents claimed the club had changed since the pandemic, evolving from a traditional community bowling club into an entertainment venue hosting DJ nights, live music, private functions and outdoor events that attracted younger crowds, forcing neighbours to keep windows shut, avoid outdoor areas and sleep with earplugs. The club, which has operated on Old South Head Road since 1963 and typically trades until 10pm on weekends, strongly rejected those claims and argued the “order of occupancy” principle was firmly in its favour, given it had been operating in the area for decades before the lead complainant moved nearby about five years ago. Liquor and Gaming NSW found that the venue had “not seriously disturbed the quiet and good order of the neighbourhood.” James Brickwood The club’s general manager Neve Storey said the club had spent more than $200,000 on noise mitigation measures after becoming aware of the complaints, including installing double-glazed windows, acoustic treatments, sound barriers, building upgrades and introducing operational changes designed to reduce impacts on neighbours. “We ran in the red for two years to put money into the club to do everything we could to address the concerns that were raised,” she said. “We’re not a big RSL or a major club – it’s been very traumatic for a little club, the amount of scrutiny we’ve been under.”



Regulatory inspections of the venue revealed mixed findings. Liquor & Gaming NSW conducted multiple covert observations of the venue, including inspections in late 2024 when officers found intoxicated patrons stumbling as they left the club, while others were seen running across the bowling greens, yelling, late at night. The venue was also subject to separate assessments by Waverley Council environmental health officers, who concluded amplified music and patron noise were likely to be offensive inside nearby homes when windows were open. However, Eastern Suburbs Police reached a different view, reporting that while music was audible from nearby locations, noise levels were comparable to those generated by other licensed venues in Sydney’s east and were not considered offensive. In its submissions to the regulator, the bowling club argued one neighbour had been responsible for co-ordinating many of the complaints and had encouraged other residents to lodge reports with authorities.



Related Article Opinion

City life If you buy a house near a pub, don’t complain about the noise Elizabeth Barry Sydney writer The club also rejected suggestions it had become a nightclub, arguing it had expanded its food, beverage and entertainment offerings simply to remain financially viable and had never marketed itself as a dance venue targeting an 18-to-25-year-old demographic. Storey said responding to the investigation had come at a significant financial and emotional cost through legal fees, consultant reports and staff resources. “At one point we felt like we’d become the fun police, shushing customers at 9.30pm on a Saturday just so we didn’t inflame the situation any further,” she said. “We’ve never had an alcohol-related incident. We’ve never had violence. We’ve never had sexual misconduct. How could we, as a small bowling club in Vaucluse, be the most complained-about club in NSW?”



Liquor & Gaming NSW acting director of hospitality and gaming operations Darren Duke, in his ruling, concluded the complaint could not be upheld under the legal framework introduced through the vibrancy reforms, which established a higher threshold for regulatory action against long-established venues. NSW Night-time Economy Minister John Graham said the decision was in line with laws designed to protect entertainment venues from noise complaints. Michael Quelch While declining to impose additional licence conditions or other sanctions, Duke issued the club with a formal warning, saying it was intended “to formally remind the club of its obligations to minimise disturbance and ensure the operation of the club does not detract from the amenity of the surrounding community”. NSW Night-time Economy Minister John Graham said the ruling demonstrated the intent of the government’s reforms. “This ruling proves the days of moving in next to an established venue and complaining until it gets closed down are coming to an end,” Graham said.



“While this is a good outcome, this was a costly process for the venue, which shows there is still more work to be done to cut red tape and help our venues survive.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The omission in Jacinta Allan’s departing statement as premier
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election The omission in Jacinta Allan’s departing statement as premier Kieran Rooney Updated July 28, 2026 — 11:24am ,first published 11:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Follow live updates: ALP leadership showdown As Jacinta Allan bid farewell to the job she has held for the past 1036 days, she used her final speech as Victoria’s premier to highlight her government’s achievements: tougher bail laws, a budget back in surplus, free public transport and improvements in women’s health. But as she emphasised Labor’s record upgrading the state’s infrastructure, Allan remained defiant about the corruption scandal that has plagued those same Big Build projects, even as some of her colleagues publicly moved to call for a royal commission. Loading “We’ve removed 92 level crossings, finished the West Gate Tunnel. We’re building the North East Link and the Suburban Rail Loop, and then there’s the Metro Tunnel,” she told reporters.



“Not too many people get to see a project of this size and scale through from the start to the end. I am so goddamn proud of it.” Ben Carroll, who is set to be Victoria’s new premier, is expected to announce a royal commission into the scandal surrounding the Big Build and the CFMEU as one of his first acts. Several Labor ministers pressed for such an inquiry during a tense cabinet meeting on Monday, and then did so publicly on Tuesday morning before Allan’s resignation. Jacinta Allan during her final press conference on Tuesday. Getty Images In her statement to reporters, Allan did not mention the revelations in The Age that the scandal-plagued construction union inflated the cost of the government’s signature projects, delayed construction, and employed criminals, including bikies, to work on them. Forced from office in large part because of her refusal to call a royal commission into the Building Bad scandal, Allan intimated that Victorians were benefiting from completed projects without focusing on the corrupt conduct on building sites during their construction.

World.title: Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline
World.content:
MoneySavingBudgeting Living at home in your 20s used to be taboo. Now it’s a financial lifeline Nina Hendy July 28, 2026 — 11:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Living at home with her parents well into her 20s has resulted in a huge financial saving that has helped 25-year-old Chloe Henry get ahead in life and also helped the communications professional save for her first overseas holiday. Henry doesn’t pay any rent to her parents, instead contributing by buying some groceries and helping with the housework. Other than that, her income is hers to do with as she pleases. Communications professional Chloe Henry says she hopes to take her parents on a holiday to thank them for letting her live at home. “I’m lucky that my parents have allowed me to stay at home for as long as I want and that they’re happy to have me there. I’m off to Japan in September for my birthday, and I can’t wait,” she says. Each morning, she travels via public transport from Berwick into Melbourne, a journey that takes 90 minutes each way. But the sacrifice has been worth it, enabling her savings to quietly grow.



“Living at home means I’m not feeling like I’m under a price crunch. I have a savings goal in mind, and I’ve been able to reach that goal a lot faster,” she says. But the future of life on her own isn’t entirely clear. The hope is that one day, she could be in a strong enough position to be able to rent with her partner, who is still in university. “I’m pretty pessimistic about the housing market and being able to save up to move out or put a deposit on a home. A lot of my friends still live at home and don’t have plans to move out anytime soon either.” Staying put Henry is not alone. New research from AMP shows that for many, support is no longer just about the bank of mum and dad, it’s also about the house of mum and dad, with extended families open to sharing housing, costs and care in more practical ways.



The shift has been driven mostly by younger singles as housing affordability, rate increases and cost of living pressures combine to make living alone increasingly unaffordable. Editor's pick Opinion

Housing affordability A new type of class divide is emerging – and property is to blame Victoria Devine Money columnist The growing number of shared living arrangements is in direct response to the constant rise in living costs, which shows no sign of easing. While common in some cultures, multi-generational living isn’t the norm in Australia. But what started during the pandemic as a way to save money as housing costs bolted has now become a way of life for many. At a time when so many people are seeking financial stability, it’s understandable that living with a flatmate could be undesirable for some given that factors outside their control – such as job losses or a large unexpected bill – could impact on their ability to cover rent.



Generational shift Ben Hillier, general manager of retirement solutions at AMP. Natalie Boog AMP’s research found that 68 per cent of 20- to 39-year-olds support multi-generational living, but fewer than two in five people aged 65 and over do. This points to a generational shift in expectations around independence and home ownership. “As housing pressures intensify and Australia becomes increasingly multicultural, younger Australians are rethinking what the ‘Australian dream’ looks like,” explains Ben Hillier, AMP’s director of retirement. “This shift also tells us something important about confidence for retirement, which in Australia has long been tied to home ownership. Alongside super, Australians’ sense of financial security will increasingly be shaped by the household around them – how families live, what support they can provide one another and how costs and care are shared.”



Mortgage brokers have noticed the change in property demand too as they’re asked to help families find homes that will accommodate extended family members, says Rebecca Jarrett-Dalton of Two Red Shoes. “Our job as brokers is no longer just about securing a rate – it’s about providing creative pathways, whether it’s navigating generational wealth when buying property, or helping families explore shared ownership,” she says. As for Henry, she admits she doesn’t have all the answers about housing in the future, but does hope that one day she can thank her parents for letting her stay home well into her 20s. “Maybe I can pay for them to take a holiday one day,” she says.
