World.title: Melbourne businessman found guilty of rape, but his name remains a secret
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCourts Melbourne businessman found guilty of rape, but his name remains a secret Erin Pearson July 28, 2026 — 11:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A high-profile Melbourne businessman has been found guilty of raping a 27-year-old personal assistant. The man, who cannot be named due to a suppression order preventing his identity from being released, had been on trial for rape and sexual assault in the County Court of Victoria since July 8. The man cannot be named as his lawyers argue it could be detrimental to him. Tamara Voninski The prosecution had alleged the much older man had offered the young woman work, including on his autobiography, when she attended his “larger than life” converted warehouse to discuss the role. It was alleged that after a night of drinking and consuming cocaine the man raped the woman.



Related Article Courts Rape trial begins for Melbourne man who cannot be named Defence barrister Dermot Dann, KC, maintained his client was innocent and urged the jury to find the complainant was an unreliable witness who had a financial motive to lie. “She’s like a fiction writer,” Dann said. “She was telling [the accused man] this night that she loved him for his spirit. “What the prosecution has served up to you is a horrible mixture of lies, fabrications, recent inventions, inconsistencies and evidence that had been proved to be demonstrably false.



“This case is a powerful demonstration that there are cases when complainants make false evidence, false statements. This is one of those cases.” However on Tuesday, a jury of nine women and three men rejected the defence argument and found the man guilty after three days of deliberations. The accused had pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault and two counts of rape. The rapist was immediately taken into custody with the prosecution applying to revoke his bail minutes after the three guilty verdicts were returned because of the likelihood the man would ultimately be sentenced to an immediate term of imprisonment. During the trial, the court heard the pair met in 2022 after the woman contacted him to express interest in working for him while she studied. While the job was initially unavailable, when it opened up the student was told she could help work on projects including his autobiography and a film script.



Prosecutor Matthew Fisher said an Uber was sent to collect the woman and bring her to the man’s house to discuss the employment position. Related Article Courts Doctor charged with filming naked pool patrons wins three-month secrecy order But, when she arrived he attempted to kiss her, prompting her to reply, “If I let you do this, if I let you f--- me, you’ll never respect me as your employee. I don’t want that to be the role I play in your life. I’ll never want to have sex with you.” The woman quit months later before reconnecting with the man in March 2023 when she was again offered work on his book. When she visited the man’s home to discuss the project days later, the jury were told the two allegedly consumed wine and cocaine and watched television at an associate’s home in South Melbourne.



On their return to his home, the prosecution alleges the woman began to cry and speak of the breakdown of a recent relationship when the accused man pulled her from a lounge and onto his bed, telling her he’d take care of her. “You’re so sexy, I can’t stop, I need your help to sleep, help me, I need to,” he allegedly said. The woman, who gave evidence for more than a week, said she was then raped before she punched the man in the nose and was told to leave. The woman went to a spare room where she texted her mother, who called the police. The man will face a plea hearing at a later date.



Last month, this masthead revealed that almost 500 suppression orders in various forms were issued in Victorian courts last year, with the highest number being issued on safety grounds, including for mental health reasons. Of those suppression orders granted, 247 were made in the County Court. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘Completely unprecedented’: Europe races to fight out-of-control blazes ahead of new heatwave
World.content:
WorldEuropeBushfires ‘Completely unprecedented’: Europe races to fight out-of-control blazes ahead of new heatwave David Crowe Updated July 28, 2026 — 11:01am ,first published July 28, 2026 — 8:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has warned of more devastating wildfires across Europe, with climate change making heatwaves more frequent, as emergency crews raced to contain blazes in Spain and France before temperatures soar later this week. Sanchez pledged more funding for fire shelters ahead of a meeting of national ministers that is tipped to commit to new measures on climate change during a growing debate on the country’s worst wildfires in decades. Burnt vehicles in a parking yard in Chapinería, Spain, on Monday. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez A firefighter monitors flames in La Adrada, in Spain’s Avila province. Anadolu via Getty Images The Spanish fires appeared to slow on Monday after spreading over the weekend in the Avila province west of Madrid, but a fire near Valencia in the south of the country continued to burn out of control.



In south-western France, a vast fire heading toward Bordeaux slowed as winds died down, but government officials warned of mounting risks when temperatures reach 39 degrees in the coming days. French authorities have evacuated about 220,000 people, including local residents and people on holiday, while Spanish authorities have told some 100,000 people to leave their homes or seek shelter. A charred bicycle in Lège-Cap-Ferret, outside Bordeaux, France. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva Firefighters work to suppress a blaze near Lacanau, France, on Monday. AP Photo/Baz Ratner Sanchez visited La Vall d’Uixo in Castellon province, north of Valencia, to step up his calls for a “state pact” across governments to do more to address climate change.



“What we’re experiencing isn’t a succession of isolated events,” he said. “It’s the most painful expression of a climate emergency ​that is making sixth-generation wildfires more ferocious, heatwaves more frequent, and our territory more vulnerable.” The Spanish Civil Guard released dramatic drone footage on Monday (shortly after 10pm, AEST) that showed the Avila fire spreading quickly through dense forests. The agency has deployed more than 8000 personnel to fight the fires. The State Meteorological Agency in Spain, AEMET, forecast another heatwave – the fourth of this northern summer – to begin on Wednesday and continue until at least Sunday.



“The wildfire danger level will continue to increase, reaching extreme levels and making firefighting efforts more difficult due to high temperatures, locally gusty southerly winds and widespread low humidity,” it said in a statement. Fires across Spain have scorched 150,000 hectares and killed 13 people since the start of this year, according to Sanchez. Waterbombing outside Bordeaux. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva Houses destroyed in Navas del Rey, Spain. AP Photo/Manu Fernandez The Avila blaze alone, which is now within 100 kilometres of Madrid, has burned an estimated 47,000 hectares, which would make it the country’s worst wildfire since official records began in 1968.



While the fires heightened arguments about climate change, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu revealed concerns about arson in police investigations into suspected criminals. Related Article Updated

Extreme weather Fire ‘at the gates’ of Bordeaux as Europe battles blazes Lecornu said fires across France had burned 116,085 hectares since January, surpassing the record year of 2022, when 72,000 hectares burned. “Our country is going through an unprecedented fire season,” he said, noting that there had been 13,566 “fire starts” recorded since January. “The fight against wildfires begins with prevention. Nine out of 10 fires are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution.



“But not all these fires are accidents. Some are deliberately set. Since July 6, 162 arrests have already taken place. “Security forces are fully mobilised to identify arsonists. They will be found, arrested, and held accountable for their actions before the courts.” Loading Lecornu said deliberately lighting a fire was a crime punishable by 15 years in prison.



In a visit to Bordeaux, French President Emmanuel Macron thanked firefighters for their hard work, warning the coming weeks would remain difficult. French President Emmanuel Macron at the fire and rescue operational centre in Bordeaux on Monday. Kenzo Tribouillard/Pool AFP via AP “We must hold on. We are going ​to win this battle together. The whole nation is behind you,” he said. “We’re facing a completely unprecedented fire,” Macron added, describing the situation as the country’s worst fire-related crisis since World War II. A pyrocumulonimbus – a giant cloud created by a large bushfires – near France’s Lège-Cap-Ferret late last week. AP Photo/Caroline Blumberg



Macron said more than 200 houses had burned down and that “all those who have lost everything” would be supported by the government. Smoke emanating from the Lege-Cap-Ferret fire in south-west France. AFP The fire in French south-west remains about 15 kilometres west of the main entry points to Bordeaux, a city of about 1.3 million people across metropolitan region. Officials said 80 firefighters had been injured tackling the blaze. Related Article Heatwave Europe’s summers are changing. The continent isn’t ready The fire was so powerful its smoke column became a thunderstorm that generated lightning that struck the ground and ignited new fires beyond the original blaze, French officials told the Associated Press.



The thundercloud also produced violent, erratic winds capable of driving the flames in new directions. The phenomenon, called a pyrocumulonimbus, is rare in Europe and more commonly documented in North America and Australia, where it occurs only over some of the most extreme fires. France’s national firefighters federation said it had never before recorded one in the country. Scientists in Australia drew attention to the pyrocumulonimbus events, also known as pyroCb firestorms, in February 2020 after some of the country’s most horrific bushfires that summer. With Reuters, AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Former long-time Taupō mayor David Trewavas dies
World.content:
Former long-time mayor of Taupō, David Trewavas, has died, age 63.

Trewavas served the Taupō District Council for 24 years - 13 of which he did so as mayor.

He died on Tuesday.

Current Taupō mayor John Funnell gave tribute to Trewavas, saying he was a people person, who always had a genuine interest in others.

"David served the district with professionalism, dedication and a commitment to helping others; and for that he was hugely loved."

Trewavas stood for re-election last year, but lost to Funnell.

"He was widely respected, within the district but also in local government throughout New Zealand and nationally, for his kindness, integrity and the effort he put into building relationships - he was known for remembering the name of everyone he met."

Trewavas' work for Taupō included a new airport terminal, the CBD redevelopment, and a $3.5 million sports facility.

Council chief executive Julie Gardyne said Trewavas' self-deprecating humour and outgoing personality were a real asset to him in his role as mayor.

"He had a great way of breaking the ice with others. He built connections everywhere he went."

The council said it extended its condolences to his whānau and former colleagues.

Taupō Funeral Services also shared the news to social media.

"David James passed away suddenly on 28 July 2026, aged 63 years."

It said the former mayor was deeply loved and forever remembered by his family and all who knew him.

World.title: City Rail Link: Another meeting, but still no opening date
World.content:
Auckland councillors are frustrated they are still in the dark about when the city's new underground commuter train network will open, despite a meeting updating them on its progress.

Auckland Transport will hold public open days for the City Rail Link (CRL) from next month, but is waiting for sign-off from the rail safety regulator, the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA).

At a committee meeting on Tuesday, project leaders from Auckland Transport, KiwiRail and CRL updated councillors about the network's progress.

However before discussion began, Auckland Council director of resilience and infrastructure Barry Potter said they could not answer questions about the opening.

"We won't be talking today about the opening date except to say it is getting closer day by day, and hopefully it's not too far away from announcements.

"We'll just leave that, if we can avoid questions around that that would be great."

Councillor Richard Hills said people were getting frustrated knowing it was close with no confirmed date.

"Is there any way in the next couple of days that it can be announced what month? Because there are a lot of people getting upset, concerned. There's a lot of businesses who just want hope."

Councillor Richard Hills. LDR/SUPPLIED

Soon after, Councillor Daniel Newman tried a backdoor question: "The new timetable, on what date does that apply?"

Auckland's rail network closed earlier this month for a final dress rehearsal for the long anticipated CRL.

Auckland Transport said that went well and formal testing had been completed, with regulatory approval the last step. That would come from NZTA and the director of land transport.

An NZTA spokesperson said a significant volume of documentation and evidence had been submitted, and this was being assessed thoroughly by the regulator.

"For the CRL, three separate safety case variations have been submitted for approval - covering the new rail infrastructure as well as changes to freight operations and passenger services due to the CRL opening.

"This process provides independent assurance that everything 'so far as reasonably practicable' has been, and will continue to be, done to reduce the risk of harm."

Auckland's rail network had a major shut down for a month - from the end of December until 28 January - to test the CRL and allow for final track rebuilding.

The CRL update showed there would be future shutdowns this summer, but these would be shorter and only partial closures so KiwiRail could complete network maintenance.

Deputy Mayor Desley Simpson said it would be crucial to ensure any partial shutdowns did not happen when there were big events in the city.

"I know we're not going there with the opening date, but if you think it's got to be somewhere between now and Christmas, there's going to be a very short period of time when everything opens up, then you begin to do partial shutdowns again."

Auckland Transport group manager for rail services Mark Lambert said the train network would remain open until January 2026, then there would be a series of partial closures that would be well publicised on the southern and western lines. He said there would be two weekends this November when there would also be partial closures.

Councillor Mike Lee said such closures were unacceptable for a modern city.

"I'm not too sure when it will be open, obviously, but if this practice in terms of disrupting the network… is going to carry on, any idea of getting a serious passenger commuter rail service in Auckland to be viable… is not going to happen," he said.

"If this sort of disruption is going to carry on there's going to be a real problem… from the people of Auckland. That is just not acceptable"

Passenger information screens at Karanga-a-Hape Station during a City Rail Link operational test. LDR / Taelegalolo'u Mary Afemata

CRL open days

The opening date was a tightly held secret, but Auckland Transport had released some information about the lead-up. It had a new journey planner tool that showed the new timetable for when the CRL opens, allowing commuters to check if it will be faster to take a train.

Auckland Transport, City Rail Link Limited and KiwiRail were also opening the new stations to the public through a series of 'First Look' events. These will be free, ticketed sessions, but numbers will be limited.

They will be held over consecutive Saturdays in August: 8 August - First Look at Maungawhau, 15 August - First Look at Karanga-a-Hape, 22 August - First Look at Te Waihorotiu.

The free tickets for these will be available one week ahead of each event.

World.title: Christopher Luxon says ruling out working with Opportunity Party 'not a surprise'
World.content:
Christopher Luxon says nobody should be surprised by his call to rule out working with the Opportunity Party - despite the new position being revealed without notice at the very end of a media conference.

In response to a question at his usual Monday briefing, Luxon said he could not work with Opportunity due to its advocacy for a land tax. He declined to give a direct yes-or-no answer, but his office later confirmed that amounted to a formal rule-out.

Previously when asked, the National leader would say only that a vote for Opportunity looked "like a vote for Labour and the Greens" and that he had not "given them any thought".

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Luxon insisted the party's position had been discussed among National's caucus and board "for several months".

"Pretty obvious to us - and I know a big surprise to you, apparently - but you know, this is a party that wants extreme policy on taxes. We're a party of low taxes. It's not a surprise we don't want to work with them."

Luxon also disputed Opportunity's attempt to position itself as a kingmaker which could go with either the left or right.

"They're as centrist as I am an All Black, frankly," he said.

When reminded he was working with New Zealand First, which wanted to buy back BNZ, Luxon replied: "I ruled that policy out, it's all good".

He then walked away from reporters, having taken questions for about three-and-half minutes.

Opportunity Party leader Quilae Wong speaks to Guyon Espiner Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Not a 'Trojan horse' - Wong

In response, Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong told Midday Report she was certain Luxon would change his tune if the alternative was going into opposition.

"If they need us, I'm sure they would rather have a chat with us than just give up altogether. When that day comes, we are still here and willing to chat and have a good-faith conversation."

Wong said both right- and left-wing supporters had been trying to paint Opportunity as a Trojan horse for the other side. She said in reality, Opportunity had a lot of common ground with both parties, noting it could work with National to grow the economy.

"It would be great if we could put that ideology aside and not... just cast us off as the other team."

Wong said Opportunity would lay out its clear bottom lines closer to the election so voters knew its priorities in negotiations.

In the lead-up to the 2023 election, Luxon called a special media conference to formally rule out working with Te Pāti Māori, as they had "no philosophical alignment".

Labour's leader Chris Hipkins says Luxon got caught on the hoof and just made it up as he went along. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Speaking separately on Tuesday, Labour's leader Chris Hipkins said anyone watching Luxon's announcement would have described it as "rushed and haphazard" .

"I think he got caught on the hoof and just made it up as he went along," Hipkins said.

"It's clear that... a lot of scrambling went on in the hour or two after that to figure out exactly what their position on it was."

But other National MPs reiterated their leader's talking points on the way into their Tuesday morning caucus meeting.

National deputy Nicola Willis said Luxon's position reflected "widely held views" across National and did not come as a surprise.

"It's good we have a prime minister that, when he's asked a clear question gives a clear answer, which distinguishes him from Chris Hipkins, who refuses to be clear about who he would work with."

Hipkins has said he will lay out which parties Labour could work with before Parliament rises near the end of September.

Campaign chair Simeon Brown said National had long been "very clear" that it would not work with parties with "radical left" policies.

Erica Stanford said the announcement had come as no surprise given her discussions with other senior ministers. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Chris Bishop said the rule-out was "nothing out of the ordinary" and suggested reporters were "jumping at shadows".

"It would be wrong to characterise it as some great big pronouncement. He was asked the question, he answered it."

Bishop added that he did not think Opportunity would make it over the 5 percent threshold: "Vibe-based political parties don't go so well."

Erica Stanford said Luxon's Monday announcement had come as no surprise given her discussions with other senior ministers.

"I'm not surprised. The public aren't surprised. No one should be surprised."

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Bowls format 'brutal' as two NZ teams miss out on medals
World.content:
New Zealand lawn bowler Shannon McIlroy has described the format at the Commonwealth Games as brutal.

Mcilroy, who is competing at his fifth Games, was knocked out of contention for a medal in the singles despite losing just one game in sectional play.

Under a new format to help streamline and speed up the competition at the Glasgow Games only the section winners advance to the semi-finals, unlike previous events where multiple players could advance.

It also meant that despite finishing tied at the top of the women's pair, Katelyn Inch and Selina Goddard, missed out on the semi-finals on countback.

"I'm sure it will be discussed," McIlroy told RNZ, on what the change of format may mean for the future.

"I think it's pretty cut-throat to have just one go through, there are so many good players here, you could be outplayed for half an hour and then you're out of the tournament so its pretty brutal."

However the 39-year-old, who played his 400th game for New Zealand on Tuesday, isn't despondent.

"We're fortunate that the Commonwealth Games is still happening and we're part of it."

But McIlroy is unsure about his future in the sport.

"To be honest it all depends on my children, they're getting to an age where they're going to chase their sporting endeavours so if that requires me to be there then I'll just have to see what the balance looks like and it might mean that I don't play as much domestically."

Mcilroy has been competing internationally for nearly 20 years. He won his first medal at the Asia Pacific Championships in 2007 and in 2016 won a singles world title.

"I can still remember the first one (international match) like it was yesterday.... I was a lot skinnier!

"To get the opportunity to play for New Zealand is incredible, I still get the same feelings as I did when I first started so that will never change."

"Really fortunate that I've played with some really good players over the years that helped me get there. As long as that drive is still there and my support network still wants me to play for New Zealand then I'll go as long as I can."

World.title: Deadly Mount Maunganui landslide still active and moving
World.content:
Experts have found the main landslide on Mauao is still active and moving.

Six additional slip events have been recorded on the deadly landslide above the Mount Maunganui Beachside Holiday Park since last weekend.

Tauranga City Council recovery manager Charlie Rahiri said geotechnical specialists had identified fresh cracking and evidence of groundwater emerging from the slope, which indicated it's highly susceptible to further movement.

He said it was now considered active and ongoing and this was why a cautious, evidence-based approach remained essential.

Victims of the landslide on Mount Maunganui in January. RNZ

"Our monitoring systems are designed to detect changes in slope behaviour and provide early warning when conditions change. The recent movement triggered established response procedures, allowing us to act quickly and put appropriate safety measures in place.

"While this movement is a reminder that Mauao remains an active environment, it does not change our commitment to restoring access where it is safe to do so. We've made substantial progress over recent months and will continue to be guided by specialist advice as recovery work progresses."

He said repair works on the base track Te Ara Tūtanga were continuing as planned, with other known landslide sites not currently showing signs of "significant change".

RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

Initial assessments had also not identified damage to the summit 4WS Motukauri track, but those inspections would continue.

"Public safety remains our priority. We will continue to work closely with our geotechnical advisers and mana whenua partners to ensure decisions are informed by the latest information and reflect the long-term wellbeing of the maunga and those who use it."

The closure of Adams Avenue would remain in place for the foreseeable future while experts continued to assess the site and monitor conditions.

World.title: Protection for hoiho around Otago Peninsula to be made permanent
World.content:
A set net ban to protect hoiho off the Otago Peninsula will be made permanent to reduce the risk of fishing bycatch.

A temporary emergency closure was imposed by the Oceans and Fisheries minister last year to protect the nationally endangered yellow-eyed penguin.

Shane Jones said he decided to make the closure permanent.

"I am also establishing a new escalating response framework called a fishing related mortality limit so I can act quickly and decisively to increase protections if needed," he said.

The plan included setting an accidental capture limit of four northern hoiho per year.

Jones called that a "bottom line" and did not rule out putting further restrictions on fishing in place to ensure the limit was not exceeded.

"Last year's risk assessment projected that to stabilise the northern hoiho population we must cut deaths from all causes by half and I consider the new protections will achieve this goal for fisheries bycatch," he said.

Disease, predation and starvation were the major risks to hoiho but the changes to reduce risk of fisheries bycatch would help, he said.

The changes would come into force on 16 September.

Seafood New Zealand chief executive Lisa Futscheck said the decision gave fishers in the area more certainty but that was undermined by the addition of a fishing related mortality limit.

"Fishers will continue to do everything they can to minimise risk and avoid hoiho capture," she said.

"We want to see hoiho thrive and have the best chance at recovery and survival."

Futscheck said it was important that threats to hoiho were addressed using an evidence-based approach.

When Fisheries New Zealand was consulting on the changes last year, it said commercial set net fishing was estimated to be the third largest cause of hoiho mortality in recent years.

World.title: First bills going out from Wellington's new water provider Tiaki Wai
World.content:
Wellington's new water services provider Tiaki Wai will begin sending out its first bills.

Ratepayers across Wellington, Porirua, Lower Hutt and Upper Hutt are now receiving two separate rate bills, one for water from Tiaki Wai, and one for all other services from their council.

Property owners in Wellington City, Hutt City and Upper Hutt City would start receiving Tiaki Wai bills from this week and those in Porirua City from next week.

Tiaki Wai said the first bill was due for payment across the region on 1 September 2026.

Property owners could pay by direct debit, online or phone banking, or over the counter at NZ Post stores offering the 'pay a bill' service. Lower Hutt property owners could use the Payble online platform.

Tiaki Wai said water services charges would vary from property to property, in the same way council rates bills varied, and would also be charged every three months.

For the first year the property's bill would be calculated using a mix of rateable capital value (CV) and fixed charges, similar to the mix each council had been using.

Long term, Tiaki Wai aimed to make the way the bill is calculated consistent across all four council areas and to install residential water meters, so the bill reflected usage.

"Every day, pipes across the Wellington region's water network deliver safe drinking water, remove wastewater from sinks and toilets, and take stormwater away from downpipes, streets and other public areas. Your Tiaki Wai bill covers the cost of these essential water services," said Tiaki Wai Chief Customer Officer Liza Gunn.

This coming year, Tiaki Wai would need to invest around $800 million. About half would go into keeping essential water services working, and the other half into replacing and upgrading aging pipes and other critical assets.

World.title: Knee injuries might soon be fixed with a pill
World.content:
Scientists make breakthrough for damaged knees Nine To Noon Download MP3 12m

Stanford University scientists have had a major breakthrough that could lead to future knee injuries being repaired with a simple injection or oral medication.

The researchers also say it could mean far fewer people in the future needing knee and hip replacement surgeries.

The work was done with mice, the researchers targeting a specific protein that causes cartilage to break down.

Lead authors Dr Helen Blau and Dr Nidhi Bhutani said by blocking that protein in older mice, they found cartilage that had thinned had actually grown thicker.

"Osteoarthritis affects about 240 million people worldwide," Blau told Nine to Noon.

"Right now, the only thing that is offered is pain medications to deal with the pain of osteoarthritis, and also when it's particularly bad, then you can get knee replacement or hip replacement surgery."

The scientists discovered an enzyme which, if blocked, could restore muscle mass and muscle strength - and further testing allowed them to do the same with cartilage.

"What we see is that these cells are now able to reprogram into a younger phenotype," Bhutani said.

Blau said the drug had been through a phase one clinical trial which showed it is safe for use in humans.

"We have the green light from the [US Food and Drug Administration] to proceed to phase 2b trials in sarcopenia, muscle wasting for ageing."

World.title: Sabalenka, Djokovic lead mixed doubles teams for US Open
World.content:
Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic headline the initial list of 16 teams entered into the US Open mixed doubles championship.

The tournament was overhauled last year, with a $US1 million ($1.43 million) prize going to the winners, in an effort to get top singles players to compete. Many of those types of stars were listed among the teams announced Monday by the US Tennis Association.

Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud, the runners-up in 2025, are entered again, along with Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz, the Japanese duo of Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori, along with Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper.

The main draw will be played over two days on August 25-26, with all the matches set to be held in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, the two biggest venues at the US Open.

Teams can enter up until August 17, when the six duos with the best combined singles rankings at the time will be automatically entered into the main draw.

That means Sabalenka, the two-time defending US Open women's champion and Djokovic, still ranked number five on the men's tour at age 39, will be safely into the field.

Eight teams will be given wild cards by the USTA, and two other teams will play their way into the field through a qualifying tournament to be held from August 24.

Defending champions win US Open mixed doubles final Italian pair Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori accomplish their "mission" by winning the US Open mixed doubles title for the second straight year in a controversially revamped format.

The remainder of the teams that were entered as of Monday:

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev; Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli; Diana Shnaider and Daniil Medvedev; Amanda Anisimova and Learner Tien; Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime; Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe; Taylor Townsend and Alexander Zverev; Elena-Gabriela Ruse and Nuno Borges; Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori; Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten; and siblings Peyton Stearns and Preston Stearns.

Errani and Vavassori are the two-time defending US Open champions. The Italians needed a wild card to get into last year's event because their singles ranking was too low, and that will be the case again this year.

The US Open was initially criticised last year because the format of the event shut out doubles specialists such as Errani and Vavassori, but the tournament certainly seemed a success, helping draw 78,000 fans to the grounds and selling out Ashe both days.

"Any time you can bring women and men together on the same team, you showcase tennis at its best. This is exactly what the mixed doubles championship does," USTA CEO Craig Tiley said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The mixed doubles championship is an innovation that will engage new audiences and give our fans another opportunity to see the biggest stars compete together."

Errani and Vavassori were the only traditional doubles team in last year's tournament.

There is a chance for more this year — Siniakova and Patten are doubles specialists — with the addition of the eight-team qualifying tournament, which will include six direct entries and two wild cards.

The format will be best-of-three-set matches with sets to four games, tiebreakers at 4-all and a 10-point match tie-break instead of a third set, through the semifinals. The final will be standard scoring with sets to six games and a tiebreaker at 6-all, and a 10-point match tiebreaker if necessary.

AP

World.title: 'A gorgeous human' gets her solo moment and still shares it with her mates
World.content:
There aren't many legacies in sport as dominant as Australia in the women's 4x100m freestyle relay.

The first night of the Glasgow program marked the team's 19th victory in the past 21 major international finals across the Olympics, long-course world championships, Pan Pacs and Commonwealth Games.

It also marked the sixth time Meg Harris had stood on the top step of the podium with her teammates in those events, bridging the gap from the Campbells era to these Commonwealth Games and onwards towards Brisbane 2032.

But on Tuesday morning (AEST), when Mollie O'Callaghan and Shayna Jack joined her up there, they did so with her blessing, of course, after she became the solo 100m champion for the first time.

Meg Harris (centre) pipped superstars Shayna Jack (left) and Mollie O'Callaghan to the wall. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"It's pretty incredible, I've never done that before. I've never been in that position," Harris said.

"Hopefully this is just the start of my journey. I'm pretty happy with that. These girls are absolutely incredible, so any chance I get to stand on the podium with them is great."

The trials in June marked the first time she had made the team as an individual 100m swimmer.

Glasgow 2026 day four live Australia wins nine gold medals across the pool, athletics track and in the gymnastics on day four in Glasgow.

The 24-year-old admitted to struggling with motivation in the 100m after the Paris Olympics, rediscovering her love for the sport through her pet 50m event, where she won the world title in Singapore last year.

"I've always loved the [100m] race," she said.

"The 50m was something I've always loved and always known I've enjoyed racing that … but the 100m is always the one I've been working towards in the long run. I guess I need to take a step back and enjoy it for a while."

Harris's win was one of seven gold medals on the night for Australia, with Alex Perkins in the 100m butterfly and Jenna Forrester in the 400m individual medley also enjoying a breakout meet.

Jenna Forrester has enjoyed a breakout Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Forrester's victory added to her surprise 200m backstroke victory three nights earlier.

"We all really get around each other, and that's what makes Team Australia really special and successful," Perkins said.

Little did she know how true that was.

Minutes earlier, Harris had made an immediate pivot from star performer to cheer captain, stepping away from her media obligations to cheer Perkins on with every stroke as she powered to victory.

"She's amazing; all those girls are in the 100m freestyle," Perkins said.

"[They're] so successful in that event and [Harris is] just also a gorgeous human. I was really proud; it was really inspiring to watch her before my event."

100m butterfly gold medallist Alex Perkins is a big fan of Meg Harris. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Perkins and Harris are kindred spirits, two swimmers winning their favourite events for the first time after years of toil while in their mid-20s (Perkins celebrating gold on her 26th birthday).

Along with Forrester, Sam Short, Lani Pallister and a slew of other gold medallists on the night and at these Games, it's all part of a moment of transition for the Dolphins in Glasgow.

It's not so much a passing of the baton as simply getting more hands on it.

"We've got a home [Olympic] Games in 2032, we're all trying to do our best and make the most of every moment," Perkins said.

And Harris is a key part of that.

The 4x100m freestyle squad featured eight swimmers in Glasgow: Brittany Castelluzzo (25), Inez Miller (19), Jessica Cole (19) and Hannah Casey (20) in their heat; and Harris, Perkins, Jack and O'Callaghan in the final.

The jewel in Australian swimming's crown is central to the rejuvenation that never really stops for this all-conquering team.

In among the Dolphins, they call themselves "the starfish", according to the retiring Jack.

Swimming is perhaps the loneliest of all elite sport pursuits, so finding that connection is crucial to, if you'll pardon the pun, keeping your head above water.

"Meg's my roommate here, which I'm really grateful for because we do have a lot of events together and being able to share in those moments with her is extremely special to me," Jack said.

"Swimming is such an event that can be quite isolating. That's also why I love the relays because you get to share in those special moments with somebody else, and being able to go 1-2-3 tonight, it's just another moment I get to share with these amazing girls."

World.title: How this 'old couple' is shooting for gold at Glasgow
World.content:
In sport, trust between teammates is imperative, but it's hard to imagine a scenario where it's more important than the world of paracycling.

Born with albinism and affected by vision loss associated with the condition, legally blind cyclist Kane Perris rides in tandem with his pilot, Luke Zaccaria.

Now the pair is among the favourites in the men's "tandem b", for vision-impaired cyclists, at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

The trust between them took some time to develop.

"Giving up my control and going against what human nature and the brain says to do, which is … you're riding a bike that I don't have control over steering … on a bunch of wooden planks that are at 44 degrees," Perris said.

Luke Zaccaria and Kane Perris can hit blistering speeds on the track. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"To me, it did take a long time to build that trust in the sport and build that trust in Luke."

The right stuff

Zaccaria discovered Perris on a talent search day, and was immediately struck by his mental strength.

"There were definitely some qualities that really stuck out to me," Zaccaria said.

"We ran the testing, Kane walked in and [impressed with] his attitude and his mindset, which for me is a big thing, it kind of sets people apart.

" But that's something that's not really trainable, that's an inherent quality within him and that really stood out. "

Now they describe their relationship as similar to an old married couple.

Perris and Zaccaria say their relationship resembles that of an "old couple" much of the time. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"We're constantly bickering in the training environment but Luke and I have, like, forged our strength through trust in the relationship we've built over the last six years in riding together," Perris said.

"We have this clear expectation that we're both doing the work.

"Ultimately, it's that trust that makes us go fast."

Speed bumps

Perris is not exaggerating: on a good day, the duo can hit 75 kilometres per hour.

But sometimes the consequences can be disastrous.

It took Perris some time to recover after a harrowing crash at the paracycling world championships in Rio in 2024. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

The pair crashed out on the opening day of the paracycling world championships in 2024, and Kane was left with a fractured shoulder, three broken ribs and a punctured lung.

But they licked their wounds and finished fourth in the 1 kilometre time trial at the Paris Paralympics later that year.

Kane says he was at a low ebb mentally when he came to cycling in 2020, in need of a new challenge.

"I really needed something in life that could be the vessel for growth and I never knew that it would be riding bikes in circles at 75km/h but this guy came along and the opportunity came up and I've never looked back.

" What a vessel it's been for my growth as a person, and an athlete. "

Kane Perris and LUke Zaccaria kept the bickering to a minimum during this training session. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

Six years after their fateful meeting, Perris and Zaccaria head to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow to compete in the 1km time trial and sprints, with gold firmly on their mind.

Young star rising

Liliya Tatarinoff has just turned 20, but is already attracting attention for her performances on the track.

She only relocated to Perth a year ago from the New South Wales Central Coast, leaving her family behind to pursue her sporting dreams by training at the WA Institute of Sport under cycling guru Shane Perkins.

"It's been a tough transition, but definitely a worthwhile one," she said.

Liliya Tatarinoff has had her heart set on the Commonwealth Games for years. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"I've had a huge improvement since moving here."

Tatarinoff is a reserve in the team sprint in Glasgow, and will compete in the sprints, keirin and 1 kilometre time trial.

Tatarinoff competed in the world championships last year, her first elite international competition, and said the Commonwealth Games was the "next step".

Tatarinoff is focused on improvement in Glasgow. (ABC News: Ruby Stammers)

"Being selected for the Comm Games is just a huge achievement for me, it's always been a dream of mine ever since I was a little girl," she said.

World.title: Cabo Verde stunner gets people's vote as best World Cup goal
World.content:
Cape Verde has made more World Cup history with Sidny Lopes Cabral winning the public vote for goal of the tournament.

Lopes Cabral's curling shot into the far top corner of the Argentina net was a stand-out moment at the World Cup where the unheralded African team made a stellar debut.

His goal tied defending champion Argentina at 2-2 in extra time of their thrilling Round of 32 game in Miami Gardens. Cape Verde would eventually lose 3-2.

Lopes Cabral's goal was voted best of the 308 goals scored at the tournament, ahead of Eldor Shomurodov's delicate lob for Uzbekistan against DR Congo and Wilson Isidor of Haiti scoring with a powerful rising shot against Morocco.

FIFA drew up a shortlist of 12 goals for public voting that closed Monday.

Sidny Lopes Cabral headed for the stands to celebrate with fans and family after scoring a screamer for Cabo Verde against Argentina. (Getty Images: ISI Photos/Eston Parker)

Lopes Cabral's celebration also entered World Cup lore as he broke free of teammates reaching to grab him before climbing into the tribune to hug his girlfriend and look for his mother.

"Before the game, I'd told my mom and my girlfriend that if I scored, I'd run over to them," he said.

"When I got there, I saw my mom crying. She hadn't even realised I was right there. Everyone was busy tending to her because she had fainted when I scored."

Cape Verde defied both World Cup finalists in its four games, after goalkeeper Vozinha's stand-out display saw his team open with a 0-0 draw to stun eventual champion Spain.

AP

World.title: Aussie Rohan Browning clips 'unfair' 100m surprise sprung on sprinters
World.content:
Just a day or two before the start of the athletics program at the Commonwealth Games, the public was made aware that the top eight 100 metre sprinters in the rankings would be given a free ticket into the semifinals in a break from tradition.

It left the rest of the field, including Australians Rohan Browning and Eddie Nketia, to duke it out in a mass time trial across 11 heats.

It was a significant change to the usual system where everybody runs the heats and the top two in each race are automatic qualifiers, with the remaining runners trying to get through on times.

Both Australians finished second in their heats, but Browning could not enjoy the moment after going through in 10.24 seconds in heat seven with four more to come.

Browning said the new rules were as much of a surprise to him as they were for the rest of us.

Glasgow 2026 day four live Australia wins nine gold medals across the pool, athletics track and in the gymnastics on day four in Glasgow.

"It's an unheard of progression, it's extremely weird. It's really hard to know, I have no idea what times have been run, I have no idea where I sit in the placings," he said, asking reporters to clue him in on where he sat in the standings.

"It's gusty out there, so when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of us goes through on a time trial rather than first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will have better conditions than others, so I don't know what's going on."

Browning made the cut in 16th as the second slowest qualifier and compatriot Eddie Nketia was fourth fastest overall with his 10.07

Browning, who was a controversial inclusion in the team ahead of Josh Azzopardi, said he always turns up prepared to run three rounds but the other folks, including countryman Lachie Kennedy, do not have to.

Eddie Nketia looked powerful as he finished second in his heat. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"It's not fair, clearly it's not fair," he said.

"It's clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever's motivated that decision, I don't know what it is or if it's reasonable or not, but clearly it's not fair. I think everyone would agree on that."

Nketia said it was out of his control so he was not going to worry too much about it, and Browning acknowledged the best response is probably to just run fast.

Aussie sprinter feels 'robbed' Josh Azzopardi opens up after missing out on selection as a 100 metres runner in Australia's athletics team for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

"At the end of the day this sport is meritocracy at its finest; if you're quick enough you go through, so I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place," he said.

"In all likelihood they were probably the guys paying the best odds to make the final regardless, but you just don't know. Some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. I don't even know when they took the performances from."

National record holder Torrie Lewis is experiencing both sides of the coin in the women's events, running the heats in the 100m but granted the automatic progression in the 200m.

"Having a day off in the middle is perfect, so I'm really happy with that," he said after winning her heat in 11.15 seconds to finish as the second-fastest qualifier.

"It would've been better if it was first [past the post], just to eliminate the wind because it's so gusty going around, but what can you do? Just be the fastest no matter what."

World.title: Dolphins dominate once more as McDonald, Hardy get in on gymnastics medals
World.content:
Mollie O'Callaghan has been sensationally dethroned as Commonwealth Games 100m freestyle champion by Meg Harris as Australia's tsunami of swimming medals continued in Glasgow.

Harris's shock triumph came after Jenna Forrester extended her brilliant meet with a second gold medal, adding the 400m individual medley title to her 200m backstroke crown.

O'Callaghan had been expected to again battle through the pain barrier to defend her crown but instead had to settle for the silver in another Australian 1-2-3, as Shayna Jack, in her final competition, grabbed the bronze.

Meg Harris (left), Shayna Jack and Mollie O'Callaghan swept the podium in the Women's 100m freestyle. (Getty Images: Andrew Milligan/PA Images)

But this time, it was Albury's Harris, the 24-year-old double Olympic relay champion, who had the measure of the five-time Olympic winner, leading her at the halfway mark, with O'Callaghan turning in third.

The Queensland star could not peg back the lead as Harris touched the wall in 52.90 seconds to O'Callaghan's 53.25 and Jack's 53.38.

"Very happy. Look, I wasn't meant to be here," O'Callaghan told reporters.

" So, to be on the podium with these two amazing ladies; Meg absolute killed it tonight, so did Shayna. Like, honestly, I'm just so happy. "

Alex Perkins marked her 26th birthday with a perfect present as she lifted the 100m butterfly crown, her second triumph in three days after years of near-misses at major individual international events.

Perkins continues to enjoy the most extraordinary meet, winning her fourth gold in as many nights, and on a landmark day.

The 50m fly champion was in a different class from her chasers, stopping the clock at 56.38, with Scotland's Keanna MacInnes second, almost a second behind.

Sam Williamson had to learn to walk again after an injury a year ago. He's leaving Glasgow with two gold medals. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

Sam Williamson, already champion in the 100m, again upset the odds to produce a thunderous late burst to get up for gold in the 50m breaststroke dash.

Williamson's charge for the wall in the one-lap breaststroke was one of the highlights of the meet as he powered through the second half of the race to prevail in 26.50, 0.27sec clear of South African Michael Houlie and 0.44 ahead of English Olympic great Adam Ramsay-Peaty.

Para swimmer Beau Matthews added another gold in the 100m breaststroke SB9 final, while Sam Short powered home to win the 800m freestyle final.

Matthews, seen as a future para star, came of age, clocking 1:09.41 to better Tim Hodge, Australia's baton bearer at the opening ceremony.

Hodge, who had won the 100m backstroke S9 the night before, had to settle for bronze behind New Zealander Joshua Willmer.

'Don't be poo': McDonald quells doubts with gold

Kate McDonald had a rather novel strategy to follow to claim gold in the uneven bars. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Fighting off the voices in her head that tell her "don't be poo", Kate McDonald won Australia's second gymnastics gold medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

It was sweet redemption for McDonald, who banished haunting memories of her "pretty poo" finish at the 2022 Birmingham Games with a near-flawless performance at Glasgow International Stadium, scoring 14.333 points.

So dominant was the 25-year-old that she was the only gymnast to hit the 14.000-point mark and blitzed next-best, Canadian great Ellie Black, by 0.433 points, with Wales's Emily Roper following for bronze.

"I'm over the moon," McDonald said.

"I bombed in that (2022) final, and that's obviously in the back of my head.

" I did want this medal really badly. "

Wearing her headphones during warm-up, McDonald said cycling through her competition playlist — from AC/DC to Dom Dolla — helped her fight off memories of the 2022 final.

Whether a coincidence or a good omen in her 2028 Los Angeles qualifying campaign, her final song before competing was a remix of California Dreamin'.

"Putting music in helps ground me, and that helps the voice in my head stay nice," McDonald said.

"''Don't be poo, don't fall. Be perfect, it's not going to be perfect.' There's a lot of background noise.

"I'm just going to again try and learn from this experience and bring it into LA; hopefully, we qualify a team for LA, hopefully I'm on that team for LA."

James Hardy competes in the Men's Rings. (Getty: Lintao Zhang)

As McDonald led the charge in the women's field, James Hardy claimed bronze on the rings and the floor routine exercise.

Just as the team bronze was Australia's first since the 2010 Delhi Games, Hardy's two individual bronze medals ended the nation's 16-year drought on the apparatuses in the men's field.

The 23-year-old competed with a pink ribbon painted on the nail of his right hand ring finger in tribute to his mum, Sally, who has breast cancer.

She is in remission after undergoing surgery, but she and the Hardy family were unable to travel to Glasgow.

"It's been in the back of my mind, but obviously nice to know that she's just doing really well," Hardy said.

"Spoken to mum and dad before, they're absolutely, you know, just so, so, so proud.

"It's very emotional. They would have loved to be here."

Catch up on all the action from day four of the games in our blog below.
